public_statements.boeing:
A few years ago we said we had three jobs to do before anything else: stabilize the factories, finish the airplanes we'd started, and repair the balance sheet. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and 10 are delivering, and our net debt is back where it was before the hard years. I'm proud of this team for that. We still work on safety and quality every day, and that doesn't stop.

People ask me whether now is the time for the next airplane. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're ready on our end. The other two aren't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane to win a news cycle. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it, and not before.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month. The line is stable and the data is good, and the demand in front of us doesn't need another step right now. I'd much rather run a steady line than chase a number. On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep investing in it and in Charleston.

Going slow is what let us go fast. It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, with entry into service planned in the second half of the 2030s. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s: on the clock of technology maturity, with a disciplined and controlled ramp-up. To serve our customers through the transition, we will keep the A320 family in production for longer on our proven lines while the new aircraft ramps up. We have invited CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power the new aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp. We will fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. The LEAP is flying on every 737 MAX and on the A320neo, and our job today is to deliver those engines on time and support that fleet. We'll keep at it with our suppliers, and with our partners at Safran.

Here's what we don't know: when the airframers will launch their next single-aisle, and what they'll want under the wing. That's really not for us to say. We don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM will offer our engines to both airframers, and we will commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer.

RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran. The airframers will set the date for that architecture.

On the widebody, we're investing in a GEnx upgrade so the 787 fleet stays competitive for our customers.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Control what you can control. The last few years on the GTF fleet were hard on our customers, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine.

Here is our commitment. In any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney for a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside a partner, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan that same round. It is planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036 for a commitment made this year. Its durability will be proven before it enters service. That means time on wing ahead of fuel burn in the specification, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet, also at standard terms. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us, where seven years of development fit before its entry into service. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't compress maturity for anyone. Partnership is our preference, not our need: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit the round they do. UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 MAX at 57 a month under the KPI gates; request no further rate step
boeing.detail: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line. The KPIs are stable (no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem). The demand in front of us does not call for another step: 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34. Rates stay agreed with the FAA and gated on data [BX-1259, B-2351].

boeing.move: Keep growing 787 capacity at Charleston
boeing.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787, the most efficient airplane in its segment [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board does not price this.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for the transition
airbus.detail: Long-term agreements for A320neo engine slots with CFM and P&W to cover the longer A320 tail, and NGSA engines from CFM, the only maker certain to be ready. Titanium and rare-earth supply secured for the combined A320/NGSA peak in the mid-2040s, the follow-on to the 2025 de-risking [AX-0062, AX-0063]. These are for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

airbus.move: Engineering recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: Normal hiring and internal redeployment to staff NGSA development, sized so the A320 sustaining teams and the A350F are not stripped [A-0366, A-0485]. This is not targeted at any competitor's programme and is not a Delay Tactics move.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: Continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

cfm.move: LEAP derivative offered to both airframers for any new narrowbody
cfm.detail: CFM offers its engines to both airframers on any new single-aisle they launch, and will commit a new engine with a committed airframer (H1: no airframer refused or locked out). No price, no terms, no dates. Any pricing goes to Safran first [CX-0184]. Unpriced on the board.

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
cfm.detail: Funded as technology, not cancelled for cost (H5). No product launch, no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public (Ali's advice; H6). The product decision returns to the CFM partners in 2035. Unpriced.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section durability kit across the in-service A320neo GTF fleet. It is sold at standard terms with pass-through pricing: no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We report progress as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration, not as a dated AOG recovery (Eddy's advice; my own dated recoveries have slipped) [PX-0098][PX-0104]. It changes no payoff on the board.

rolls_royce.move: Public invitation to Pratt & Whitney on the Joint Venture
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce invites P&W to commit to a narrowbody Joint Venture. Rolls-Royce commits in the round P&W's commitment is on the public record, on terms that credit the technology each side brings [RX-0118, RX-0072]. No Rolls-Royce commitment is made this round. Gating is partner first, and the Board vetoes a first commit.

rolls_royce.move: Commercial discipline: standard terms through the Investment Committee
rolls_royce.detail: No price concessions to buy share. Any airframer or airline campaign is priced 'win-win' with value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan technology and Trent durability continue inside existing R&D
rolls_royce.detail: The UltraFan demonstrator programme and its technology keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing. In-service Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine durability work continues inside the existing durability budget. This is not the board's $2B t1000_upgrade order and makes no grid adjustment [RX-0123, RX-0094].

boeing.move: Prepare the 2035 fps case; do not announce it
boeing.detail: 10-year ramp, which beats the 7-year by $2.65-3.63B in every column. The Renton site is on the table (+0.36 to +0.69 in every column, about $3.0B of capex avoided), alongside Pope's plan for the MAX wind-down: the waiting backlog grows to 792 by 2047 in Do Nothing, so Renton winds down only as fps capacity comes on. The engine code is set at launch. My lean is to keep CFM named (Code 3, an inference), and I will test Codes 5 and 6 against what P&W and Rolls-Royce would need to see to have a second source ready by EIS. Development contracts carry risk-share or cost-plus terms, not fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304]. No date before launch [B-2315].

boeing.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine ready in reserve
boeing.detail: A low-cost study with GE on a GEnx-derivative route that meets a 5-year EIS; engine durability first [BX-1298]. Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB arrives a year late on a 2030 launch. It comes back to the Board in 2035, with both outcomes shown, if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half). Pairing with a 2035 10-year fps gives 2 years of overlap (H4-legal, $1.2B strain undiscounted).

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot; run supplier and LEAP-1B readiness reviews
boeing.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Supplier readiness stays a hard gate on any future rate step or launch.

airbus.move: Consolidate the A320 tail on the fewest lines (Wagner's quality watch)
airbus.detail: Under the Alt plan the 14-a-month tail runs about four years while staff move to NGSA. Concentrate it on the fewest lines to keep skills and quality. Publish no A320 rate numbers for the 2040s.

airbus.move: Board paper fixes the phasing of the Alt plan's $0.75B
airbus.detail: Spend about $0.094B a year in 2037-44 as the longer A320 lines run, after NGSA development spend rolls off. Any pre-EIS commitment is capped at $0.10B in any 2030-36 year, inside the $0.126B headroom. Peak programme cash stays at $5.074B a year against the $5.2B line.

cfm.move: Private 2035 readiness work on a defensive Ducted
cfm.detail: A cross-functional team sets up the hot-and-harsh durability gate and test plan Ali asked for. The yardstick is the LEAP durability gap in harsh conditions. The aim is a launch-ready case if an airframer code puts CFM on a new narrowbody alongside a rival. No commitment, no date, no spend on the board. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208, CX-0012].

cfm.move: Private LEAP supply operating review
cfm.detail: Ali runs the review of the constrained suppliers (80% of shortages from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613, CX-0633]) while NB engine volumes rise from 2,131 in 2030 to 2,615 in 2037. OE engines come first and spares do not crowd them out. This is the gate Ali named for lifting his objection to a second project in 2035.

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet-first priority on pacing parts
pratt_whitney.detail: This is an internal rule and is not published. If GTF2 triggers, GTF fleet spares and MRO material rank ahead of GTF2 production installs on the pacing-parts list from the 2036 ramp onward. Development to 2036 draws engineers and test hardware, not production castings. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. Eddy's condition is adopted as written.

pratt_whitney.move: 2035 review gates written into the plan
pratt_whitney.detail: This is internal. If GTF2 has triggered, Eddy reports severe-environment endurance test data and maturity gates against the 2036 ready date before the 2035 round, and the bad number comes first. We do not compress testing to hold the date. On the Joint Venture, we revisit only if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). The gear and core technology are never on the table [P-1233].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan before EIS (condition of Watson's concurrence)
rolls_royce.detail: This sits in the package and becomes live only if launch_if_selected triggers. It sets up a partner-shop MRO network on the Singapore joint-venture model with repair technology invested in those shops, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team. All of it is built inside the seven development years and in place before any narrowbody EIS: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. It builds on the V2500 aftermarket base (inference). With a Joint Venture, P&W's network shares the load (inference) [RX-0283, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: Supplier and engineering capacity readiness (no spend unless triggered)
rolls_royce.detail: Contingency plan if selected. Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, and gearbox capacity is sized early. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work is ring-fenced while a narrowbody line ramps. The narrowbody runs to roughly 1,100-1,900 engines a year by 2050 if selected (Watson's approximation, not a board output). Money is redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not added [RX-0214, RX-0284, RX-0286].

boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold; fps_engine_code null; fps_site new_site (no effect with fps on hold).
- rate_737 hold; re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, company doctrine (profile §7's read of the A350 Re-engine odds) drove the call, not my record. My evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES (Board recommendation 2)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have lapsed:
  - the 777X entered service in 2027 [BX-0550];
  - the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873];
  - net debt reached $0.0B in 2029, and 2030 in the stress case (brief §2) [BX-1305, B-2327, B-2326].
  - The condition is met, not waived. An fps still has to win on the grid and pass Malave's buffer test, and this round none does.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and the 777X is done.
- H3, second half: confirmed. No 787 Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the public record. None is on it today.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine.
  - A 2030 Re-engine with a 2030 10-year fps overlaps 2 years (legal); with a 2030 7-year fps, 5 years (barred).
  - Nothing ordered here engages H4.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's KPI check passes and her veto is not invoked.
(2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
- Balance sheet: yes.
- Market: not for an fps. Under this demand case Airbus's unmet demand falls to us, so NGSA alone costs only $0.64B (S2), or $0.83B on the A320 Alt plan (S3).
- Technology: no. At a 2040 EIS every engine code gives CFM only.
- So we are not ready on all three [BX-1296].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? Malave ran S6 as the baseline (section 4).
(4) Is this doing less, better? I compared every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

3. THE TESTED CASE AGAINST DO NOTHING AND S6 (Board recommendation 1)
Each row reads S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6.
- Submitted, Do Nothing: 0.00 / -0.64 / -0.83 / -2.62 / -3.26 / -0.64. S6 equals Do Nothing's own S6.
- There are no Board items, so there are no default rows to show.
- Rejected rows, for the record:
  - B, 787 Re-engine: +3.30 / +2.67 / +2.47 / -5.10 / -5.74 / +2.67. Against Do Nothing: +3.30 / +3.31 / +3.30 / -2.48 / -2.48 / +3.31.
  - C, Rate Increase: -0.21 / -1.20 / -1.66 / -2.83 / -3.83 / -1.20. Against Do Nothing: -0.21 / -0.56 / -0.83 / -0.21 / -0.57 / -0.56.
  - D, best fps (10-year at Renton + Re-engine): -2.19 / -3.24 / -3.90 / -10.59 / -11.64 / -3.26.
  - E, 10-year at Renton: -4.39 / -5.44 / -6.09 / -7.01 / -8.06 / -5.45.
  - F, 7-year at Renton: -7.91 / -8.18 / -8.76 / -10.53 / -10.80 / -8.18.
  - G, best via Embraer row: -21.08 / -22.13 / -22.79 / -29.48 / -30.53 / -22.15.
- Expected column: S2 and S5 at even odds.
  - Do Nothing scores -1.95 on that blend, and the Re-engine -1.535 (+0.41, inside ε).
  - On S2 alone the Re-engine is best (+2.67).

4. MALAVE'S MEMO: binding on the fps, advice on the rest
Buffer test (limit: S6 no lower than -2.64):
- Do Nothing passes at -0.64, $2.00B clear of the limit.
- The Re-engine passes at +2.67, $5.31B clear.
- The Rate Increase passes at -1.20.
- All 24 fps rows fail:
  - D at -3.26, short by $0.62B;
  - E at -5.45, short by $2.81B;
  - F at -8.18, short by $5.54B;
  - G at -22.15, short by $19.51B.
- His veto on any fps launch binds under the team rule. I accept it in full.
"Fundable when the 777X turns":
- 10-year fps: pass. Stress-case net debt is held at $0.0B in all 8 rows.
- 7-year fps: fail. Stress peak $0.7B, $2.8B with the Re-engine, $3.1B in S4/S5. Only the 7-year at Renton without the Re-engine holds.
- Via Embraer: fail. Stress peak $1.0-6.3B.
- Re-engine alone and Rate Increase: pass at $0.0B.
Undiscounted debt penalties, for scale only (the grid already nets them): 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B.

5. POPE'S SEAT
- No live problem, so the KPI veto cannot bind.
- The Rate Increase fails capacity-follows-demand.
- The Re-engine passes every operations test:
  - zero overlap;
  - about $1B a year, 7% of base free cash flow;
  - a GEnx derivative meets 2035; Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB arrives in 2036, a year late;
  - Charleston can absorb the volume.
- Her hold on the Re-engine is deference, not a finding.
- She backs the 10-year ramp, and finds that Embraer adds nothing Boeing lacks [BX-1330].

6. THE 787 RE-ENGINE, THE ONE LIVE DECISION
Its value hangs on a sealed Airbus move I cannot see.
- Gain against hold: 3.31 - 5.79p, where p is the odds of an A350 Re-engine this round.
  - Break-even is 57%.
  - The gain falls inside ε at 40% or more.
  - Holding breaks the $2B H8 cap only below 23%.
- Doctrine §7 (an inference; my own record is Low here) expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt: Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446].
- At even odds the gain is +0.41, a tie. Doing less [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the higher worst column (-3.26 against -5.74) all break it toward hold.
- The call is robust: at one-in-three odds, holding gives up about $1.38B, still inside the cap. I have no evidence to put the odds under 23%.
- The upside is fragile. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and a 2035 A350 Re-engine would stop our gains at 2040 and cut the margin (Malave).
- It fails the Board's -$1B downside limit in S4 and S5 (-2.48), and the Board named hold as the acceptable alternative. A launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
- Doctrine's "Chicken game" inference: sealed same-round orders give no first mover. A same-round match is the -2.48 outcome. Holding keeps the option to stand aside under H3.
- Cost of waiting, which I accept:
  - a 2035 launch is worth about 0.61 times as much;
  - it would overlap a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain undiscounted, H4-legal);
  - it rules out pairing with a 2035 7-year fps.

7. RATE INCREASE
- KPIs pass, but the business case fails in every column: -0.21 to -0.83.
- 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34.
- This is the only round it is offered. Letting it lapse gains $0.56B in S2.
- Not decided with reference to Airbus (H6).

8. fps
- Malave's veto binds, and every row sits below Do Nothing in every column.
- An objective premium of at least $4.39B would exceed the $2B cap.
- I prepare the 2035 case (10-year ramp, Renton, engine code) and announce no date [B-2315, B-2313].

9. PREMIUM LOG
- Doctrine premium: $0.41B (Re-engine hold, even odds).
- Objective premium: $0.
- Total: $0.41B, within the $2B cap.
- It breaks if the odds of an A350 Re-engine fall below 23%.

10. RED LINES
- None is breached:
  - no rate request without stable KPIs;
  - no concurrency of production and certification;
  - no cancel;
  - no fixed-price development;
  - no blame on the FAA;
  - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus.
- The overrides list is empty.

memo_weighing.cfo:
I gave this memo full weight, and it binds on the fps. Malave is my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. His figures match the brief cell for cell.
- Buffer test: all 24 fps rows fail; the closest, D, misses by $0.62B. His veto binds under the team rule, I accept it, and I have no override.
- "Fundable when the 777X turns": the 10-year ramp passes; the 7-year and via Embraer fail; the Re-engine and the Rate Increase pass.
- His hold on the Re-engine (+0.41 at even odds, a $0.41B premium, with break points at 40%, 23% and 57%) is advice, not a veto. I adopted it because it matches my doctrine read and the Board's downside rule.
- I took his deferral arithmetic (x0.607) and his point that the grid assumes nobody moves after this round.
- Thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and his even odds of an A350 Re-engine come from doctrine §7, not his record. I weighed his view beyond the buffer test as advice.
memo_weighing.ops:
I gave this memo full weight on KPIs, strain and readiness, which is the doctrine it is built on.
- No live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so her KPI veto does not bind.
- The Rate Increase fails on demand, not on KPIs: 66, 42 and 20 idle slots in 2032-34.
- The Re-engine passes every operations test: zero overlap, about $1B a year, a GEnx derivative ready for 2035 (UltraFan WB arrives in 2036, a year late), and room at Charleston. Her hold is deference to me, not a finding.
- She backs the 10-year ramp for 2035, and finds that Embraer adds nothing Boeing lacks.
- I took her caution on Renton: wind the MAX down only as fps capacity comes on, because the Do Nothing backlog reaches 792 by 2047.
- Thin seat: her record is Global Services (Very low on airplanes), and the gates are [NOW] doctrine. I used her numbers and weighed her judgement on the A350 as none.

boeing.expected_scenario: S2 and S5 at even odds. Airbus launches NGSA, and the odds are about even that it also launches the A350 Re-engine in the same round. Those odds come from doctrine §7, an inference: Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446]. My own record is Low on Airbus. I read S6, the risk case, as Malave's slip-leg baseline; for Do Nothing it equals S2 (-0.64). Do Nothing scores -1.95 on the blend.
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: On the S2/S5 even-odds blend, the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, at -1.535 against Do Nothing's -1.95. That is +0.41, inside ε, so it is a tie, and Do Nothing wins it on doing less [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the higher worst column (-3.26 against -5.74). FOR THE 787 RE-ENGINE:

cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.64 in S6, so the limit is -2.64. Every fps row fails. The closest, the 10-year at Renton with the 787 Re-engine, sits at -3.26, short by $0.62B. The 10-year at Renton alone misses by $2.81B and via Embraer by $19.51B or more. Under the team rule that is a binding veto on any fps launch this round. The 10-year ramp does pass "Fundable when the 777X turns", with stress net debt at $0.0B. The 7-year at a new site or with the Re-engine fails it ($0.7-3.1B), and so does Embraer ($1.0-6.3B).

The Rate Increase passes the buffer but loses $0.21-0.83B in every column. I would not fund it.

The 787 Re-engine passes the buffer by $5.31B and holds net debt at zero in stress, at about $1B a year. My concern is its worst column, -5.74 in S5: $2.48B below Do Nothing's worst, more than my own buffer. Doctrine, not my record, puts an A350 Re-engine at roughly even odds. On that read the Re-engine is worth +0.41, a tie, and the higher-confidence plan wins it. I advise holding, which is not a veto, and logging a $0.41B premium.

That holds barring a firm sign that Airbus leaves the A350 alone. Below 40% odds I would take the Re-engine to the Board; below 23%, holding breaks the $2B cap.

It is a baseline we can meet and potentially beat. We're bullish on our outlook.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: 787 Re-engine (EIS 2035) [record, applied by inference; slip prior is doctrine]
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read the risk-case column (S6) and the doctrine slip prior, and say how much of the value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers: S6 +2.67 = S2 +2.67: the risk case (NGSA + Delay Tactics) acts only from fps EIS, so it does not touch the Re-engine. The board prices no Re-engine slip. The doctrine prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). Shifting the whole item at 10.5% WACC leaves S1 at about +2.70 for a 2-year slip (x0.819) and +2.21 for a 4-year slip (x0.671) (inference). So it stays positive in S1-S3 and S6. Engine route: a GEnx derivative is the one that meets 2035 (doctrine, §6). Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 = 2036, a year late (rules.md). Customers name engine durability as their concern [BX-1298].

tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read S6 against the nominal column.

The value is negative before any slip: Solo rows run -3.26 to -8.56 in S6. The doctrine slip prior for a clean sheet is +3 years central (range +2 to +5) and the board does not price it (787-8 and 777X record). No new narrowbody engine is on the record: every code gives CFM only at a 2040 EIS. I cannot certify a 2040 or 2037 EIS today.

tests.name: Two-front strain: 787 Re-engine 2030, alone or with a 10-year fps [doctrine; board arithmetic]

tests.numbers: Re-engine 2030-35 alone: 0 years, $0. With a 2030 10-year fps (window 2033-40): 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, H4-legal. With a 2035 10-year fps (window 2038-45): 0 years, $0, and still only 1 year ($0.6B) if the Re-engine slips 4 years. A Re-engine deferred to 2035 (2035-40) overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B). The 777X (in service 2027) and the MAX 7/10 (certified 2026) are done, so the Re-engine would be the one major development in work [B-0341]. It also lands on the backside of the last programme, as the doctrine says new programmes should [B-1393].

tests.threshold: Overlap at most 2 years (H4).

It gives no strain relief: the Re-engine is worth +1.36 with it and +2.19 with the Solo 10-year (S1). Stress-case net debt peaks at $1.5-6.3B. The partner takes value and adds nothing Boeing lacks. Solo passes.

The brief does not show KPI history at each step up to 57, or supplier and CFM readiness for about 200 more LEAP-1B engines a year [B-2308, BX-1264]. Passing the gate is not a case for the step; see the demand test.

tests.threshold: Add capacity only where demand is visible and the step adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column (S2).

ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes: the KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. Nothing is live. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so my KPI veto does not bind. The Rate Increase fails on demand, not on KPIs: at 57 a month we already leave 66, 42 and 20 slots idle in 2032-34, and the step loses $0.21-0.83B in every column. Hold it.

Second, engineering capacity: one development at a time [B-0341]. The 787 Re-engine passes every operations test. It has no overlap, costs about $1B a year (7% of base free cash flow), and net debt holds in stress. 2030 is its cleanest window: it finishes before a 2035 10-year fps opens its strain window in 2038. Deferred to 2035, it adds 2 years of overlap to that fps ($1.2B of strain) and rules out a 7-year one. Launching turns on the A350, where I have no record. I defer to Kelly and the Board. We see about $0.58B of expected value for every 10 points of A350 odds; break-even is 57%.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. No fps passes today. The 10-year ramp beats the 7-year by $2.65-3.63B in every column; a same-round 7-year fps plus the Re-engine overlaps 5 years (H4). Embraer trails Solo by $18B and adds no IP or capacity we lack [BX-1330]. Prepare the 2035 case on the 10-year ramp.

The demand in front of us does not call for another step: 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34. Rates stay agreed with the FAA and gated on data [BX-1259, B-2351].

The Renton site is on the table (+0.36 to +0.69 in every column, about $3.0B of capex avoided), alongside Pope's plan for the MAX wind-down: the waiting backlog grows to 792 by 2047 in Do Nothing, so Renton winds down only as fps capacity comes on. The engine code is set at launch. My lean is to keep CFM named (Code 3, an inference), and I will test Codes 5 and 6 against what P&W and Rolls-Royce would need to see to have a second source ready by EIS. Development contracts carry risk-share or cost-plus terms, not fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304]. No date before launch [B-2315].

decision.public_statement:
A few years ago we said we had three jobs to do before anything else: stabilize the factories, finish the airplanes we'd started, and repair the balance sheet. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and 10 are delivering, and our net debt is back where it was before the hard years. I'm proud of this team for that. We still work on safety and quality every day, and that doesn't stop.

People ask me whether now is the time for the next airplane. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're ready on our end. The other two aren't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane to win a news cycle. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it, and not before.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month. The line is stable and the data is good, and the demand in front of us doesn't need another step right now. I'd much rather run a steady line than chase a number. On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep investing in it and in Charleston.

Going slow is what let us go fast. It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold; fps_engine_code null; fps_site new_site (no effect with fps on hold).
- rate_737 hold; re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, company doctrine (profile §7's read of the A350 Re-engine odds) drove the call, not my record. My evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES (Board recommendation 2)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have lapsed:
  - the 777X entered service in 2027 [BX-0550];
  - the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873];
  - net debt reached $0.0B in 2029, and 2030 in the stress case (brief §2) [BX-1305, B-2327, B-2326].
  - The condition is met, not waived. An fps still has to win on the grid and pass Malave's buffer test, and this round none does.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and the 777X is done.
- H3, second half: confirmed. No 787 Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the public record. None is on it today.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine.
  - A 2030 Re-engine with a 2030 10-year fps overlaps 2 years (legal); with a 2030 7-year fps, 5 years (barred).
  - Nothing ordered here engages H4.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's KPI check passes and her veto is not invoked.
(2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
- Balance sheet: yes.
- Market: not for an fps. Under this demand case Airbus's unmet demand falls to us, so NGSA alone costs only $0.64B (S2), or $0.83B on the A320 Alt plan (S3).
- Technology: no. At a 2040 EIS every engine code gives CFM only.
- So we are not ready on all three [BX-1296].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? Malave ran S6 as the baseline (section 4).
(4) Is this doing less, better? I compared every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

3. THE TESTED CASE AGAINST DO NOTHING AND S6 (Board recommendation 1)
Each row reads S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6.
- Submitted, Do Nothing: 0.00 / -0.64 / -0.83 / -2.62 / -3.26 / -0.64. S6 equals Do Nothing's own S6.
- There are no Board items, so there are no default rows to show.
- Rejected rows, for the record:
  - B, 787 Re-engine: +3.30 / +2.67 / +2.47 / -5.10 / -5.74 / +2.67. Against Do Nothing: +3.30 / +3.31 / +3.30 / -2.48 / -2.48 / +3.31.
  - C, Rate Increase: -0.21 / -1.20 / -1.66 / -2.83 / -3.83 / -1.20. Against Do Nothing: -0.21 / -0.56 / -0.83 / -0.21 / -0.57 / -0.56.
  - D, best fps (10-year at Renton + Re-engine): -2.19 / -3.24 / -3.90 / -10.59 / -11.64 / -3.26.
  - E, 10-year at Renton: -4.39 / -5.44 / -6.09 / -7.01 / -8.06 / -5.45.
  - F, 7-year at Renton: -7.91 / -8.18 / -8.76 / -10.53 / -10.80 / -8.18.
  - G, best via Embraer row: -21.08 / -22.13 / -22.79 / -29.48 / -30.53 / -22.15.
- Expected column: S2 and S5 at even odds.
  - Do Nothing scores -1.95 on that blend, and the Re-engine -1.535 (+0.41, inside ε).
  - On S2 alone the Re-engine is best (+2.67).

4. MALAVE'S MEMO: binding on the fps, advice on the rest
Buffer test (limit: S6 no lower than -2.64):
- Do Nothing passes at -0.64, $2.00B clear of the limit.
- The Re-engine passes at +2.67, $5.31B clear.
- The Rate Increase passes at -1.20.
- All 24 fps rows fail:
  - D at -3.26, short by $0.62B;
  - E at -5.45, short by $2.81B;
  - F at -8.18, short by $5.54B;
  - G at -22.15, short by $19.51B.
- His veto on any fps launch binds under the team rule. I accept it in full.
"Fundable when the 777X turns":
- 10-year fps: pass. Stress-case net debt is held at $0.0B in all 8 rows.
- 7-year fps: fail. Stress peak $0.7B, $2.8B with the Re-engine, $3.1B in S4/S5. Only the 7-year at Renton without the Re-engine holds.
- Via Embraer: fail. Stress peak $1.0-6.3B.
- Re-engine alone and Rate Increase: pass at $0.0B.
Undiscounted debt penalties, for scale only (the grid already nets them): 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B.

5. POPE'S SEAT
- No live problem, so the KPI veto cannot bind.
- The Rate Increase fails capacity-follows-demand.
- The Re-engine passes every operations test:
  - zero overlap;
  - about $1B a year, 7% of base free cash flow;
  - a GEnx derivative meets 2035; Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB arrives in 2036, a year late;
  - Charleston can absorb the volume.
- Her hold on the Re-engine is deference, not a finding.
- She backs the 10-year ramp, and finds that Embraer adds nothing Boeing lacks [BX-1330].

6. THE 787 RE-ENGINE, THE ONE LIVE DECISION
Its value hangs on a sealed Airbus move I cannot see.
- Gain against hold: 3.31 - 5.79p, where p is the odds of an A350 Re-engine this round.
  - Break-even is 57%.
  - The gain falls inside ε at 40% or more.
  - Holding breaks the $2B H8 cap only below 23%.
- Doctrine §7 (an inference; my own record is Low here) expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt: Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446].
- At even odds the gain is +0.41, a tie. Doing less [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the higher worst column (-3.26 against -5.74) all break it toward hold.
- The call is robust: at one-in-three odds, holding gives up about $1.38B, still inside the cap. I have no evidence to put the odds under 23%.
- The upside is fragile. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and a 2035 A350 Re-engine would stop our gains at 2040 and cut the margin (Malave).
- It fails the Board's -$1B downside limit in S4 and S5 (-2.48), and the Board named hold as the acceptable alternative. A launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
- Doctrine's "Chicken game" inference: sealed same-round orders give no first mover. A same-round match is the -2.48 outcome. Holding keeps the option to stand aside under H3.
- Cost of waiting, which I accept:
  - a 2035 launch is worth about 0.61 times as much;
  - it would overlap a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain undiscounted, H4-legal);
  - it rules out pairing with a 2035 7-year fps.

7. RATE INCREASE
- KPIs pass, but the business case fails in every column: -0.21 to -0.83.
- 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34.
- This is the only round it is offered. Letting it lapse gains $0.56B in S2.
- Not decided with reference to Airbus (H6).

8. fps
- Malave's veto binds, and every row sits below Do Nothing in every column.
- An objective premium of at least $4.39B would exceed the $2B cap.
- I prepare the 2035 case (10-year ramp, Renton, engine code) and announce no date [B-2315, B-2313].

9. PREMIUM LOG
- Doctrine premium: $0.41B (Re-engine hold, even odds).
- Objective premium: $0.
- Total: $0.41B, within the $2B cap.
- It breaks if the odds of an A350 Re-engine fall below 23%.

10. RED LINES
- None is breached:
  - no rate request without stable KPIs;
  - no concurrency of production and certification;
  - no cancel;
  - no fixed-price development;
  - no blame on the FAA;
  - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus.
- The overrides list is empty.

- "Fundable when the 777X turns": the 10-year ramp passes; the 7-year and via Embraer fail; the Re-engine and the Rate Increase pass.
- His hold on the Re-engine (+0.41 at even odds, a $0.41B premium, with break points at 40%, 23% and 57%) is advice, not a veto. I adopted it because it matches my doctrine read and the Board's downside rule.
- I took his deferral arithmetic (x0.607) and his point that the grid assumes nobody moves after this round.
- Thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and his even odds of an A350 Re-engine come from doctrine §7, not his record. I weighed his view beyond the buffer test as advice.

decision.premium_reason:
This is a doctrine premium of $0.41B for holding the 787 Re-engine.
- At even odds of an A350 Re-engine this round, the Re-engine's expected gain is 0.5 x 3.31 - 0.5 x 2.48 = +0.41. I give that up for doing less, the higher-confidence plan and the higher worst column.
- The objective premium is $0: no fps is launched for the 50/50 objective, because it would need at least $4.39B, above the cap.
- Holding the fps and the Rate Increase costs nothing; both gain against the alternatives.
- Total: $0.41B, within the $2B H8 cap.

decision.objective_note:

- Hold the 50/50 split: not met. 41.6% in 2040, 45.3% in 2045, 40.0% in 2050.
- Defend incumbency: met. Worst year 40.0%.
- Balance-sheet repair: met in base and stress (net debt $0.0B from 2029, 2030 in stress, held to 2050).

Only an fps can move the split and the engine sources. Every fps row loses at least $4.39B against Do Nothing and fails Malave's buffer test, so I take no objective premium. The objective never changes the payoff. I carry the engine-source goal into the 2035 fps preparation (Codes 5 and 6 tested against Code 3).

- Airbus is not part of the reasoning (H6). The 737 stays at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed gates.

board_response.recommendation: Prepare but do not announce the 2035 fps case: 10-year ramp, consider Renton, an engine code with a maker ready by EIS; no date before launch, conservative EIS.
board_response.response:
Taken up, as a non-public move.
- Ramp: 10-year, which beats the 7-year by $2.65-3.63B in every column.
- Site: Renton is under study (+0.36 to +0.69), with Pope's wind-down plan (Everett up to 15 a month) phased to the fps ramp, because the backlog grows to 792 by 2047.

board_response.recommendation: Log every premium; an fps launch would need at least $4.39B of objective premium, above the cap; surplus cash is reserved to the Board.
board_response.response:
Logged.
- Doctrine premium: $0.41B (Re-engine hold at even odds).
- Objective premium: $0 (no fps launched).
- Total: $0.41B, within $2B. It breaks below 23% odds of an A350 Re-engine.

cfo.red_line: None. No launch, no cancel (H5), no Re-engine near an A350 Re-engine (H3), no rate step under a live problem, no fixed-price development. The premium log is $0.41B, inside the $2B H8 cap.
cfo.note:
I concur.

THE BUFFER TEST, RE-RUN ON THE EXACT PLAN ORDERED
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold. fps_site new_site has no effect while the fps is on hold.
- That is the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold' in the brief's grid, which is Do Nothing.
- Risk-case column S6 (NGSA + Airbus Delay Tactics, covert): -0.64.
- The limit is Do Nothing's S6 less $2B, which is -2.64.
- Result: pass, $2.00B clear of the limit. Run as the baseline, not as a sensitivity [BX-0553].
- Net debt is held at $0.0B from 2029 in all six columns, in both base and stress.

MY ADVICE AND THE CEO'S USE OF IT
- My binding veto on every fps launch (all 24 rows fail S6; the closest, D, is at -3.26, short by $0.62B) is respected. No fps row is ordered.
- The CEO also took my two non-binding points:
  - He holds the 787 Re-engine as the higher-confidence plan. At even odds of an A350 Re-engine it is worth +0.41, a tie. Its worst column is -5.74, against -3.26 for Do Nothing. The hold is logged as a $0.41B doctrine premium.
  - He lets the Rate Increase lapse. Its item value is -0.21 to -0.83 in every column.

RED LINES
- None is breached:
  - nothing is launched or cancelled (H5);
  - no Re-engine is ordered (H3);
  - no rate step (KPIs stable, H6 not engaged);
  - no fixed-price development.
- Total premium is $0.41B, within the $2B cap (H8).
- The CEO's rulings lifting H1 and H3's first half change no order this round, so I have no finding on them here.

THE CONDITION THAT WOULD BREAK THIS
- If the odds of an A350 Re-engine fall below 23%, holding the Re-engine breaks the $2B cap.
- Below 40%, I would take the Re-engine to the Board as one tested case.
- The 2035 fps case comes back to my buffer test on that round's grid. My lean is the 10-year ramp at Renton, which keeps net debt at $0.0B in stress.

In my voice: this is a baseline we can meet and potentially beat. Do Nothing costs us nothing against the slip leg, and it keeps "fully restoring the health of our balance sheet" [BX-0556] intact. The reset to a higher-confidence plan is the right call [BX-0548]. We're bullish on our outlook. The Re-engine and the fps come back with full numbers in 2035.

ops.red_line: None. The orders are all hold: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold, and fps_site new_site, which has no effect with fps on hold. H4 is not engaged: there is no Re-engine and no fps, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0. H5 is not engaged because nothing is cancelled. H6 is not engaged: there is no Rate Increase, and the hold is reasoned on demand, not on Airbus. H1 and H3 are lifted on evidence, and they would not bind on an all-hold package in any case. The second half of H3 is confirmed.

board_review.note: No Board items: every order is the default.

Titanium and rare-earth supply secured for the combined A320/NGSA peak in the mid-2040s, the follow-on to the 2025 de-risking [AX-0062, AX-0063]. These are for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, with entry into service planned in the second half of the 2030s. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s: on the clock of technology maturity, with a disciplined and controlled ramp-up. To serve our customers through the transition, we will keep the A320 family in production for longer on our proven lines while the new aircraft ramps up. We have invited CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power the new aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp. We will fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
airbus.rationale:
ROUND 1 (2030). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Order of argument:
- Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- A disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409].
- What the Board can carry: one programme, inside a year's FCF, with no item losing more than $2B in any column [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine:
  - Rule 6: two launches in one round, with a 5-year overlap from 2030 to 2035.
  - Peak cash: $6.674B a year against $5.2B.
  - Its item value is -2.15 in S6 and S7. It is on the Board's would-veto list. This is the raw best in S1 to S5 (+15.83 in S1); it is a red-line deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Integrity pillar.
  - The Board vetoes bottleneck and both always, and poaching now.
  - One move is worth -15.74 in S1 and -15.75 in S6 against the lean.

2. SOFT VETOES ACCEPTED
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails Toepfer's robustness test and Wagner's A350F/Spirit absorption test. It trails the lean by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no override is possible. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash ($5.824B). Remedied by phasing it over 2037-44.

3. SURVIVORS
| Row | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5 | S6 | S7 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Do Nothing | 0.00 | -2.72 | -2.55 | -4.07 | -2.72 | -0.86 | -3.58 |
| NGSA, base plan (doctrine default) | +11.49 | +2.37 | +3.55 | -0.70 | +2.37 | +10.62 | +1.51 |
| NGSA, Alt plan, A350 hold (ordered) | +14.09 | +4.46 | +5.43 | +1.04 | +4.46 | +13.23 | +3.60 |

The ordered row is the best survivor in every column, so the choice does not depend on my scenario call. It beats the doctrine default by +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09, more than the $1B margin in every column, so I depart from the base-plan default. Its worst column (S4 at +1.04) stays positive, which meets my robustness preference; the base plan's worst column (-0.70) does not. The within-$1B tie-breaks do not apply.

One tie-break note for the record: after a one-year slip, NGSA's EIS would be 2038, outside 2035-2037. No alternative exists, because 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window and the board offers no earlier launch. Holding NGSA would give up the window, so I accept the exposure. The public window, "the second half of the 2030s", covers a one-year slip; the internal target stays 2037.

4. ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD, COLUMN BY COLUMN
- With each Board item at its default: the ngsa item at hold is the Do Nothing row (the Alt plan has no effect without NGSA). The a320_plan item at base is the NGSA base row.
- NGSA item against Do Nothing (base plan): +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09.
- Alt item against the base plan: +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09.
- Package against Do Nothing: +14.09 / +7.18 / +7.98 / +5.11 / +7.18 / +14.09 / +7.18.
- No item loses money in any column, so every item passes the Board's -$2B line.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
- `ngsa: launch`, engine code 7 (Qualified Majority):
  - Five pillars: pass. Wagner reports no safety or quality event and no open finding.
  - Toepfer: pass. Peak cash is $5.074B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B ($0.126B headroom), with no overlap; robustness passes.
  - Wagner: pass on engineering capacity, production readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Grid ΔPV against Do Nothing: as above, minimum +3.37 (S4).
  - Engine sources: at a 2037 EIS, on today's record only CFM is fitted. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no slack) are fitted only if they launch on our selection this round.
- `a320_plan: alt` (read with the package):
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: pass, with the $0.75B phased over 2037-44 and any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
  - Wagner: pass on all five tests. The A320 runs at 82 a month at most, below today's 85, so this is a run-down on mature lines, not a ramp.
  - Grid ΔPV against the base plan: as above, minimum +1.74.
- `rea350: hold` and `delay_tactics: none` are defaults and are not Board items.
- No override is used, and the budget of one per game is intact.

6. DELAY TACTICS
The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it shifts share, not EIS, so read literally it keeps Delay Tactics off. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off. I would revisit only if an fps is on the public record, and then only one poaching move while NGSA is in development, with the grid showing at least $1B and every Board condition met.

7. OWN CLOCK
Boeing's posture played no part in the launch. The launch rests on the technology window and the grid. No future Boeing move will re-time or cancel NGSA (rules 2 and 7).

8. SUPPLY ATTRIBUTION
Wagner's illustrative ramp shows neither A320 plan closing the early-2040s capacity gap during the transition. The binding constraints are engines and structures at the combined peak. Hence the supply moves: A320neo engine slots, titanium and rare earths for our own ramp.

9. RECORDED GAPS
- Toepfer's cash-timing disclosure: the grid books NGSA at EIS. In a cash-timed view, before any offset, the base-plan NGSA item would be about -2.4 in S4 and the lean about -0.6 against Do Nothing. That is a further reason for the Alt plan.
- At a 48% payout on flat FY2025 FCF, net cash would approach nil around 2034. I would take a payout reset toward the 30% floor to the Board, never an equity raise.
- The Board reads the grid as given, and so do I. Both points go in the Audit Committee paper.

Doctrine premium: $0B.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence).

Passed for the ordered package:
- Peak cash for NGSA: $5.074B against $5.2B, $0.126B headroom.
- Alt plan: passes when the $0.75B is phased over 2037-44 (about $0.094B a year), with any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
- Net cash, payout and buyback, with no equity raise: net cash €12.2bn; the buyback completes by 2029; state support counts as upside only; the debt penalty is in the grid.
- Robustness: the lean is positive in all seven columns, worst S4 at +1.04.
- The Board's downside line: item minimums are +3.37 for NGSA and +1.74 for the Alt plan.

Failed, and binding:
- NGSA + A350 Re-engine: peak cash $6.674B, rule 6, and -2.15 in S6 and S7. A red line; deleted.
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails robustness. A soft veto; it trails the lean by at least $1.85B. Accepted.
- Any Delay Tactics: rule 4, fine exposure. A red line; deleted.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one year: fails at $5.824B. A soft veto, accepted by adopting his phasing.

I took his recommended orders in full, with no override.

I also took two disclosures into the Board paper:
- The cash-timing gap: the grid books NGSA at EIS, about $5.7B of PV uncharged before the debt-penalty offset.
- The payout stress case: a reset toward the 30% floor goes to the Board, never an equity raise.

The cash-timing gap does not change the decision, because the Board and I test on the grid. It strengthens the case for the Alt plan over the base plan.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence).

Passed for NGSA on both the base and Alt plans:
- Engineering capacity (zero overlap, A350 on hold)
- Production readiness (EIS 2037 is after the 2035 technology-ready year)
- Safety
- Quality
- A320 ramp shield (the end-2027 commitment is behind us; no ramp problem reported)
- Supply crunch (none reported; the Alt tail is a run-down at 82 a month or less)

He passed the A350 hold on A350F and Spirit absorption, and recommended engine code 7, which I took. The code has no payoff effect, and only a 2030 selection can bring a second source in by 2037.

Failed, and binding:
- Any A350 Re-engine in 2030: with NGSA it is rule 6, a red line; alone it is his absorption test, a soft veto that trails the lean by at least $1.85B.
- Any Delay Tactics: rule 4, a red line, and integrity.

All of these I accepted.

I adopted his quality watch: consolidate the 14-a-month tail on the fewest lines, publish no 2040s A320 rates, and give windows, not dates. I also took his supply-first list into other moves: A320neo engine slots, NGSA engines from CFM, titanium and rare earths.

His capacity reading informs the objective note: neither plan closes the early-2040s gap, but the Alt plan narrows it most.

His change-of-mind triggers carry into round 2. A quality escape, safety event or A320neo engine crunch would send us back to the base plan; an engine maturity slip would re-time NGSA, never cancel it.

airbus.objective_note:
Briefing goal: 'Defend 60/40; protect the A320 family; stable engine supply'. It is scored by the GM, and I trade no PV for it.

Defend 60/40 (preference ≥60% in 2040, 2045 and 2050):
- Do Nothing fails it: 58.4% in 2040 and 54.7% in 2045, as Boeing takes our capacity slack.
- With NGSA in service from 2037 and no fps in service, Boeing loses 1 pp a year. Customers would want about 63% from us in 2040 and 68% in 2045.
- The brief gives no share table for NGSA rows, and the slack floor applies. On Wagner's illustrative ramp, 2040 is at risk on either plan because of the transition trough. The Alt plan narrows it most (about 1,000 deliveries against about 650 on the base plan). 2045 and 2050 should be met as NGSA reaches about 100 a month with capacity creep.

Protect the A320 family (≥60% in every listed year before NGSA EIS):
- Likely not met. In 2035 our preference is 58.7%, because the firm backlog runs out while we are capacity-bound at 1,020 a year. No order this round acts before 2037.

Stable engine supply:
- In 2050, with NGSA: 1 source / 1 maker if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold; 3 / 3 on code 7 if both launch on our selection. Do Nothing gives 2 / 2.
- Code 7 is the only route to three makers and costs nothing on the grid.

board_response.recommendation: Present the peak-cash arithmetic to the Audit Committee standard; confirm net cash carries the payout and the €5bn buyback with no equity raise; state support upside only.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
- Peak cash: NGSA is $35.52B over seven years, $5.074B a year against $5.2B (€4,753m FCF at $1.10), leaving $0.126B of headroom.
- Net cash and returns: €12.2bn of net cash ($13.42B). The €5bn buyback completes by 2029, before NGSA spend starts. There is no equity raise. State support and refundable advances count as upside only. The debt penalty is in the grid.
- Disclosed in addition: the stress case (a 48% payout on flat FY2025 FCF takes net cash to about nil by 2034, while the 30% floor keeps it positive) and the cash-timing gap (the grid books NGSA at EIS). If FCF tracks below FY2025, a payout reset would come to the Board, never an equity raise.

board_response.recommendation: In the public statement give windows rather than dates, stress a disciplined and controlled ramp with safety first, and make no reference to Delay Tactics.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement opens on the five pillars and gives the EIS as 'the second half of the 2030s'. It speaks of a disciplined and controlled ramp-up, keeping the A320 family in production longer without rate numbers, a multi-source engine invitation and zero-for-zero trade. It does not mention Delay Tactics.

priorities: Launch NGSA on its own clock this round. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window, which gives entry into service in 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. Against Do Nothing, the launch gains in every column of the grid: +3.37 (S4) to +11.49 (S1) on the base A320 plan, and +5.11 to +14.09 with the A320 Alt plan. The Board will not veto it for its spend or its cost to near-term earnings.

Protect liquidity and the rating: one programme at a time. NGSA alone costs $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year, which passes the $5.2B line (about one year's FCF) by only $0.13B. No second programme can enter development alongside it.

Integrity: no Delay Tactics. No fps is on the public record, so every move would be naked and expose the company to the $48.32B fine. A single move is worth -15.74 in S1 and S6 and -0.27 to -0.41 elsewhere. That fails the integrity test, the downside test and hard rule 4.

Safety, quality and the A320 ramp come before output. The operating head's tests on keeping the A320 lines running longer under the Alt plan, and on the NGSA ramp, must pass on their own terms. The Board accepts no override of them.
A stable engine supply: an NGSA engine code with CFM plus a second maker. Code 7 is the only route to three makers in 2050 (3 / 3 in the brief's metrics against 1 / 1).
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Averse, 4 of 5. The Board will back one programme, funded inside a year's FCF ($5.2B), on its technology clock. No Board item may lose more than $2B in any plausible column. Boeing has launched nothing, so all seven columns (S1-S7) count.
board_guidance.expect_to_see:
The package should contain the following.
(1) The grid row of the submitted orders. If the ExCo proposes NGSA with the A320 Alt plan and A350: hold, that row reads +14.09 / +4.46 / +5.43 / +1.04 / +4.46 / +13.23 / +3.60.

(3) The CEO's expected scenario and the worst plausible column. On the Board's reading the worst column is S4 (fps 7-yr): +1.04 for NGSA with the Alt plan and -0.70 on the base plan.
(4) The CFO's peak-cash arithmetic. NGSA is $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line. The CFO should show when the Alt plan's $0.75B is spent: spread over development it peaks at $5.18B, which passes, but lumped into a single development year it reaches $5.82B and fails. He should also confirm that net cash still carries the payout and the €5bn buyback with no equity raise.
(5) The operating head's results on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield, supply crunch and production readiness, for both NGSA and the Alt plan's longer A320 lines.
(6) The veto checks, and any override with its margin.
(7) The engine code and its fitted sources.
(8) A rationale recording that the team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands, and that Delay Tactics are off.
(9) A public statement that gives windows, not dates, and does not mention Delay Tactics.
The brief's rules already encode this run's assumptions (the conservative demand curve; Boeing losing 1 pp a year from NGSA entry into service while no fps is in service; Airbus raising capacity 1% a year while it is short). The Board reads the grid as given.
would_approve: ngsa: launch in 2030 (entry into service 2037), with ngsa_engine_code 5, 6 or 7 (7 preferred). Against Do Nothing it is worth +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09 on the base plan. It passes the technology clock (2037 is not before 2035), liquidity ($5.07B against $5.2B) and the downside test (it gains in every column). This needs a Qualified Majority, and the case carries it.

One clean sheet: two launches in one round, with a 5-year development overlap from 2030 to 2035. Downside: its item value is +1.74 in S1-S5 but -2.15 in S6 and S7, a loss beyond $2B in columns the bulletin has not ruled out. Override review: it is a Qualified Majority item and falls $2.15B behind the best passing plan in its worst column. Acceptable alternative: hold.

recommendations.text: Launch NGSA this round, inside the window. 2030 is the last year of 2028-2030, and entry into service in 2037 matches the company's stated 'around 2037'. The Board would not veto a later launch for lateness alone. But under this run's rules every year without NGSA in service costs share and leaves Boeing an open field for an fps lead. Show the item value against Do Nothing column by column, and the worst plausible column (S4).

Take the A320 Alt plan with NGSA if the operating head confirms that keeping the A320 lines running longer (82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month) does not create a supply crunch during the NGSA ramp. It gains $1.74-2.61B in every column. The CFO should show when the $0.75B is spent: lumped into one development year it would breach the $5.2B line.

Keep the A350 Re-engine on hold until NGSA spend rolls off after its 2037 entry into service. Under these bills a 2035 launch would still overlap NGSA for 2 years at $6.67B a year and fail the liquidity line. A launch in the 2045 round would not overlap NGSA. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine, stay out (hard rule 3).

Keep Delay Tactics off this round and record it in the rationale. No fps is on the public record, any move would be naked against a $48.32B fine, and integrity has been a pillar since the 2020 settlement. Revisit only if Boeing launches an fps, and then only talent poaching and only if every one of the Board's conditions holds.

Select NGSA engine code 7, or 5 or 6 if the ExCo prefers: CFM plus at least one second maker. Code 7 appears in no barred code pair. It is also the only selection that can trigger both Pratt & Whitney's and Rolls-Royce's conditional launches, which take the 2050 engine metrics from 1 / 1 to 3 / 3. The engine code does not change the payoff and is not a veto ground.

Present the peak-cash arithmetic to the Audit Committee standard: NGSA $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line, which leaves $0.13B of headroom. Confirm that net cash still carries the 30-50% payout and the €5bn buyback with no equity raise, and that state support is upside only, never assumed in the case.
In the public statement, give windows rather than dates ('the second half of the 2030s'), stress a disciplined and controlled ramp with safety first, and make no reference to Delay Tactics.

frame.question: Do we launch NGSA now, in 2030, the last year of our 2028-2030 window (entry into service 2037, "around 2037"), and if so on which A320 supply plan and engine code, with the A350 on hold and Delay Tactics off, so that the Board can carry it on one programme, inside a year's FCF and positive in every Boeing column?
frame.situation: Public record: no programme has been launched by anyone. Boeing has made no public move. Its MAX runs at 57 a month from 2030, and its fps would be built at new sites if launched. We delivered 60.6% of the narrowbody market in 2026-2029. Rules for this run: demand follows the conservative curve, 1,406 aircraft in 2030, peaking at 2,019 in 2045, then 1,852 in 2050. Our firm backlog (4,925 in 2030) runs out around 2035. Once NGSA is in service and no fps is, Boeing loses 1 pp a year from 40%. Customers we cannot serve go to Boeing as slack. We add 1% of capacity a year while we are short. If we Do Nothing (+0.00): from 2035 we are capacity-bound at 1,020 a year, rising only to 1,127. Our preference share falls to 58.4% in 2040 and 54.7% in 2045 as Boeing takes the slack. Both 'Defend 60/40' and 'Protect the A320 family' are not met (worst year 54.7%). Of the engine-supply goal, dual sources are met (A320neo on CFM and P&W) and three makers are not. With NGSA, the 2050 engine metric is 1 / 1 if the engine makers hold, and 3 / 3 on code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch when we select them. Board guidance (non-binding, but its veto binds): launch NGSA on its own clock this round. One programme at a time, funded within about $5.2B a year. No Delay Tactics. No override of the operating head's safety and ramp tests. Engine code 7 preferred. No Board item may lose more than $2B in any of the seven columns, all of which count because Boeing has launched nothing. Its would-veto list: rea350 launch alongside ngsa; any Delay Tactics; a320_plan alt if Lars fails it on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch; any override outside its review. No safety, quality or supply event is reported in the brief.

ngsa_engine_code: 1-7 (a request; makers not ready by 2037 are dropped; no payoff effect; rides with the NGSA Board item; can be changed in any round until EIS)

rea350: hold / launch (Board item)
delay_tactics: none / bottleneck / poaching / both (covert; Board item; off by the team's stricter condition)
No cancel option exists this round: nothing has been launched

The NGSA item against Do Nothing is +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09, a gain in every column. Worst column S4 at -0.70, which fails my robustness preference.

Tested only to delete, for the record: NGSA (Alt) + A350 Re-engine. Row: +15.83 / +6.21 / +7.17 / +2.78 / +6.21 / +11.08 / +1.45. It is the raw best in S1-S5, $1.74B above the lean. But the Re-engine item is -2.15 in S6 and S7. It breaks rule 6 (two launches in one round, with a five-year overlap from 2030 to 2035). It breaks peak cash ($5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B a year against $5.2B). It is on the Board's would-veto list, and my position is no Re-engine in round 1. It is deleted whatever its PV.

red_lines: Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security): never overridden. Every order and every public word must stand up on them [AX-0073, AX-0081].
Rule 1, the NGSA clock: no entry into service before the 2035 technology-ready year. The launch window is 2028-2030, so 2030 is the last launch year (EIS 2037) [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409].
Rules 2 and 7, our own clock: no Boeing move, now or later, re-times or cancels NGSA. Boeing's public posture does not enter the launch decision.

Rule 6: at most one new launch this round. No NGSA plus A350 Re-engine, and no NGSA / A350 overlap above 2 years unless the grid shows at least $1B more and it passes cash. Here the overlap would be 5 years and fail cash.

Peak cash (Thomas's test and the Board's liquidity line): programme spend at most about $5.2B a year (about one year's FCF of €4.75bn) [AX-0104]. NGSA alone is $5.07B, leaving $0.13B of headroom. The Alt plan's $0.75B must not land in a single NGSA development year ($5.82B fails).

Rules 4 and 5 and the team's stricter condition: Delay Tactics stay off. No fps is public, the fine for a naked move is $48.32B, and the Board vetoes bottleneck and both always, and poaching now. Never named in public.
Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine. It is not active (no 787 Re-engine is public), but it is carried forward. The A350 stays on hold in round 1 (A350F absorption) [AX-0082, AX-0019].
Board downside test: no Board item may lose more than $2B in any of S1-S7. It approves one programme at a time, on its technology clock, and NGSA needs a Qualified Majority [AX-0026, AX-0008].
Lars's safety, quality, A320 ramp-shield and supply-crunch results cannot be overridden. If he fails the Alt plan on any of them, we revert to the base plan.

Override budget: at most one in the game, only with at least $1B over the best passing option in the expected column, and also in the worst plausible column on a Qualified Majority item. It must be recorded as a Board item. None is planned this round.
Disclosure: windows, not dates, for EIS and rate. Internal long-term-plan targets are never disclosed [AX-0005, AX-0004].
frame.asks_cfo:
Thomas, please bring the cash, overlap and robustness memo against the brief's grid only.
(1) Peak cash: NGSA at $35.52B over 7 development years is $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line (€4.75bn FCF at $1.10). Confirm the $0.13B headroom and the development-year profile from 2030 to 2037.
(2) The Alt plan's $0.75B: when is it spent? If it falls after the 2037 entry into service, when NGSA development spend has rolled off, the peak stays at $5.07B. Spread over development, the peak is $5.18B, which passes. Lumped into one development year, it is $5.82B, which fails. Propose a phasing that keeps every year under $5.2B, or tell me it cannot be done.
(3) Confirm that net cash (€12.2bn today [AX-0102]) still carries the 30-50% payout and the €5bn buyback with no equity raise. State support counts as upside only. Is the debt penalty already in the grid?
(4) Robustness: confirm the worst plausible column for each surviving row. As I read it, S4 is +1.04 for the lean, -0.70 for the base-plan NGSA and -4.07 for Do Nothing. Confirm the lean is positive in all seven columns.
(5) Record the cash view of NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine ($6.67B a year) as a fail. Pre-read the next rounds: does a 2035 Re-engine launch overlap NGSA by 2 years and fail the line, while a 2045 launch clears it?
(6) Draft the Board-gate lines for ngsa: launch (Qualified Majority, with the engine code) and for a320_plan alt (read with the package): five pillars, your test, Lars's test, and the grid ΔPV against Do Nothing and against the base plan, column by column.
(7) Your pass or fail on each candidate row, and whether any failure is a soft veto.
frame.asks_ops:
Lars, please bring the production, supply and quality memo.
(1) Engineering capacity: can we launch NGSA in 2030 while we run the A320 at 85 a month and absorb the A350F, without starving the ramp of engineers and suppliers [A-0366, A-0485]? The rate-75 commitment for end-2027 [AX-0054] is behind us by then. Pass or fail.
(2) The Alt plan: it keeps the A320 lines at 82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month for about eight years after the 2037 EIS, while NGSA ramps to 50 a month around EIS+4, 80 around +6 and 100 around +8. Give me a result on each of safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield, supply crunch (CFM and P&W A320neo engines plus the NGSA engines and structures at the combined peak) and production readiness. Then give me the same five results for NGSA on the base plan. The Board accepts no override of the first four, so a fail means base.
(3) Capacity against demand: on the conservative curve we are capacity-bound from 2035, and Boeing takes our slack. (4) Engine code: your supply recommendation among 5, 6 and 7. GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready in 2036. UltraFan NB would be ready in 2037, which is our EIS year with no slack. A maker that is not ready is dropped, and NGSA does not wait. Code 7 is in no barred pair. Do you see any reason not to name all three [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360]?
(5) Confirm the A350 stays on hold in round 1 (A350F absorption [AX-0082]), and give your pre-read on a later Re-engine window.

frame.initial_lean:
My lean: ngsa launch in 2030 (EIS 2037, "around 2037", in "the second half of the next decade" [A-0409, AX-0020]); ngsa_engine_code 7, subject to Lars's supply recommendation; a320_plan alt, if Lars passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch and Thomas phases the $0.75B to keep every year under $5.2B; rea350 hold; delay_tactics none.

On the grid this row reads +14.09 / +4.46 / +5.43 / +1.04 / +4.46 / +13.23 / +3.60. It is the best surviving row in every column, so my choice does not depend on which scenario I expect. My working expectation is S1: Boeing holds this round, given its stated preconditions and our prior of no fps before the next round. S4 (fps 7-yr, same EIS year, Boeing climbing toward 50%) is the worst plausible column at +1.04, still positive. Against Do Nothing, NGSA gains in every column (+3.37 to +11.49 on the base plan). The Alt plan adds a further $1.74B to $2.61B in every column, more than the $1B doctrine margin, so I depart from the base-plan doctrine default unless a test fails. If Lars fails the Alt plan, I take the base plan (worst column S4 at -0.70) without override, because the Board accepts none there.

The raw best plan, Alt plus an A350 Re-engine, scores $1.74B more in S1-S5. It is deleted on rule 6, on peak cash ($6.67B) and on the Board's veto, and it is not a premium I am paying for doctrine. tests.numbers: Five pillars: no breach on my side; Lars confirms safety and quality. CFO: peak cash $5.074B against $5.2B passes ($0.126B headroom); no overlap; robustness passes. Operating head: Lars's result, not mine. Delta PV against Do Nothing (base plan): +11.49/+5.09/+6.10/+3.37/+5.09/+11.48/+5.09. Engine code 7 rides with the item. It has no payoff effect, and I defer to Lars.

tests.name: Board gate line: a320_plan alt, read with the package (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Five pillars, CFO test, operating-head test, grid delta PV against the base plan and against Do Nothing
tests.numbers: Five pillars and operating head: Lars's results on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch decide, and none can be overridden. CFO: passes with the $0.75B phased 2037-44 (peak $5.074B); fails if lumped ($5.824B). Delta PV against the base plan: +2.60/+2.09/+1.88/+1.74/+2.09/+2.61/+2.09. Package against Do Nothing: +14.09/+7.18/+7.98/+5.11/+7.18/+14.09/+7.18.
