tests.threshold: Within $1B, prefer fewer Board items and the later capex start
tests.numbers: The lean carries 2 Board items (ngsa launch; a320_plan alt), the base plan 1. The Alt plan is $1.74B-$2.61B ahead, outside the $1B band, so the tie-break does not bite. NGSA in 2030 is the last window year. The Alt cost phased after EIS is the later capex start.

tests.name: Cash-timing disclosure: the grid books at EIS (disclosure, not a pass/fail test)
tests.threshold: Disclosure only: lead with the grid, never hide a charge
tests.numbers: PV at 2026 of $35.52B booked in 2037 = $15.23B. PV of $5.074B a year over 2030-36 = $20.97B. Gap: $5.74B unloaded, partly covered by the grid's debt penalty of about $1.2B. Before any offset, it would move S4 to about -2.4 for the base-plan NGSA item and about -0.6 for the lean against Do Nothing; S1 stays at about +5.8 and +8.4. I test on the grid, as the Board does, and record the gap.

tests.name: Candidate rows, summary (ask 7)
tests.threshold: Pass or fail on each row, and whether a failure is a soft veto or a red line
tests.numbers: Do Nothing: no cash fail; worst S4 -4.07; gives up the last NGSA year (Faury's call, not a cash test). NGSA base: passes all. Lean: passes all, on the Alt phasing condition. NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine: fails peak cash, overlap and robustness; red line rule 6, binding. A350 Re-engine alone: fails robustness; soft veto, binding, and it trails the lean by at least $1.85B. Any Delay Tactics row: fails fine exposure, and `both` also fails the second-move test; red line rule 4, binding. Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash; soft veto, binding, margin 0.00 against the phased version.

vetoes.plan: NGSA (base or Alt plan) plus rea350 launch in 2030
vetoes.ground: Red line, rule 6: two new launches in one round with a 5-year development overlap (2030-2035), and the Re-engine item is -2.15 in S6 and S7, so not at least $1B. It also fails peak cash ($6.674B a year, $6.781B with the Alt cost spread, against $5.2B) and robustness. Grid margin against the best passing option (the lean): +1.74/+1.75/+1.74/+1.74/+1.75/-2.15/-2.15. Deleted whatever its PV; no override can restore it.

vetoes.plan: rea350 launch with ngsa hold (A350 Re-engine alone)
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test: item against Do Nothing is -0.64 in S6 and S7. Soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing option (the lean): -10.83/-3.92/-4.72/-1.85/-3.92/-14.73/-7.82, so it is behind in every column and the $1B override test cannot be met.

vetoes.plan: Any delay_tactics order this round (bottleneck, poaching or both)
vetoes.ground: Red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked against a $48.32B fine. `both` is a second move and buys nothing (-0.51 to -0.63 over one move). `bottleneck` is also an integrity flag under the five pillars that I could not defend to the Audit Committee. One move is worth -15.74/-0.27/-0.41/-0.31/-0.27/-15.75/-0.28 against the lean. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: a320_plan alt with its $0.75B lumped into a single NGSA development year (2030-2036)
vetoes.ground: Failed peak-cash test: $5.074B + $0.75B = $5.824B against $5.2B. Soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing option (the same Alt plan phased after EIS, 2037-44): 0.00 in every column, so no override can meet $1B. Remedy: phase the spend after EIS, or cap it at $0.10B in any development year.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: I would move from the lean to NGSA on the base plan in two cases: (1) Lars fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch; or (2) the $0.75B cannot be kept to $0.126B or less in every 2030-36 year. NGSA alone still passes all my tests ($5.074B a year; item +3.37 to +11.49). I would change the package if the grid showed an option at least $1B better than the lean in every plausible column that also passed peak cash, or if the Board decided otherwise. On liquidity, I would take a payout reset to the Board, never an equity raise, if 2030-36 FCF tracked below FY2025's €4,753m with no offset, so that even the 30% floor drew net cash below zero. If the Board asks for the cash-timed view (bill spread over 2030-36 rather than booked at EIS), the base-plan NGSA item reads about -2.4 in S4, beyond its -$2B line, while the lean stays about -0.6. That makes the Alt plan more important, not less. A public fps or 787 Re-engine next round does not reopen NGSA (rules 2 and 7). It does re-run Delay Tactics fine exposure, and robustness and the rule-3 check for any A350 Re-engine; a 2035 Re-engine still fails cash at $6.674B in 2035-36.
cfo.memo:
Round 1 (2030), on the brief's grid. Recommended: ngsa launch, engine code 7 (I defer to Lars on the code), a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none.

Peak cash. NGSA is $35.52B over seven development years, 2030-36: $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line (FCF of €4,753m at $1.10). Headroom $0.13B. Pass, narrowly; nothing else can enter development beside it.

Alt plan. Spend the $0.75B as the longer A320 lines run, 2037-44, about $0.09B a year, after NGSA spend rolls off: the peak stays $5.07B. Spread over development it is $5.18B, a pass with no buffer; lumped into one year, $5.82B, a fail. The Board paper should fix that phasing.

Robustness. All seven columns count. The lean row is +1.04 at worst (S4) and gains +5.11 to +14.09 on Do Nothing. NGSA on the base plan gains +3.37 to +11.49. The Alt plan adds +1.74 to +2.61 in every column, above the $1B premium.

Net cash. The €5bn buyback runs off by 2029, before NGSA spend. No equity raise. On flat FY2025 FCF, a 48% payout takes net cash to about nil by 2034; the 30% floor keeps it positive. State support is upside only. The debt penalty is in the grid.

Disclosure: the grid books NGSA at EIS; cash leaves in 2030-36, about $5.7B of PV at 8% the grid does not charge.

Deleted: an A350 Re-engine beside NGSA ($6.67B a year, rule 6, -2.15 in S6-S7); the Re-engine alone (-0.64); any Delay Tactics (naked $48.32B fine).

tests.name: Engineering capacity: NGSA alone (2030 launch, A350 on hold) [Faury ask 1]
tests.threshold: Rule 6 allows one new launch per round. NGSA/A350 development overlap must be 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more.
tests.numbers: NGSA development runs 2030-2037: $35.52B, or $5.07B a year. The A350 is held, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0. The A320 runs at a steady 85 a month (capacity 1,020 a year). It delivers 852 in 2030 and 951 in 2032, and is capacity-bound only from 2034-35. That is sustaining engineering, not a ramp, so a 2030 launch does not starve the line of engineers or suppliers. The end-2027 rate commitment is behind us.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6: NGSA + A350 Re-engine both launched in 2030
tests.threshold: Rule 6 allows one new launch per round. NGSA/A350 development overlap must be 2 years or less, unless the grid shows at least $1B more.
tests.numbers: Two new launches in one round. NGSA develops 2030-2037 and the A350 Re-engine 2030-2035: a 5-year overlap, $3.0B of strain ($0.6B a year), $6.67B a year in the overlap years. Against the best passing row (NGSA Alt + A350 hold) the grid gives +1.74 / +1.75 / +1.74 / +1.74 / +1.75 / -2.15 / -2.15 (S1-S7). That is not $1B or more in every column. Two launches in one round is a red line whatever the margin.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption: A350 on hold in round 1 [Faury ask 5]
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed: not in round 1 (2030), round 2 (2035) at the earliest.
tests.numbers: rea350 hold is confirmed. Pre-read for round 2: a 2035 launch (EIS 2040) overlaps NGSA development in 2035-37. That is 2 years and $1.2B of strain ($0.6B a year), exactly at my limit, and it passes only if no supply crunch is reported. Its EIS also lands at NGSA EIS+3, inside the ramp to 50 a month. On cash it means $6.67B a year in 2035-36, which is Toepfer's test. A launch in the 2045 round has no overlap. Never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption: any A350 Re-engine launch in 2030, with or without NGSA
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine in round 1.
tests.numbers: The A350 Re-engine alone scores +3.26 / +0.54 / +0.71 / -0.81 / +0.54 / -1.50 / -4.22. It trails the best passing row by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no $1B override can apply. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year. For the version with NGSA, see the rule 6 entry.

tests.name: Production readiness: NGSA launch in 2030, base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: Launch inside the 2028-2030 window, once the wing is buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft. Rule 1: no EIS before 2035.
tests.numbers: Launch in 2030, the last year of the window. EIS 2037 is 2 years after the 2035 technology-ready year. NGSA ramp anchors are 50 a month at EIS+4 (2041), 80 at +6 (2043) and 100 at +8 (2045). On the base plan the A320 winds down 72, 52, 42, 14, then none about 5 years after EIS, which bets on NGSA hitting its anchors. On the Alt plan it runs 82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 for about 8 years in all: about 1,500 more A320s on proven lines. That hedges the 1-2 years of ramp slip our own record shows (rate 75 slipped about 2 years). Both plans pass, and Alt is the more robust production plan.

tests.name: Safety: NGSA launch, base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: Five pillars: no order that compromises safety. Never overridden.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no safety event, and no order touches an open safety finding. The Alt plan runs existing, certified A320 lines longer at lower rates (82 a month at most after EIS).

tests.name: Quality, and public explanations: base and Alt plans [Faury asks 2 and 6]
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality.
tests.numbers: In public the Alt plan reads as extended A320 family production through the NGSA transition, which is consistent with the pillars. Quality watch: the 14-a-month tail runs about 4 years (around 2041-44) while staff move to NGSA, so consolidate it on the fewest lines to keep skills. Flags: no Delay Tactics move can be explained publicly. Give NGSA EIS and rates as windows ('second half of the 2030s'), not dates. Publish no 2040s A320 rate numbers.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield: base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment. On this board it passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment (70-75 a month, then 75) is behind us. The A320 runs at 85 a month (capacity 1,020 a year), and no ramp problem is reported. After EIS the Alt plan holds the A320 at 82 a month or less, never above today's rate, for about $0.75B. Phasing that $0.75B under the $5.2B line is Toepfer's test.

tests.name: Supply crunch: base and Alt plans (CFM and P&W A320neo engines, plus NGSA engines and structures at the combined peak) [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency.
tests.numbers: No crunch is reported, so the trigger does not fire. Forward check: today's 85 a month needs 2,040 engines a year (CFM 1,224, P&W 816 at 60/40). The Alt tail peaks at 82 a month (1,968 engines a year), then falls to 14 a month (336 a year). That is a run-down, not a ramp. My straight-line reading of the rules' ramp anchors (illustrative, not a board number): Alt runs about 64-82 a month in 2037-42 and peaks around 104 in 2044 (90 NGSA + 14 A320). Base runs about 52-72 a month in 2037-42 and reaches 100 in 2045. Both carry about 9-10% of capacity creep on top. Alt's peak is about 4% above base, and the extra 14 a month are on mature lines. Secure first: A320neo tail engine slots (CFM, P&W), NGSA engines at CFM (the only certain maker), titanium and rare earths.

tests.name: Capacity against demand [Faury ask 3; for information, not a veto test]
tests.threshold: Report only.
tests.numbers: Do Nothing: capacity-bound from 2035 at 1,020 a year, creeping to 1,127. In 2045 we would want 1,211 (60% of 2,019) against 1,105 of capacity, and the whole market has 1,789 slots (1,105 + 684) against 2,019 demand. With NGSA our preference rises 1 pp a year from 2037 (about 63% in 2040, 68% in 2045), so we would want about 1,135 in 2040 and 1,373 in 2045. On my illustrative ramp, base supplies about 650 and Alt about 1,000 in 2040. In 2045 both supply about 1,330 (100 a month with creep). Neither plan closes the gap in the early 2040s. Alt narrows it most in 2037-44, and the gap nearly closes around 2045. The brief has no supply table for the NGSA rows. The grid's Alt item (+1.74 to +2.61 in every column) confirms the extra A320s sell.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (a recommendation, not a veto ground) [Faury ask 4]
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7). Code 7 when I cannot tell which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS.
tests.numbers:
Readiness by the 2037 EIS:
- CFM: always ready.
- P&W GTF2: if launched in 2030, ready in 2036 (1 year of slack).
- Joint Venture: if formed in 2030, ready in 2036.
- RR UltraFan NB: if launched in 2030, ready in 2037 (no slack).
An engine launched in the 2035 round would be ready only in 2041-42, too late for 2037, so only a 2030 selection can add a second source at EIS. 2050 metric: 1/1 if the makers hold (CFM alone, against 2/2 on Do Nothing); 3/3 on code 7 if both launch. Code 7 is in no barred pair. I recommend code 7. Operating cost the board does not price: up to three engine integrations in 2030-37 on teams that already bind. An unready maker is dropped, so NGSA never waits (rule 8 cannot bind).

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year. Never cancel.
tests.numbers: No slip is reported in the brief.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers: No Boeing move is on the public record. The MAX runs at 57 a month from 2030. This changes none of our programmes.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, any move in 2030 (rules 4-5, five pillars, team's stricter condition)
tests.threshold: No move before an fps is launched. At most one move (`both` is two). `poaching` only while a programme is in development. `bottleneck` only as a first claim on capacity for our own ramp.
tests.numbers: No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine. One move on the lean scores -15.74 / -0.27 / -0.41 / -0.31 / -0.27 / -15.75 / -0.28 against it. `both` scores -16.26 to -0.83. Neither changes who enters service first. The recommended order, `none`, passes.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch alongside ngsa: launch, on either the base or the Alt A320 plan
vetoes.ground: Company red line rule 6, which cannot be overridden: two new launches in one round, with a 5-year NGSA/A350 development overlap (2030-2035), $3B of strain and $6.67B a year in the overlap years. It also fails my A350F and Spirit A350 absorption test, a soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing row (NGSA Alt + A350 hold): +1.74 / +1.75 in S1-S5 and -2.15 in S6-S7.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch with ngsa: hold (the A350 Re-engine alone in 2030)
vetoes.ground: It fails my A350F and Spirit A350 absorption test (no A350 Re-engine in round 1), a soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing row: -10.83 / -3.92 / -4.72 / -1.85 / -3.92 / -14.73 / -7.82, so it can never clear the $1B override test. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.

vetoes.plan: delay_tactics: bottleneck, poaching or both (any move this round)
vetoes.ground: Company red line rule 4: no Delay Tactics before an fps is launched (none is public), and `both` is a second move. `bottleneck` and `both` also breach the five pillars (integrity). Any move is naked against the $48.32B fine and scores -15.74 (S1), -15.75 (S6) and -0.27 to -0.41 elsewhere against the lean. It fails the team's stricter condition too, because it does not change who enters service first.

ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence). None of this is in my own recorded words.

NGSA in 2030 passes. EIS 2037 comes after the 2035 technology-ready year. With the A350 on hold, NGSA overlaps nothing: zero years, zero strain. The rate-75 date (end-2027) is behind us, and no ramp problem or supply crunch is reported.

The Alt plan passes on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch and readiness, and I prefer it. Its A320 lines never exceed 82 a month, below today's 85, so CFM and P&W see a slower run-down, not a ramp. On the base plan our combined rate falls well below 85 a month while NGSA climbs to 50. Alt fills much of that trough with about 1,500 A320s, and it insures us if our ramp slips, as rate 75 did. First secure A320neo engines for the tail, and titanium and rare earths for the combined peak around 2044.

Engine code 7. GTF2 would be ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no slack. I cannot tell which maker will launch, and only a 2030 selection gets either in by EIS. Otherwise NGSA flies CFM alone by 2050.

Binding vetoes: an A350 Re-engine in 2030, with or without NGSA, fails A350F absorption. With NGSA it also breaks rule 6: two launches, a five-year overlap, $3B of strain and -$2.15B in S6-S7. Any Delay Tactics breaks rule 4, because no fps is public.

In public: windows, not dates, and a disciplined and controlled ramp.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for the transition
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements for A320neo engine slots with CFM and P&W to cover the longer A320 tail, and NGSA engines from CFM, the only maker certain to be ready. Titanium and rare-earth supply secured for the combined A320/NGSA peak in the mid-2040s, the follow-on to the 2025 de-risking [AX-0062, AX-0063]. These are for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

other_moves.move: Engineering recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Normal hiring and internal redeployment to staff NGSA development, sized so the A320 sustaining teams and the A350F are not stripped [A-0366, A-0485]. This is not targeted at any competitor's programme and is not a Delay Tactics move.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: Continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

other_moves.move: Consolidate the A320 tail on the fewest lines (Wagner's quality watch)
other_moves.detail: Under the Alt plan the 14-a-month tail runs about four years while staff move to NGSA. Concentrate it on the fewest lines to keep skills and quality. Publish no A320 rate numbers for the 2040s.

other_moves.move: Board paper fixes the phasing of the Alt plan's $0.75B
other_moves.detail: Spend about $0.094B a year in 2037-44 as the longer A320 lines run, after NGSA development spend rolls off. Any pre-EIS commitment is capped at $0.10B in any 2030-36 year, inside the $0.126B headroom. Peak programme cash stays at $5.074B a year against the $5.2B line.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, with entry into service planned in the second half of the 2030s. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s: on the clock of technology maturity, with a disciplined and controlled ramp-up. To serve our customers through the transition, we will keep the A320 family in production for longer on our proven lines while the new aircraft ramps up. We have invited CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power the new aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp. We will fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
ROUND 1 (2030). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Order of argument:
- Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- A disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409].
- What the Board can carry: one programme, inside a year's FCF, with no item losing more than $2B in any column [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine:
  - Rule 6: two launches in one round, with a 5-year overlap from 2030 to 2035.
  - Peak cash: $6.674B a year against $5.2B.
  - Its item value is -2.15 in S6 and S7. It is on the Board's would-veto list. This is the raw best in S1 to S5 (+15.83 in S1); it is a red-line deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Integrity pillar.
  - The Board vetoes bottleneck and both always, and poaching now.
  - One move is worth -15.74 in S1 and -15.75 in S6 against the lean.

2. SOFT VETOES ACCEPTED
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails Toepfer's robustness test and Wagner's A350F/Spirit absorption test. It trails the lean by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no override is possible. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash ($5.824B). Remedied by phasing it over 2037-44.

3. SURVIVORS
| Row | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5 | S6 | S7 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Do Nothing | 0.00 | -2.72 | -2.55 | -4.07 | -2.72 | -0.86 | -3.58 |
| NGSA, base plan (doctrine default) | +11.49 | +2.37 | +3.55 | -0.70 | +2.37 | +10.62 | +1.51 |
| NGSA, Alt plan, A350 hold (ordered) | +14.09 | +4.46 | +5.43 | +1.04 | +4.46 | +13.23 | +3.60 |

The ordered row is the best survivor in every column, so the choice does not depend on my scenario call. It beats the doctrine default by +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09, more than the $1B margin in every column, so I depart from the base-plan default. Its worst column (S4 at +1.04) stays positive, which meets my robustness preference; the base plan's worst column (-0.70) does not. The within-$1B tie-breaks do not apply.

One tie-break note for the record: after a one-year slip, NGSA's EIS would be 2038, outside 2035-2037. No alternative exists, because 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window and the board offers no earlier launch. Holding NGSA would give up the window, so I accept the exposure. The public window, "the second half of the 2030s", covers a one-year slip; the internal target stays 2037.

4. ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD, COLUMN BY COLUMN
- With each Board item at its default: the ngsa item at hold is the Do Nothing row (the Alt plan has no effect without NGSA). The a320_plan item at base is the NGSA base row.
- NGSA item against Do Nothing (base plan): +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09.
- Alt item against the base plan: +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09.
- Package against Do Nothing: +14.09 / +7.18 / +7.98 / +5.11 / +7.18 / +14.09 / +7.18.
- No item loses money in any column, so every item passes the Board's -$2B line.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
- `ngsa: launch`, engine code 7 (Qualified Majority):
  - Five pillars: pass. Wagner reports no safety or quality event and no open finding.
  - Toepfer: pass. Peak cash is $5.074B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B ($0.126B headroom), with no overlap; robustness passes.
  - Wagner: pass on engineering capacity, production readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Grid ΔPV against Do Nothing: as above, minimum +3.37 (S4).
  - Engine sources: at a 2037 EIS, on today's record only CFM is fitted. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no slack) are fitted only if they launch on our selection this round.
- `a320_plan: alt` (read with the package):
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: pass, with the $0.75B phased over 2037-44 and any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
  - Wagner: pass on all five tests. The A320 runs at 82 a month at most, below today's 85, so this is a run-down on mature lines, not a ramp.
  - Grid ΔPV against the base plan: as above, minimum +1.74.
- `rea350: hold` and `delay_tactics: none` are defaults and are not Board items.
- No override is used, and the budget of one per game is intact.

6. DELAY TACTICS
The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it shifts share, not EIS, so read literally it keeps Delay Tactics off. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off. I would revisit only if an fps is on the public record, and then only one poaching move while NGSA is in development, with the grid showing at least $1B and every Board condition met.

7. OWN CLOCK

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. The LEAP is flying on every 737 MAX and on the A320neo, and our job today is to deliver those engines on time and support that fleet. We'll keep at it with our suppliers, and with our partners at Safran.

Here's what we don't know: when the airframers will launch their next single-aisle, and what they'll want under the wing. That's really not for us to say. We don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM will offer our engines to both airframers, and we will commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer.

RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran. The airframers will set the date for that architecture.

On the widebody, we're investing in a GEnx upgrade so the 787 fleet stays competitive for our customers.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
I'm placing one order: genx: upgrade_genx9. Everything else holds: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. RISE stays whole as technology. The narrowbody product decision comes back in 2035, once the airframers' launches and codes are on the record.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake. It is 2030 and nothing is launched: no airframe, no code, no rival NB engine, no Joint Venture commitment. cfo.would_change_mind_if: Four things would move me. (1) An airframer launch goes on the public record with a code that puts CFM on a new narrowbody alongside a rival engine (S2 or S5 becomes the expected column), or a rival new NB engine is launched or a Joint Venture committed on the record. Then the Ducted passes volumes first and pays for itself (+2.06 or +4.44), and I would back it in that round with the volume assumptions worked. (2) Confirmed data, not early signals, puts more than about 55% on S2+S5 against the GEnx-alone plan and more than about 70-80% against waiting to 2035. (3) Ali's test and ramp evidence shows the new type reaching rate faster than the public plan, so that a 2035 Ducted would give up more than $1B in S2 or S5. (4) A 787 or A350 re-engine on a rival engine, or a Trent 1000 upgrade, changes the GEnx's value or its 2042 start.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the money on one page. Your item values check to the cent.

GEnx upgrade: +0.78 in S1, +0.77 in the worst column, no board R&D, one project, GE alone. Price/cost positive in every column; the only order that is.

Ducted: -4.00 in S1 and S6, its full bill. It pays only in S2 (+2.06) and S5 (+4.44), and both assume selections nobody has made. On your weights it is -0.52 against hold. The honest comparison is against GEnx alone, since GEnx cannot ride with a Ducted alone: -1.30, break-even at about 55% on S2 plus S5. We need to work the exact volume assumptions with the airframer first.

Waiting costs little. A 2035 Ducted is ready 2041; we give up the NGSA ramp years, when the A320 is still most of the line. Off grid, I estimate $0.5-0.7B in S2 and $0.5-0.9B in S5, under the $1B margin. Launching now beats waiting only above roughly 70-80% on S2 plus S5.

R&D per year: nil on GEnx, $0.67B for a Ducted, against about $2.5B. The 70% payout stays whole; no rating risk. Premium: zero in S1, 1.44 in S2; 4.90 in S5, above the cap.

What the case leaves out: S6 is -59.28, $60B below S1, and the grid assumes nobody moves again. But the good news is the GEnx stays positive even there.

Book +0.77, no upside until a launch is on the record. Plenty of work to do, and we are all over it.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my date veto): every ready year in options A-G
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted at launch + 6. Open Fan at launch + 10 and not before 2045. Embraer counts at launch + 7. GEnx counts at launch + 3 and not before the first re-engine (2035 at the earliest, 2042 if none). An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036 and a 2035 launch in 2041, the years Culp's frame uses. Open Fan: a 2030 launch is ready at max(2040, 2045) = 2045, and a 2035 launch at max(2045, 2045) = 2045, as the frame says. Embraer: a 2030 launch counts from 2037. GEnx upgrade (option B): 2030 + 3 = 2033, but it counts only from the first re-engine's entry into service, which is 2042 because none is on the record (2035 at the earliest, for a re-engine launched in 2030). The grid's +0.78/+0.77 in every column (row 'GEnx upgrade' minus row 'hold everything') rests on 2042. None of options A-G depends on an earlier year. What tests stand behind the Ducted date: none on a ducted product. What we do have is RISE technology testing (over 350 tests, early focus on durability; HPT dust testing on the compact core began October 2025) and LEAP fixes delivered on test (the fuel-nozzle fix in production by March 2024; LEAP-1A HPT hardware certified December 2024). 2036 is the board's date, and I hold it as a planning date.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That a Ducted is defensive only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data. Culp's frame says his 20% line binds RISE and that the Ducted is a defensive LEAP successor with 'less than half' the gain, never the next generation. That matches my words: 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics', and a ducted engine has 'less than half the fuel burn improvements'. The draft public line calls no engine the next generation. His rebuttal of his own red line stands on physics.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. Not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data, and no option trades durability for fuel burn or schedule. No flag is open in the record. RISE has over 350 tests with an early focus on durability, the earliest-ever HPT dust testing on its compact core, and an owner for open-fan durability. The yardstick if a Ducted launches is the LEAP gap: 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 in benign conditions, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh ones, caused by a handful of parts. A Ducted's hot-and-harsh durability gate goes to a cross-functional team at launch. Confirmed for Culp: durability and fuel burn, 'the genius of the AND'; no plan here trades one for the other.

D against C: -1.22 / +0.15 / +1.53 / +0.12 / +1.24 / -1.23, so +0.15 in S2 sits inside the $1B margin. D against B: -6.00 / +1.44 / -0.22 / -0.71 / +4.90 / -6.00. Whether overlapping projects still draw strain is Ghai's to check.

My 2022 'mid-decade' fly demo slipped. Outcomes after October 2025 are not in the evidence. For 2035 I need the flight test done and the compact core's durability turned on and turned off. Our NB engines climb from 2,131 to 2,615 between 2030 and 2037, and 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites. One commitment per round. If a Ducted launches, the GEnx can follow in 2035 at the same 2042 count unless a re-engine launches in 2030.

vetoes.plan: Any wording that calls a Ducted the next generation, or a public Ducted ready year
vetoes.ground: Physics and test standard (advice). A ducted engine has 'less than half' the open fan's gain, and 20% is 'practically impossible' without the open fan. 2036 is the board's development time; we have never turned a ducted product on and off, so keep the date internal.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Only test or field data, never analysis. (1) The Ducted call: a public airframer launch whose code puts CFM alongside a rival (S2 or S5) is field fact. Then a 2030 Ducted, ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 NGSA, has my concurrence on dates, provided a cross-functional durability gate is set at launch. (2) The Ducted date: a hot-and-harsh endurance test on a ducted or RISE compact-core configuration that turns the failure on and turns it off would firm up 2036. A failed test would move it, and I would report the slip in numbers. (3) Stacking: field data showing LEAP deliveries meeting rate, with the 9 constrained suppliers at 15 sites cleared, would lift my objection to running two projects. (4) The Open Fan: nothing on this board moves it before 2045. For 2035 I would need RISE ground and flight-test results and compact-core durability turned on and off, plus an airframer whose entry into service is 2045 or later.
ops.memo:
We have done what we always do here: dates first, and only on test.

Open Fan. Launched in 2030 or 2035, ready in 2045. A 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps enters service in 2037, eight years earlier; a 10-year fps in 2040, five years earlier. Airframers will not wait. Hold. RISE stays whole as technology: over 350 tests, early focus on durability. I promised a fly demo by mid-decade; it became "this decade". We failed twice. We got it done.

Ducted. Launch plus six: 2036 on a 2030 launch, one year ahead of a 2037 NGSA, four ahead of a 2040 fps. Launched in 2035, ready 2041, four years late against a 2030 NGSA. 2036 passes my test as the board's development time. But precisely: we have never turned a ducted product on and turned it off. 2036 is a planning date, not a public one. It is not the next generation, and the reason is physics: less than half the gain.

No safety or durability flag is open. If the Ducted launches, hot-and-harsh durability goes to a cross-functional team. No single person can make a safety decision.

Supply: 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers. One commitment per round; Ducted plus GEnx is -1.22 in every column. No evidence: following doctrine. On launching the Ducted, Embraer or Lobby: No evidence: following Culp.

I recommend the GEnx upgrade alone. No veto on that plan. A date before launch plus development years, or an Open Fan before 2045, I veto.

Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208, CX-0012].

other_moves.detail: Ali runs the review of the constrained suppliers (80% of shortages from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613, CX-0633]) while NB engine volumes rise from 2,131 in 2030 to 2,615 in 2037. OE engines come first and spares do not crowd them out. This is the gate Ali named for lifting his objection to a second project in 2035.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. The LEAP is flying on every 737 MAX and on the A320neo, and our job today is to deliver those engines on time and support that fleet. We'll keep at it with our suppliers, and with our partners at Safran.

Here's what we don't know: when the airframers will launch their next single-aisle, and what they'll want under the wing. That's really not for us to say. We don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM will offer our engines to both airframers, and we will commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer.

RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran. The airframers will set the date for that architecture.

On the widebody, we're investing in a GEnx upgrade so the 787 fleet stays competitive for our customers.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
I'm placing one order: genx: upgrade_genx9. Everything else holds: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. RISE stays whole as technology. The narrowbody product decision comes back in 2035, once the airframers' launches and codes are on the record.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake. It is 2030 and nothing is launched: no airframe, no code, no rival NB engine, no Joint Venture commitment. This game's rules make any shift of airframe share from Boeing to Airbus cost us. Boeing loses 1 pp a year from an NGSA EIS while no fps is in service. Airbus's slack goes to Boeing, and Airbus adds 1% a year of capacity while it is short. We are sole source on the 737 and hold 60% of the A320neo. That is why hold falls to -15.23 in S2 even with CFM selected. That loss comes from the airframers, not from anything we order. Our controllables are what we put on the airframes and when.

NO BIRTHRIGHT. I read the columns where we lose the slot as hard as those where we keep it. A rival takes the whole slot in S3 (-42.50) and S6 (-60.05), and part of it in S2, S4 and S5. A Ducted does not buy back a lost slot: S3 -0.97 and S6 -4.00 against hold. It pays only where we share a new airframe with a rival: S2 +2.06 and S5 +4.44.

THE DECISION BY TEST
(1) Additive and paid for the risk. The GEnx upgrade is +0.78 in S1 and +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. It is one project, carries no strain, and GE acts alone. It is the best grid plan in S1, S3, S4 and S6, and the only order positive in all six columns.
- The Ducted fails in the expected column: S1 -4.00, its full bill. On my weights it is -0.52 against hold and -1.30 against the GEnx-alone plan it would displace, because GEnx on a Ducted alone is -1.22 once strain is netted.
- Rahul's comparator is the right one. Break-even on S2+S5 is 41% against hold, 55% against GEnx alone, and roughly 70-80% against waiting to 2035. My 40% clears none of these.
(2) Low case first. The expected column is S1 on the public record. I plan on the backlog, not on orders not yet won [CX-0248, CX-0536].
(3) Timing. The airframer sets the date. Rahul's off-grid estimate is labelled as inference. A Ducted deferred to 2035 (ready 2041) gives up about $0.49-0.72B in S2 and $0.51-0.77B in S5 against a 2030 launch. That is up to $1.13B only with a fast 7-year fps. The years lost are 2037-40, the low part of the new type's ramp.
- That is under my $1B ε, so patience wins.
- 'GEnx now, Ducted in 2035 only if S2 or S5' is worth, against hold, +0.78 / +2.24 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +4.61 / +0.77, or +1.72 weighted. A Ducted now is -0.52 and the full package -0.62.
- Caveat for 2035: if the board still counts the 2030 GEnx as running, a 2035 Ducted carries the $2B strain and pays only in S5 (+1.83). I'll ask the GM how the board treats it before the 2035 frame.
(4) H2, the Open Fan. Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it is ready in 2045 either way. Every 2030 airframe enters service first: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. Against hold it is -8.00 / -29.21 / -8.00 / -15.22 / -32.15 / -8.00, far beyond its $8B bill. With Lobby it is still -11.00 to -27.87. Launching now adds cost and no earlier date. I'm not spending the one RISE allowance in 2030.
(5) H3. The record holds no trigger. The grid route needs about 41% or more on S2+S5. My weights give 40% and Rahul's read of the record gives less, so a Ducted launch now is not a defence. It would be a bet on selections nobody has made.
(6) Suppliers. Ali advises one commitment per round, and Rahul's no-stacking advice agrees. Strain is the board's doctrine; Ali's supply record is my own description of his job [CX-0633].
(7) Next generation. The 20% line binds RISE. No Ducted launches, so the line stands untouched this round. If a Ducted launches in 2035, I rebut the line on physics: a ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183], so it is a defensive LEAP successor and never the next generation. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].
(8) Tie-break. upgrade_genx9 and invest_genx are identical on the board. I take the upgrade: a derivative on a proven architecture, quality ahead of novelty.

ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD
- GEnx upgrade row: +0.78 / -14.46 / -41.72 / -24.25 / -35.12 / -59.28.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The last few years on the GTF fleet were hard on our customers, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine.

Here is our commitment. In any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney for a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside a partner, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan that same round. It is planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036 for a commitment made this year. Its durability will be proven before it enters service. That means time on wing ahead of fuel burn in the specification, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet, also at standard terms. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.

frame.question: Control what you can control [PX-0020]. We do not control whether Airbus launches NGSA or Boeing launches fps this year, or which engine either of them names. We do control two things. First, whether P&W is still in the running when they choose. Second, what we promise the market about durability. The question this round: what order on `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr` keeps us in the running for any new narrowbody launched in 2030, with no capital spent ahead of visible demand, the dividend and debt path untouched, and nothing promised that we have not yet proven? Round 1 is our only chance at a 2030-launched airframe. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, after a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS and after a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. If we miss this cycle, we are shut out of it for decades [PX-0071][P-1347]. That line was said of RTX's businesses in general, so applying it to GTF2 is inference.

Airbus is on its base A320 plan (85 a month until NGSA, then the lines wind down). Boeing's fps would be built at new sites. Observed 2026-29: P&W holds 24.2% of narrowbody engines, which is our 40% of the A320neo slot. This run's assumptions are in rules.md: the conservative demand case (1,406 aircraft in 2030, peaking at 2,019 in 2045), with the firm backlog lasting to about 2035; Boeing loses 1 pp a year from NGSA EIS while no fps is in service; Airbus slack goes to Boeing; Airbus adds 1% of capacity a year whenever it is short. The bad news first. Our status quo is ΔPV −0.00 (yield 100.0%). Neither objective test is met: no new P&W engine on a new airframe (credibility), and ΔPV is not above zero (capitalise). On the grid, every column in which NGSA enters service without P&W costs us −19.49, about 18% of our $110B EV, as NGSA replaces the A320neo slot. An fps 10-yr in service without us costs −2.48 (S4 on hold). `launch_if_selected` turns S2 into +5.59, S4 into +6.37 and S5 into +9.10. It is never below `hold` in any column (+25.08 / +8.85 / +28.59 in S2 / S4 / S5, 0 elsewhere). S3 and S6, where NGSA launches without us, stay at about −19 whatever we order. An unconditional launch only moves them to −19.12 and −18.35. That loss comes from the selection, not from our order, and we answer it with product, not price [PX-0055]. Readiness: a 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. That is one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, and four years inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. My own operating dates have slipped before, by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104], so a one-year margin needs Eddy's check, not my optimism. Board guidance: it approves `launch_if_selected` readily. It would veto an unconditional `launch` unless the expected edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least +$0.5B, would veto a `jv_with_rr: commit` this round, and would veto any case resting on unrecorded upside.

An unconditional `launch` is allowed only into a P&W selection already on the public record (there is none), or as the NGSA franchise hedge with Mitchill's expected edge over `launch_if_selected` ≥ 0 (his ground 2 binds; no premium buys it) and the Board's ≥ +$0.5B. It needs a named 2035 cancel. No hedge for fps alone, and never a launch for share alone.

Sole source: a shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted and declared as doctrine relief. On NGSA it is also franchise defence; we aimed at about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. This is inference.

Joint Venture [P-1233]: share risk and investment, never the gear or our core technology. A commitment is public at once. It is off unless Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). Neither holds in 2030.
Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. No plan that needs a dividend cut or reverses the debt path. Mitchill confirms.
Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement to win a selection. A rival's discount never moves the answer.
Narrowbody only [PX-0027]. We have no widebody move.
We never speak for an airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and never claim a selection or a Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record.
One premium cap: doctrine plus objective premium ≤ $1B (objectives.md §6). The Board passes an item that trails `hold` only on a declared premium of ≤ $0.5B that serves the objective.

Board's would-veto list, carried in: an unconditional `launch` with edge < +$0.5B; `jv_with_rr: commit` in round 1; any item resting on unrecorded upside (an assumed Airbus code change in 2035, an assumed Rolls-Royce commitment); any item with an unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, an unrebutted red-line flag, or an entry in `overrides` (we leave `overrides` empty); any item Eddy fails on durability or parts; any item that can lose more than its own $2B against `hold` in a plausible column.

Neil, I trust your cash numbers over my operating dates. Please give me the following.

Shane, your proposal leads. Please give me the following.
(1) Your engine-order proposal on `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr`, with the reasoning.

frame.initial_lean:
My lean is A: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` and `jv_with_rr: hold`, with premium $0B. It never trails `hold` in any column, and it is the best grid plan on any weights I find plausible. On my early sketch (S1 .30, S2 .15, S3 .15, S4 .10, S5 .10, S6 .10, S7 .10) it is worth about +7.5 against `hold`; on equal weights about +8.9. A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted and declared as doctrine relief, not a premium.

My bias is to see the next single-aisle "mid-next decade" [PX-0093]. That is exactly why I will not sit on `hold` and miss a 2030 selection. The unconditional `launch` hedge stays on the table only if Neil's weights give it an edge of at least 0 (and the Board's +0.5). On my own sketch it is about −0.63, or −0.50 with the 2035 cancel, so I expect it to fail. The S3 code-switch option is real but unrecorded, and I will not book it. The Joint Venture stays at `hold`: no Rolls-Royce commitment on the record, and no live code with Rolls-Royce in it. I revisit it in 2035 if either changes, with the gear never on the table [P-1233][PX-0014]. I will adjust on Neil's numbers and Shane's readiness check, not on any rival's price.

Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan in any round an airframer selects us, as sole source or alongside a partner. Low end first. On my weights (S1 .35, S2 .15, S3 .15, S4 .05, S5 .05, S6 .15, S7 .10), Do Nothing is worth −9.87, with −19.49 in four columns. My first read was timing: nothing hits before a 2037 NGSA EIS. It's more pervasive than that. NGSA takes the A320neo slot, and our order doesn't change whom Airbus picks.

`launch_if_selected` is the plan. It's worth −4.24, +5.63 against hold, and it's never below hold in any column. It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us. If it triggers, it costs about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, about 5-6% of a $6B self-funded envelope, even in S5. The V2500 and GTF aftermarket fund the bridge. The dividend stays covered and the debt path to pre-ASR levels is untouched. We do not want to starve the business, and this doesn't.

An unconditional `launch` fails my gate. Against `launch_if_selected` it's −2.00 / 0 / +0.37 / 0 / 0 / +1.14 / −2.00. The edge is −0.67 on my weights, −0.53 with a 2035 cancel and its $1.67B write-off. Break-even is 64% S6 against S1 plus S7; the Board's +0.5 needs 80%. Veto, ground 2, binding.

Joint Venture: hold. Rolls-Royce isn't on the record. It's 0, or −2.00 in S7, and a live GTF2 folds in at no new cost (E equals C).

Booked number: 0.00 in S1. The S3 code-switch is real option value; we name it, we don't count it. I'd like to see a few more reps first.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Calio's row A). Grid row "GTF2 Solo if selected": 0 / +5.59 / -19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / -19.49 / 0, against `hold` at 0 / -19.49 / -19.49 / -2.48 / -19.49 / -19.49 / 0. That is never below `hold`.

WHY `launch_if_selected`. An NGSA launched this year and in service in 2037 without us costs -19.49. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, after every EIS reachable from a 2030 launch, so this is the cycle. The order ties the launch to a customer, keeps engineering on the fleet until one shows up, and can only trigger if GTF2 would be ready by that airframe's EIS (rules.md). This is the seat's doctrine (GTF2 only into a selection, with the durability programme intact), not my own record, which has no launch decision in it.

WHY `jv_with_rr: hold`. Rolls-Royce's commitment is not on the record, no live airframe has code 1, 4, 5 or 7, and nothing on the board protects our gear and core [P-1233].

ANSWERS TO CALIO
(1) As above.
(2) Readiness. Launch 2030, ready 2036. NGSA EIS 2037 and fps 7-yr EIS 2037: one year of margin. fps 10-yr and Embraer EIS 2040: four years. That passes the binding test. One year is my advisory minimum and nothing more: my Advantage certification went from mid-2024 to 2025, and the company's derivative slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years. Six years is credible only if: time on wing and LLP life come ahead of fuel burn in the spec [PX-0073]; severe-environment endurance testing is done before certification, because 3/4 of the fleet flew cool and hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122], and the Advantage needed more than double the endurance testing [P-0779]; all LLPs are at full life at EIS [PX-0128]; and maturity gates are reviewed on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131]. If test data in 2035 put 2036 at risk, you get the bad number first. We never compress testing to hold the date.
(3) Joint Venture with fold-in. If both commit in 2030 it is ready in 2036. If it forms in 2035 it is ready in 2041, unless a solo programme folds in. A live GTF2 makes it 2036, but only after an unconditional launch: `launch_if_selected` leaves no GTF2 in S3 or S6. An RR UltraFan NB launched in 2030 makes it 2037, with zero margin. So the door to a 2037 NGSA exists on the board's arithmetic, but only through RR's 2030 solo, and only if Airbus moves NGSA's code to 4 or 7 in 2035, which is unrecorded and not booked. It is narrow. Zero margin fails my advisory margin. We would be signing durability on an engine we did not design or test, two years from service, built on RR's architecture, not an extended GTF. Cost: our $2B share. I would not go through that door without RR's severe-environment test data.
(4) Parts. The 2030 brief and bulletin show no live fleet, quality or supply problem, so ground 2 passes. The board does not model parts. My last numbers are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, shops waiting on parts rather than capacity, castings +40%, 60% of the fleet in the latest configuration. The CFO projected about 350 AOG through 2026 [PX-0300]. The AOG trend, hot-section parts and MRO slots for 2030 are not in my evidence, and I will not invent them. Development to 2036 draws engineers and test hardware, not production castings. The squeeze is the GTF2 production ramp from 2036 alongside NGSA's: the powder-metal escape came from a ramp [P-1040]. Condition (inference): fleet spares rank ahead of GTF2 installs on the pacing-parts list.
(5) Engineering load in S5: one development ($2B, about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2036) and two installs, NGSA in 2037 plus fps in 2040, or both in 2037 if the fps is a 7-yr. No second programme while the Joint Venture is at `hold`. There is no strain charge on the board, so this is advice and it passes.
(6) Veto rulings. Row A: passes both grounds. Row B: passes both, though it misses the cycle (not my ground). Rows C and E: pass both grounds (ready 2036, no live problem), so no binding veto, but I do not propose them because the engine would have no customer. Row D: passes both grounds, but the Joint Venture conditions fail. No binding veto on any row.
(7) The kit: yes, as a public other move at standard terms, pass-through pricing and no free upgrade [PX-0100][PX-0117]. Report the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration [PX-0116], not a dated AOG recovery, because my dated recoveries slipped [PX-0115]. The kit's hot-section parts are themselves pacing parts, so fleet first.

ops.memo:
The bad number first: an NGSA in service in 2037 without us costs $19.49B, our 40% of the A320neo slot. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late for any airframe launched this year.

I propose `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Triggered in 2030, GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, four inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer. One year is my minimum, not a cushion: my Advantage certification went from mid-2024 to 2025. So no EIS promise before launch plus six, all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, time on wing ahead of fuel burn, and no compressed testing to hold a date. If the 2035 test data say 2036 is slipping, you hear it from me first.

Parts: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem, so ground 2 passes; the board does not model parts. Development draws engineers, not castings. The squeeze comes with the production ramp from 2036, and fleet spares stay ahead of new installs.

No binding veto on any row. I do not propose an unconditional launch: no customer. The Joint Venture stays at hold: Rolls-Royce is not on the record, and our gear is not on the table.

The kit: yes, public, standard terms, reported by configuration percentage, not a dated AOG promise.

My record is one event, June 2023, before the recall. Where it is silent, this is the seat's doctrine.

It is sold at standard terms with pass-through pricing: no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We report progress as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration, not as a dated AOG recovery (Eddy's advice; my own dated recoveries have slipped) [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Development to 2036 draws engineers and test hardware, not production castings. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. Eddy's condition is adopted as written.

other_moves.detail: This is internal. If GTF2 has triggered, Eddy reports severe-environment endurance test data and maturity gates against the 2036 ready date before the 2035 round, and the bad number comes first. We do not compress testing to hold the date. On the Joint Venture, we revisit only if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). The gear and core technology are never on the table [P-1233].

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The last few years on the GTF fleet were hard on our customers, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine.

Here is our commitment. In any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney for a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside a partner, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan that same round. It is planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036 for a commitment made this year. Its durability will be proven before it enters service. That means time on wing ahead of fuel burn in the specification, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet, also at standard terms. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. This is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and it matches my frame. Premium $0.00B. `overrides` is empty.

Team rule, step by step.
(1) Start from Eddy's proposal, row A ("GTF2 Solo if selected"): 0 / +5.59 / −19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −19.49 / 0. The Board item set back to `hold` is 0 / −19.49 / −19.49 / −2.48 / −19.49 / −19.49 / 0.
(2) Strike plans that fail a binding veto. Mitchill's ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine) binds against an unconditional `launch` (rows C and E). His ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven) binds against any `jv_with_rr: commit` (rows D and E, and hold plus commit). I accept both. Neither is on a ground I would contest, and the rule gives me no override. Eddy raises no binding veto on any row. Row A passes all six ExCo grounds.
(3) Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2036. That is one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, and four years inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. Eddy's binding check passes. I note my own bias here: my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104], and Eddy's slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years. So I do not lean on the one-year margin. I write in his conditions: time on wing and LLP life ahead of fuel burn, severe-environment endurance testing before certification, full-life parts at EIS, a weekly drumbeat on maturity gates, and no compressed testing. The public statement says "planned", not a promise.
(4) Optimise inside the constraint. On my weights, expected ΔPV is: A −2.49 (+7.51 against hold); C −3.12; C with the 2035 cancel −2.99; D −2.69; hold −9.99. A is the best row on my weights, on Mitchill's (A −4.24, +5.63 against hold) and on equal weights (+8.93). It is also never below hold in any column, so it clears the return hurdle on any weights.
(5) Visible-demand test [PX-0109][PX-0009]. `launch_if_selected` spends only if a live airframe selects a code with P&W (2, 6 or 7) this round. The commitment arrives with the demand. The edge of `launch` over `launch_if_selected` is 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)]. On my weights that is −0.63 (−0.50 with the 2035 cancel at $1.67B); Mitchill gets −0.67 (−0.53) and equal weights give −0.36. Break-even needs 64% on S6 against S1 plus S7, and the Board needs 80%. The hedge fails, and no premium can buy it.
(6) Miss-a-cycle test [PX-0071]. That line was said of RTX's businesses in general, so applying it to GTF2 is inference. Any column where NGSA enters service without us costs −19.49, about 18% of EV. This round is the only one that can serve an airframe launched in 2030: a GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late. `launch_if_selected` answers that test at zero cost unless we are selected. The S3 and S6 losses come from Airbus's selection, not from our order. An unconditional launch only moves them to −19.12 and −18.35. We answer that with product, not price [PX-0055].
(7) Joint Venture: `hold`. Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the public record, and no live airframe has a code that includes Rolls-Royce. A commit is worth 0 in S1 to S6 and −2.00 in S7. My record is silent here, so this is doctrine [P-1233] plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback requires.
(8) Dividend and debt [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. A triggered GTF2 is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035, or 5.6% of the roughly $6B self-funded envelope, even in S5. Mitchill confirms the dividend stays covered and the pre-ASR debt path is untouched.
(9) Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. There is no discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement. The kit is sold at standard terms.

Doctrine relief, declared at $0. A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted against the sole-source red line [P-0746]. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we aimed at about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. That is inference.

Not booked. Three things are excluded from every number above:
- the S3 code switch (Airbus moving NGSA to a P&W code in 2035, where only a GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready by 2037);
- any Rolls-Royce commitment or 2035 Joint Venture fold-in (Eddy's door through a Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB solo launched in 2030 has zero margin and is Rolls-Royce's architecture);
- any durability gain from the kit.

Booked number in S1: $0.00B.

Round 2 contingencies, written in now:
- If GTF2 triggered, it is never cancelled while the selecting airframe is live.
- No untriggered GTF2 can exist under this order, so there is nothing to carry and nothing to cancel in S1, S3, S6 or S7.
- The Joint Venture is reopened only on Rolls-Royce's public commitment or a live code of 1, 4, 5 or 7.

Where the record is thin: my launch behaviour is rated Medium (I have made no launch decision), so the thresholds here are inference. The Joint Venture position is doctrine, not my record.

They still put row A first, at −4.24 expected and +5.63 against hold, and never below hold. His ground-2 veto on an unconditional `launch` is binding and correct: the edge is −0.67, or −0.53 with the cancel, and break-even needs 64% on S6. His ground-4 veto on `commit` is binding and correct. I accept both, with no override. His envelope check ($0.33B a year, 5.6% of about $6B) and the dividend and debt confirmation clear my 'is the dividend safe' test. I adopt his not-booked list as stated. I also take his advice to say 'planned' about 2036. His non-binding advice against `hold` agrees with mine.

Shane's seat rests on one event, June 2023, before the recall, so his own record is Low, and he says where he is applying the seat's doctrine instead. Readiness: his binding check passes (2036 against 2037 and 2040). I adopt his conditions on durability, severe-environment testing, full-life LLPs, maturity gates and no compressed testing. His advice of at least a one-year margin is met with nothing spare against a +1.5 to 2 year slip prior. Given my own slips, I treat that as the main execution risk and have written in a 2035 test-data gate. Parts: he does not invent a 2030 AOG figure, which is right, and passes ground 2 on the brief. CONCUR. I raise no veto and find no red-line breach.

I checked the orders as submitted: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`.

GROUND 1, DURABILITY AND READINESS: PASS. GTF2 is ready 6 years after launch (rules.md), so a 2030 trigger is ready in 2036. The airframes a 2030 launch could reach enter service in:

- 2040: fps 10-yr (S4, S5) and Embraer. That leaves 4 years.
`launch_if_selected` only triggers if GTF2 would be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS (rules.md), so this order cannot put GTF2 on an airframe early. One year against 2037 meets my advisory minimum with nothing to spare: my Advantage certification slipped from mid-2024 to 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785]. The 2035 test-data gate is how we watch that risk. The fleet-first rule on pacing parts from the 2036 ramp was adopted as I wrote it. My last numbers are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG and about 30 pacing parts [PX-0120][PX-0123]. I have no 2030 figure and I have not made one up.

STATEMENT, CHECKED AGAINST GROUND 1: PASS.
- "Planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036" is launch plus six, with no earlier date.
- "Will be proven before it enters service" is a future condition, not a claim that durability is already proven.
- Life-limited parts are at full life at EIS [PX-0128].
- The statement gives no airframer date.

ADVICE, NOT BINDING:

recommendations.text: Disclosure: tighten the public statement before release. It says P&W will launch 'in any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney'. The order triggers only if GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's EIS: a 2035 selection for a 2037 EIS would not trigger, because a 2035 launch is ready in 2041. Mitchill and Eddy both advised the qualifier 'where it can be ready by the aircraft's entry into service', and it is not in the final text. Add it. Also consider replacing 'alongside a partner' with 'alongside another engine maker', so the line is not read as a Joint Venture signal that is not on the record. And consider Eddy's 'from the industrial gaps on the GTF' in place of 'the prior iterations of the GTF', which keeps the ownership on industrial performance rather than the architecture. This is not a veto ground.

Durability gate to the Board. If GTF2 triggers, Eddy should report before the 2035 round, through the Governance and Public Policy Committee, which holds product safety and quality: severe-environment endurance data, maturity gates and LLP life against the 2036 ready date. The margin to a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS is one year, against his own +1.5 to 2 year slip prior. The bad number comes first, and testing is never compressed to hold the date. Time on wing comes before fuel burn in the specification.

If it triggers, write the programme discipline in now. The selecting airframe is live, so a triggered GTF2 is not cancelled while that airframe is live. Finance should review the programme's whole-life NPV against the hurdle each year, as UTC's board did in 2017. The fleet-first rule on pacing parts from the 2036 ramp, adopted internally, is endorsed: the fleet beats a new engine.

Prepare the 2035 contingency, but do not book it. In S3 and S6, NGSA would be live on code 5, which includes Rolls-Royce. That meets the first condition of the Board's Joint Venture test in 2035. Before that round, bring the Finance Committee the full case: whether Rolls-Royce launched an UltraFan NB in 2030 (public record only); its ready year against a 2037 EIS; the code change to 4 or 7 that P&W would need and that is not on the record; Eddy's durability check on a folded engine of Rolls-Royce architecture, which he puts at zero margin; and protection of P&W's gear and core technology. The weighted item value must still be at least 0, or within a declared premium of no more than $0.5B.

Miss a cycle, carried forward. If no selection triggers GTF2 in 2030, the Board expects `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` again in 2035 wherever a live airframe's EIS is 2041 or later (for example an fps or NGSA launched in 2035). An unconditional `launch` stays off unless a P&W selection is on the public record, or the franchise-defence edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least +$0.5B on Mitchill's weights.

Dividend and debt path. In 2035, Mitchill should report actual triggered spend against the ~$6B self-funded envelope and confirm that the dividend stays covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path. The Board notes that the S3/S6 exposure, about −19.49 or 18% of EV, cannot be hedged by any P&W order on the grid. That is a reason to keep the balance sheet whole, not to stretch it.

Other moves are endorsed as submitted. The GTF Advantage kit stays at standard terms with pass-through pricing, and progress is reported as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration, not as a dated AOG recovery. No launch-style discount is to be offered to buy a selection, and a rival's price does not move the answer.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us, where seven years of development fit before its entry into service. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't compress maturity for anyone. Partnership is our preference, not our need: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit the round they do. UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

DECISION (team rule: the CEO proposes and decides; tie-break CEO). Orders: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected; jv_with_pw hold; ultrafan_wb hold; t1000_upgrade hold. This is my framing proposal unchanged. McCabe co-signs launch_if_selected. Watson concurs, with no Civil veto, provided the support plan is in the package, and it is (other moves). Overrides: none.

GRID, ROW WITH AND WITHOUT EACH BOARD ITEM. The only Board item is ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected.
- 'UltraFan NB if selected', S1-S9: 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.

It fails airframers first and the +$2B team bar. McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding), and the Board vetoes it.

- UltraFan WB. Expected -3.54; worst -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record, and the gap is above the $1B sub-cap. Beside launch_if_selected it is -9.00 in S2, S4 and S5. McCabe withholds (binding), and the Board vetoes.

THE UPGRADE: DEFERRED, NOT DROPPED. This flips my profile's round-1 default, which assumes no UltraFan is due. Here launch_if_selected is ordered, so the red line binds. The upgrade alone is -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9 (expected -0.88). It earns nothing before the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none). On record it would put a permanent $5B strain on any later Solo or Joint Venture. Choosing it over launch_if_selected would cost $2.25B on base weights against the PV-best plan, and $3.73B (above the cap) on the selection-0.2 case. I want 787 share back, "Why not?" [RX-0101], but on a date it pays. I re-test it in 2035 or in the round a Re-engine is on the record, with no UltraFan in development or ordered.

READINESS (Watson). A trigger in 2030 is ready in 2037: zero margin against an NGSA or 7-year fps (2037) and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps (2040). The order fires only if the engine is ready by EIS, so it cannot fit a late engine. Zero margin is a pacing note: we hold 2037 and never compress. Watson's 'one window' point decides the timing. If we hold now, a 2035 trigger is ready in 2042 and misses every 2030-launched airframe. So waiting is not neutral on the objective, even though it is neutral on PV in S1.

BOUNDED NARROWBODY RISK LINE ($4B, brief §2). A triggered Solo spends $8B, about £0.84bn a year for 2030-36 at 1.36 $/£, or 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn. That breaks our own $4B line, but only in S2, S4 and S5, where the row is worth +12.53, +9.52 and +23.13. In the other six columns the line holds at $0.
- I accept the breach because it is selection-backed: an airframer has gone first [RX-0058]. That is inference on my part; my record has no narrowbody launch threshold. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope.
- No balance-sheet veto is invoked: no equity, no new borrowing, leverage unchanged. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn 2026-28 buyback are untouched, since that buyback ends before any trigger spend.
- Fold route, stated plainly. If triggered and P&W then commits, we judge a jv_with_pw commit on the 2035 grid against the same row without it. Spend to date would be $5.71B: the fold saves the $2.29B not yet spent and writes off $1.71B. It cannot bring us back inside $4B. Once Solo spend passes $4B, after 3.5 years, the line is breached for good in that column.
- The Joint Venture is the only route that stays inside $4B, which is why it stays open by public invitation.

PREMIUM. $0. launch_if_selected is the PV-best plan on both weight sets (next best is launch_if_selected + commit, at +0.98 / +2.49). No narrowbody premium is carried. No widebody shortfall is incurred.

COMPANY RED-LINE CHECK ON THE FINAL ORDERS. All pass.

- No disclosed EIS before launch + 7. The statement says 'no earlier than seven years' and gives no airframer dates.
- No Joint Venture commit before P&W.

rolls_royce.predictions:
The grid is read as given: conservative demand, Boeing losing 1 pp a year after NGSA EIS while no fps is in service, Airbus's unmet demand going to Boeing, Airbus adding 1% capacity a year when short, and the 737 MAX and A320neo keeping their engines. My predictions:
1. Most likely, no airframer launches in 2030 (S1, about 0.30). The backlog runs to about 2035 and the A320neo is selling out, so Airbus has little reason to hurry the NGSA.
2. If an airframer launches, it most likely stays with its incumbent CFM or P&W codes (S3 or S6, about 0.35 together). An RR selection is about 0.10 in total: S2 0.05, S4 0.03, S5 0.02.
3. P&W does not commit to the Joint Venture this round (S7 about 0.10). Its incentive grows once an NGSA or fps engine competition is live.
4. A 787 Re-engine is possible but not likely in 2030 (S8 about 0.10, S9 about 0.05). If one is announced, I re-test UltraFan WB, or the upgrade, against hold in that round.
5. No rival announces anything that forces an RR response this round. Our expected ΔPV is +1.37 $B, with a range of 0 to +23.13.
6. Next round (2035) I expect the narrowbody question to be live. If no 2030 airframe selected us, a 2035 launch_if_selected remains the default for any new airframe whose EIS is at least seven years out. If triggered, the Joint Venture fold is judged on the 2035 grid.

The engine also has to be ready in time for a 10-year or Embraer fps (EIS 2040). No disclosed EIS may come earlier than launch plus 7 years (plus 6 for the Joint Venture or UltraFan WB), and a support plan must be in place before EIS [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284, R-0970].

2. An airframe comes first. The bulletin shows no fps, NGSA or Re-engine and no Joint Venture commitment. Narrowbody therefore goes only through `launch_if_selected` this round: no unconditional launch, no Joint Venture commitment before P&W's, and no UltraFan WB before a Re-engine [R-1005, R-0994, RX-0058, R-1010, R-1574].

3. The discipline: each item stays within its own bill in every column, and the balance sheet and the £7-9bn 2026-2028 buyback plan stay untouched. Only one big programme at a time, so `launch_if_selected` and the Trent 1000 upgrade do not go together this round [RG-0033, RX-0242, RG-0059, RG-0019, RX-0214].

4. Profit over share. A narrowbody item may carry no premium. Any widebody shortfall goes in `premium_b` with its reason: at most $3B in total, and at most $1B for an UltraFan WB [R-1561, R-1582, R-1011, RX-0213].

5. The widebody core. Trent keeps 58% in every year (the brief). The Trent 1000 upgrade is durability work worth funding when it does not close off narrowbody entry. Its timing should be argued in the package, not assumed [R-1574, RX-0246, RG-0068, RG-0021].
