board_guidance.expect_to_see:
Before we approve, the package must contain the following.
(1) For each Board item, the grid row of the submitted orders and the row with that item at `hold`, column by column for S1-S9. All nine columns are plausible in round 1 because the bulletin rules none out.
(2) The CEO's expected scenario and `predictions`. Under the ExCo rule nothing is announced, so the selection weight is 0.1. Each item's sign is the same in every column, so our verdicts do not depend on the weights; only the size of the upgrade premium does.
(3) McCabe's co-signature on every `launch`, `launch_if_selected` or `commit`, with her worst column and capex a year. At 1.36 $/£: NB Solo $8B over 7 years is about £0.84bn a year; the Joint Venture share, UltraFan WB and the upgrade (over 3 years) are each about £0.49bn a year. She should also confirm that no balance-sheet veto is invoked.
(4) Watson's ready year against each live airframe's EIS (UltraFan NB 2037 against NGSA or a 7-year fps at 2037, a zero margin, and a 10-year or Embraer fps at 2040) and his support and MRO plan before EIS.
(5) Both ExCo veto checks, with any red-line flag struck or rebutted in `rationale`, and `overrides` empty.
(6) Any widebody shortfall in `premium_b` with its reason.
(7) A public statement with no EIS earlier than launch plus development years and nothing on an airframer's dates.
(8) An explanation in `rationale` of how a triggered $8B Solo fits the bounded narrowbody risk line of $4B (brief §2), and the planned route to a Joint Venture fold.
would_approve: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`, with the other fields at hold or no widebody item. Row 'UltraFan NB if selected' against row 'UltraFan NB: hold': S1 0, S2 +12.53, S3 0, S4 +9.52, S5 +23.13, S6 0, S7 0, S8 0, S9 0. It is never below 0, so it is at least as good as hold under any weights (+1.37 on illustrative weights), and its worst column of 0 is well within −$8B. It needs no premium. It triggers only if a live airframe selects a code that includes RR and the engine is ready by EIS, so it passes the maturity and airframe tests by construction. Approval requires McCabe's co-signature.

`t1000_upgrade: launch`, but only if `ultrafan_nb_solo` and `jv_with_pw` are at hold. Row 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' against 'UltraFan NB: hold': −0.98 in S1-S7 and −0.29 in S8-S9. The worst column, −0.98, is within its −$2B bill. The shortfall (−0.29 to −0.98, about −0.88 on illustrative weights) must be declared in `premium_b` with the durability reason; it is within the $3B cap. The widebody engine share rises to 63% in 2050. We would approve this, but we recommend deferring it (see recommendations).
`jv_with_pw: commit`, in a later round, once P&W's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes P&W, and its weighted value is at least 0. It does not pass this round.
`ultrafan_wb: launch`, in a later round, once a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record and its shortfall is no more than $1B. It does not pass this round.
would_veto: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch` (unconditional). No airframe is on the public record; the bulletin shows no programme launched. It does no better than `launch_if_selected` in any column and is worse in six: S1, S7, S8 and S9 at −8.00, S3 at −3.26, S6 at −1.72. Against hold it is −4.49 on illustrative weights, so it fails the profit test and the ExCo's +$2B bar. Acceptable alternatives: `launch_if_selected`, `hold`.

`jv_with_pw: commit`. P&W's commitment is not on the public record and no live airframe carries a P&W code. Against hold the item is 0 in every column except S7, where it is −4.00: the Joint Venture forms with no airframe to fly it. Its weighted value is therefore below 0 (partner alignment and profit). With the upgrade on, S7 falls to −9.00, below its −$4B bill (reasonable worst case), and the $5B strain also applies. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`ultrafan_wb: launch`. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record (airframe test). It is −4.00 in S1-S7 and −0.90 in S8-S9. The shortfall exceeds the $1B sub-cap unless S8 and S9 together carry more than 0.97 of the weight. Beside `launch_if_selected` it is −9.00 in S2, S4 and S5, which is below its −$4B bill and also an overlap. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`t1000_upgrade: launch` together with `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected` or `launch`, or with `jv_with_pw: commit`. That breaks one big programme at a time, because an UltraFan could be triggered this round. Against row 'UltraFan NB if selected' it is −5.98 in S2, S4 and S5, below its −$2B bill (reasonable worst case). Acceptable alternative: `hold` for the upgrade.

On governance grounds, any item that: lacks McCabe's co-signature; carries a binding ExCo veto that was not respected; leaves a red-line flag unresolved; has a non-empty `overrides`; carries a widebody shortfall not declared in `premium_b`; or still stands under Watson's binding Civil veto, for example over an EIS disclosed earlier than 2037 for UltraFan NB.

recommendations.text: Lead with `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected` alone. It is the only order that can meet 'enter the narrowbody market' this round, and it costs nothing unless an airframer selects us. Selected, it is worth +12.53 (NGSA on code 7), +9.52 (fps on code 5) or +23.13 (both). This is an airframe first, in the form our doctrine prefers.

Defer the Trent 1000 upgrade to a later round. First, it cannot sit beside `launch_if_selected` this round. Second, it counts no earlier than the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if there is none), so a 2035 launch loses nothing in S1-S7 and costs only in S8-S9. Third, once the upgrade is on record, any later UltraFan NB or Joint Venture carries the $5B strain for good (brief §2), which closes off narrowbody entry. The widebody franchise test is not triggered: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, with no Re-engine on the record. If the CEO still prefers the upgrade this round, he should hold the narrowbody items and declare a premium of up to $0.98B with its durability reason, and we will approve it.

Partner first, on aligned terms. Do not commit to the Joint Venture before P&W does. In S7 a Joint Venture formed with no airframe loses $4B. Instead, invite P&W publicly to commit, and say Rolls-Royce will commit once P&W's commitment is on the record. The Joint Venture is also the only narrowbody route that stays within the $4B bounded-risk line.

Make the public statement few, conditional and binding. It should say: UltraFan NB is offered to any new narrowbody that selects Rolls-Royce and is launched in the round of selection, with EIS no earlier than launch plus 7 years (2037 for a 2030 selection); partnership is our preference and the Joint Venture is open to P&W; UltraFan WB will be launched in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced. It should say nothing on an airframer's dates.

Treat the zero margin as a maturity issue. An NGSA or a 7-year fps launched in 2030 enters service in 2037, the same year UltraFan NB would be ready. Watson should state the test pacing and a support and MRO plan before EIS, since we have no narrowbody MRO scale. If the engine is triggered, he must not compress its maturity to meet the date.

Size each item to its reasonable worst case, not the base case. McCabe should show each item's worst column and its capex a year against FY2026 free cash flow guidance of £3.6-3.8bn. A triggered Solo is about £0.84bn a year. She should confirm that the 30-40% dividend and the £7-9bn buyback plan are untouched. If a Solo is triggered, the rationale should set out how it would fold into a Joint Venture to bring our own narrowbody money back toward $4B.

The run's demand and capacity assumptions are already in the grid: the conservative demand case, Boeing losing 1 pp a year after NGSA EIS while it has no fps in service, Airbus's unmet demand going to Boeing, and Airbus adding 1% capacity a year when short. Our narrowbody volumes follow aircraft actually delivered, while the 737 MAX and A320neo keep their engines. The CEO's `predictions` should therefore be read against the grid as given, not adjusted outside the brief.

frame.question: So, the question for 2030 is about cash and the quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. No airframe is on the public record. Do we put any Rolls-Royce money at risk this round? I see two candidates. (a) A conditional narrowbody commitment, UltraFan NB launch_if_selected. It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us, and it is the only order that can deliver 'enter the narrowbody market'. (b) The Trent 1000 upgrade. It loses money in every column on this board, and it would put a permanent $5B strain charge on any later narrowbody entry. Everything else waits for an airframer or for P&W's commitment: "we need airframers, obviously, to go there first" [RX-0058]. Narrowbody is optional: "We won't do anything not profitable" [RX-0058, RX-0075]. One more question has to be answered now. A triggered Solo spends $8B against our own $4B bounded-risk line. Do we accept that if an airframer picks us?
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 1). No programme has been launched. There is no fps, no NGSA, no 787 or A350 Re-engine and no P&W Joint Venture commitment. Everyone flies today's products. Observed 2026-29: NB airframes Boeing 39.4% / Airbus 60.6%; WB 787 58.8% / A350 41.2%; NB engines CFM 75.8% / P&W 24.2% / RR 0%; WB engines GE 42% / RR 58%. Production plans: Airbus A320 at 85 a month until NGSA, then the base wind-down plan; Boeing fps at new sites.

MARKET RULES IN THIS RUN (as given in the grid). Demand is the conservative case: 1,406 aircraft in 2030, 1,724 in 2035, 2,019 at the 2045 peak, 1,852 in 2050. Firm backlog is 4,769 MAX and 7,330 A320neo, lasting to about 2035. Boeing loses 1 pp a year from NGSA EIS while no fps is in service. Customers Airbus cannot serve buy from Boeing. Airbus adds 1% capacity a year when short. Our narrowbody volumes follow aircraft actually delivered. The 737 MAX and A320neo keep their engines, so our moves reach only the fps and NGSA as they ramp.

WHAT A 2030 AIRFRAME WOULD MEAN FOR US. An NGSA launched 2030 enters service in 2037. An fps on a 7-year ramp enters in 2037; on a 10-year ramp or via Embraer, in 2040. UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against NGSA or a 7-year fps, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps. A Joint Venture formed in 2030 would be ready in 2036. A 787 or A350 Re-engine enters service 5 years after launch, so 2035 at the earliest. UltraFan WB launched in 2030 is ready in 2036 and counts only once a Re-engine is in service. The upgrade counts no earlier than the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none).

OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief §2):
- Enter NB: NOT MET (0% in 2045 and 2050).
- Keep WB dominance: MET (58% in every year; worst year 58.0%).
- Bounded NB risk (own NB money ≤ $4B): MET ($0).
- WB never starved (no NB and WB programme both on record; one-off $5B strain, permanent unless one is cancelled before it is ready): MET ($0).

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto follows). Risk appetite is 4 of 5.
- It would approve launch_if_selected alone (needs McCabe's co-signature).
- It would approve the upgrade alone with a declared premium, but recommends deferring it.
- It would veto: an unconditional Solo; a Joint Venture commit before P&W's; UltraFan WB with no Re-engine; the upgrade beside any UltraFan order; and any item whose worst column exceeds its own bill.
levers_in_play: ultrafan_nb_solo: hold | launch | launch_if_selected. $8B over 7 years (about £0.84bn a year at 1.36 $/£); ready 7 years after launch, so 2037 for a 2030 launch. RR +15 pp of NB engines once fitted to an fps or NGSA in service. launch_if_selected triggers only if a live airframe not yet in service selects a code with RR this round and the engine is ready by its EIS. Otherwise nothing is spent.

jv_with_pw: hold | commit. $4B RR share (about £0.49bn a year over 6 years). Public and standing at once. Forms only when P&W has also committed; ready 6 years after formation. RR and P&W each +5 pp NB, CFM −10 pp, then equal NB shares. A live Solo folds in, and its spend beyond $4B is written off.

ultrafan_wb: hold | launch. $4B over 6 years (about £0.49bn a year). RR +10 pp WB from CFM, counting only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. With no Re-engine the R&D is spent for nothing. Exclusive with the upgrade.

t1000_upgrade: hold | launch. $2B over 3 years (about £0.49bn a year). RR +5 pp WB, counting 3 years after launch and not before the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none). Raises WB share to 63% in 2050.

Strain: $5B one-off whenever an NB programme (Solo or Joint Venture) and a WB programme (UltraFan WB or upgrade) are both on record. It applies whatever their dates and even after one is ready; only cancelling one before it is ready removes it.
cancel: not available this round (nothing launched).
options_to_test: WEIGHTS. Base weights for S1-S9: 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.20 / 0.03 / 0.02 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05. The selection weight (S2+S4+S5) is 0.10 because nothing is announced. All gains below are against the 'UltraFan NB: hold' row, which is 0 in every column.
A. Do Nothing (all hold). 0 in every column; worst 0. It passes on cash, but the NB-entry objective stays unmet with no route open. It is the fallback, not the plan.

B. ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected alone (LEAD). S2 +12.53, S4 +9.52, S5 +23.13; 0 in S1, S3 and S6-S9. Expected +1.37 (base) or +2.89 (selection 0.2); worst 0, well within the −$8B bill. Four-part gate: passes by construction when triggered. Differentiated: UltraFan is 10% better. Large market: NB. Viable: we spend only against a selection. Synergy: shared UltraFan technology. Premium 0. One issue: a triggered Solo is $8B, against the $4B bounded-risk line.

C. hold + t1000_upgrade. −0.98 in S1-S7, −0.29 in S8-S9; expected −0.88 (base), −0.84 (sel 0.2); worst −0.98, within the −$2B bill. WB share rises to 63% in 2050. Gate: it fails a viable business model this round, being negative in every column. It is also the only order that blocks NB entry: any later Solo or Joint Venture carries the $5B strain for good. D. launch_if_selected + t1000_upgrade. Expected −0.00 (base); worst −0.98. In S2, S4 and S5 it gives +6.55, +3.54 and +17.15, which is −5.98 against B ($5B strain plus the upgrade). It breaks the red line on an upgrade while an UltraFan is ordered, and the Board vetoes it. Tested only to show the cost. STRIKE.

E. ultrafan_nb_solo: launch (unconditional). −8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9; −3.26 in S3; −1.72 in S6; positive only in S2, S4 and S5. Expected −3.94 (base), −2.18 (sel 0.2); worst −8.00. It fails airframers-first, fails the +$2B team bar, and is no better than B in any column. Speculative. STRIKE.

F. jv_with_pw: commit (alone or with B). Against the same row without it: 0 everywhere except S7, at −4.00 (the Joint Venture forms with no airframe). Expected −0.40; worst −4.00. P&W's commitment is not on the record, so it breaks partner-first and the Board vetoes it. Replace it with a public invitation to P&W. STRIKE this round.

G. ultrafan_wb: launch. −4.00 in S1-S7, −0.90 in S8-S9; expected −3.54; worst −4.00. Beside B it gives −9.00 against B in S2, S4 and S5. No Re-engine is on the record, the shortfall exceeds the $1B sub-cap, and it overlaps. STRIKE.
red_lines: Safety and maturity first [RX-0053]. Never disclose an EIS earlier than launch + 7 years for UltraFan NB (2037 for a 2030 launch), or + 6 for the Joint Venture or UltraFan WB [R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296]. Never compress maturity to meet an airframer's date.
Airframers first. No unconditional UltraFan NB launch without an RR selection on the public record. In round 1 there is none, so launch_if_selected or hold only [RX-0058, R-1005, R-0994].
Partner first. No jv_with_pw commit until P&W's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes P&W (Board veto) [RX-0118, R-1010].
No UltraFan WB without a 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. Any WB shortfall goes in premium_b: at most $3B in total, at most $1B for UltraFan WB [R-1574].

One big programme at a time. No t1000_upgrade in any round where an UltraFan is in development, launched or ordered launch_if_selected. No UltraFan WB and NB Solo together unless both are selected. The $5B NB+WB strain is permanent once both are on record (Board veto; profile red line).

Each item's worst column stays within its own bill: Solo −$8B, Joint Venture −$4B, UltraFan WB −$4B, upgrade −$2B (Board). A narrowbody item needs a weighted value of at least 0 against hold, and carries no premium.
cancel only a programme no live airframe flies (nothing to cancel this round).
No options management. Nothing standing that no airframe can use [RX-0051, R-1573].
Balance sheet (McCabe's vetoes): no equity raise; leverage no higher than about 1.5x; no levering for buybacks. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn 2026-28 buyback stay untouched.
Governance: McCabe co-signs every launch, launch_if_selected or commit [RX-0213, R-1579]; overrides stay empty; every red-line flag is struck or rebutted in the rationale.
Public statement: conditional and binding, nothing on any airframer's dates or rates.

Helen, I need these numbers before I decide. Cash is an input, not an outcome [RX-0042].

(1) Confirm each row's expected gain over hold and its worst column, on my base weights (S1-S9: 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.20 / 0.03 / 0.02 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05; selection 0.10) and on the selection-0.2 case. My figures:
- launch_if_selected: +1.37 / +2.89, worst 0
- upgrade: −0.88 / −0.84, worst −0.98
- launch_if_selected + upgrade: −0.00, worst −0.98
- unconditional Solo: −3.94 / −2.18, worst −8.00
- Joint Venture commit: −0.40, worst −4.00
- UltraFan WB: −3.54, worst −4.00

(2) The unselected loss: 0 for launch_if_selected. For an unconditional Solo it is −8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9.

(3) Capex a year in £ at 1.36 $/£, against FY2026 free cash flow guidance of £3.6-3.8bn:
- triggered Solo: about £0.84bn a year for 7 years
- Joint Venture share, UltraFan WB or the upgrade: about £0.49bn a year each
Confirm that no balance-sheet veto is invoked, and that the 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn buyback are untouched in every column.

(4) Joint Venture against Solo: $4B against $8B. The Joint Venture halves the bill and is the only narrowbody route within the $4B bounded-risk line, but it is closed this round because P&W has not committed. Tell me the round in which a fold pays. Note the costs: a 2030 Solo folded or cancelled in 2035 carries $5.71B of spend to date. The 2035 cancel write-off on an orphan Solo is also $5.71B.

(5) The bounded-risk line. A triggered Solo breaks our own $4B narrowbody line ($8B, or $5.71B if folded in 2035) while it scores NB entry and +$9.5-23B. Will you co-sign launch_if_selected on that basis? Check it against the mid-to-high-teens hurdle on the selected columns [RX-0213, R-1579].

(6) The premium against the best grid plan. I read launch_if_selected as the best plan, so the premium is 0. If we chose the upgrade instead, the WB premium would be $0.88B. Give me your number.
frame.asks_ops:
Rob, I need these before I decide.

(1) Readiness. UltraFan NB launched 2030 is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2040. launch_if_selected triggers automatically if an airframer selects us and 2037 counts as 'ready'. So I need your answer now, not after the trigger: can we meet a 2037 EIS without compressing maturity? If not, say so, and I will not order it against a 7-year airframe [RX-0296, RX-0124]. Also give me the Joint Venture's ready year if it formed in 2030 (2036) or in 2035 (2041).

(2) Strain. With the upgrade held there is no strain this round. Confirm that the $5B NB+WB strain is permanent once both are on record. That means an upgrade now taxes every later narrowbody entry.

(3) Capacity. We have no NB MRO scale. Give me your support plan before EIS (2037 or 2040): MRO, spares and the field team. Then supplier and engineering capacity: castings, forgings and the gearbox, shared with Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work [RX-0283, RX-0284].

(4) Widebody franchise. Confirm 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on hold in every column, S8 and S9 included, and 63% with the upgrade. Is the 50% line at risk anywhere this round?

(5) Upgrade timing. It counts only from the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none). Is there a fleet durability need that forces a 2030 launch? Or does 2035, or the round a Re-engine is on the record, lose nothing? I still want 787 share back: "Why not?" [RX-0101, RX-0117]. But I want it on a date it pays.

(6) A maturity check on my draft public statement: no EIS earlier than launch plus 7 years.
frame.initial_lean:
Orders I propose (subject to McCabe's co-signature and Watson's readiness check):
- ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected
- jv_with_pw: hold
- ultrafan_wb: hold
- t1000_upgrade: hold

Why: launch_if_selected is 0 or better in every column: +12.53 if NGSA selects us, +9.52 on a 10-year fps, +23.13 on both. That is +1.37 expected at selection weight 0.1, with a worst column of 0. It honours a selection without a speculative $8B. "We don't commit that easily" [RX-0124], and this commits only when an airframer does.

I am deferring the upgrade. That is a flip from my profile's round-1 default, which assumes no UltraFan is due. On this board the upgrade is −0.98 in S1-S7 and −0.29 in S8-S9. It counts only from 2042, it cannot sit beside launch_if_selected (red line, Board veto), and it would put a permanent $5B strain on any later narrowbody entry. I want 787 share back, but not at a loss in every column and not by closing the narrowbody door. Re-test it in 2035, or in the round a Re-engine is on the record.

Joint Venture: hold. I will invite P&W publicly, as an other move. We commit in the round P&W's commitment is on the record, on terms that credit the technology we bring [RX-0118, RX-0072]. That is also the planned fold route, and the only path back toward the $4B line.

UltraFan WB: hold until a Re-engine is announced.

Premium: 0. The open point is the $4B bounded-risk line. A triggered Solo spends $8B. I lean to accept it, because it is selection-backed, scores NB entry and is worth +$9.5-23B. I want Helen's view before I decide.

Other moves, all public:
- an invitation to P&W
- standard terms ("win-win", value remunerated) through the Investment Committee
- the narrowbody demonstrator continues, self-funded

Draft public statement: "So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. Partnership is our preference: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit the round they do. UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced. We won't do anything not profitable."

Expected scenario: rivals hold, or an airframer launches on CFM or P&W; the selection weight is 0.10. Expected gain is +1.37 over hold.

tests.numbers: 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' against hold: -4.00 in S1-S7 and -0.90 in S8-S9. Expected -3.54 (base) and -3.38 (sel 0.2); worst -4.00. The gap is above the $1B sub-cap. Beside launch_if_selected, the row 'if selected + UltraFan WB' against 'if selected' is -4.00 in S1/S3/S6/S7, -9.00 in S2/S4/S5 (the $5B strain plus $4B) and -0.90 in S8-S9. Expected -4.04; worst -9.00, beyond its $4B bill.

tests.name: Hurdle (co-signature): t1000_upgrade launch
tests.threshold: The row must beat hold, or the CEO must declare the gap as a premium within $3B. No UltraFan may be in development, launched or ordered launch_if_selected (red line). The worst column must stay within the $2B bill.
tests.numbers: Alone ('hold + T1000 upgrade' against hold): -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9. Expected -0.88 (base) and -0.84 (sel 0.2); worst -0.98, within the $2B bill. It does not beat hold in any column. It could be co-signed only alone, with the gap declared as a premium (see the premium test). Beside launch_if_selected ('if selected + T1000 upgrade' against 'if selected'): S1/S3/S6/S7 -0.98, S2/S4/S5 -5.98, S8-S9 -0.29. Expected -1.38 (base) and -1.84 (sel 0.2); worst -5.98, beyond its $2B bill. The CEO's 'LIS + upgrade' figure of -0.00 against hold is confirmed (-0.002). It breaks the red line.

tests.name: Unselected downside (worst column of every row)
tests.threshold: State every row's worst column. launch_if_selected spends nothing unless triggered. An unconditional launch carries the full bill ($8B NB, $4B WB) or, on cancel, the write-off (bill x years elapsed / development years). Each item's worst column must stay within its own bill.
tests.numbers: Recommended package (launch_if_selected alone): unselected loss 0 in S1, S3 and S6-S9; worst column 0 against an $8B bill. Worst columns of the other rows against hold: upgrade -0.98 (bill $2B); LIS + upgrade -0.98 (the upgrade item against the LIS row is -5.98); unconditional Solo -8.00 in S1/S7/S8/S9 (unselected), -3.26 in S3 and -1.72 in S6; Joint Venture -4.00 in S7; UltraFan WB -4.00 in S1-S7. Cancel write-off on an orphan 2030 Solo in 2035: 8 x 5/7 = $5.71B. A Solo folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 also counts $5.71B of spend, of which $1.71B (beyond the $4B share) is written off.

tests.name: Capex a year in GBP
tests.threshold: Informational: state it. My evidence sets no threshold.
tests.numbers: At 1.36 $/GBP: a triggered Solo is $8B/7 = $1.14B, about GBP0.84bn a year for 2030-36, 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance of GBP3.6-3.8bn. The Joint Venture share and UltraFan WB are each $4B/6 = $0.67B, about GBP0.49bn a year (13-14%). The upgrade is $2B/3 = $0.67B, about GBP0.49bn a year for 3 years. Recommended package, untriggered: GBP0 a year. These ratios are inference: my evidence ends in July 2025.

tests.name: Flat R&D envelope (advice, not a sign-off ground)
tests.threshold: Report any overlap and the $5B strain the grid already includes. Red lines: no UltraFan NB Solo beside UltraFan WB unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or ordered launch_if_selected. New money is redeployed, not added (inference).
tests.numbers: Recommended package: no NB and WB programme both on record, so strain is $0 in every column (objective metrics row 'UltraFan NB if selected': $0B strain in S1-S9). The overlaps, already in the grid and not deducted again: LIS + upgrade has $5B strain in S2/S4/S5, LIS + UltraFan WB $5B in S2/S4/S5, and JV + upgrade $5B in S7. Once on record the strain is permanent, so an upgrade now taxes any later narrowbody entry. If triggered, the Solo's ~GBP0.84bn a year has to be redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not added on top of it.

tests.name: Balance sheet
tests.threshold: No equity raise; no new borrowing to rebuild the balance sheet; leverage only up to about 1-1.5x and only for the right opportunity; never lever up for buybacks (inference on this board: debt $40B on EV $110B).
tests.numbers: No balance-sheet veto is invoked. The largest item, a triggered Solo, is about GBP0.84bn a year against GBP3.6-3.8bn of FY2026 FCF guidance, so it is funded from operating cash with no equity and no borrowing, and leverage is unchanged. The 30-40% payout and the GBP7-9bn 2026-28 buyback are untouched in every column. The buyback programme ends in 2028, before any 2030 trigger spend begins (inference). The board has no cash line, so this is my judgement on the PV grid.

tests.name: Joint Venture cost against Solo
tests.threshold: Read the Joint Venture row against hold, column by column. Fold write-off and share equalisation are already in the grid and are stated only as explanation (inference).
tests.numbers: No Solo is live, so there is no fold this round. Bills: Joint Venture $4B (RR share) against Solo $8B. The Joint Venture halves the downside and is the only narrowbody route inside the $4B line, but it is closed until P&W commits. A fold after a 2030 trigger cannot get back inside $4B: Solo spend passes $4B after 3.5 years, and the next round is 2035, when spend to date is $5.71B. Folding then saves the $2.29B not yet spent ($8B - $5.71B) and writes off $1.71B, but cuts RR's NB share to P&W's level. Whether that pays shows only on the 2035 grid, against the hold row with the same other orders. I book nothing for it now.

tests.name: Bounded narrowbody risk line (brief section 2 objective; priced, not a sign-off ground)
tests.threshold: RR's own NB development money of $4B or less (Control's objective; the CEO decides any objective premium).
tests.numbers: Objective metrics, row 'UltraFan NB if selected': $0.0B in S1, S3 and S6-S9; $8.0B in S2, S4 and S5, the triggered columns. So the line breaks only where the row is worth +12.53/+9.52/+23.13, with weight 0.10 (base) or 0.20 (sensitivity). A 2035 fold or cancel still counts $5.71B. A triggered Solo carries no strain and leaves the widebody at 58%. I accept the breach because it is selection-backed. It is not a veto ground.

tests.name: Short payback first
tests.threshold: State when each order starts to earn. The brief gives no payback years (inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB: ready 2037 (launch + 7). It earns only once an fps or NGSA is in service with RR fitted: 2037 (NGSA or 7-year fps) or 2040 (10-year or Embraer fps). Joint Venture: ready 6 years after formation (2036 if formed 2030). UltraFan WB: ready 2036, earns only once a Re-engine is in service (2035 at the earliest). Upgrade: earns 3 years after launch and not before the first Re-engine EIS, so 2042 if there is none (12 years after a 2030 launch); 2035 in S8/S9. A 2035 launch would lose nothing in S1-S7.

tests.name: Premium
tests.threshold: Price every doctrine or objective premium in $B against the PV-best order. Above $3B in a round, the PV-best order applies. The Board caps a premium at $1B for UltraFan WB, and a narrowbody item carries none.
tests.numbers: launch_if_selected alone is the PV-best plan on both weight sets (+1.37 base, +2.89 sel 0.2; the next best is 'if selected + commit to JV' at +0.98 / +2.49), so the premium is $0. If the CEO chose the upgrade instead, the shortfall against hold would be $0.88B (base) or $0.84B. My number, measured against the PV-best order, is $2.25B (base: 1.37 + 0.88), within the $3B cap, or $3.73B on the selection-0.2 case, above the cap, where the PV-best order applies. The Board's $0.98B limit is measured against hold. A narrowbody item may carry no premium.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_nb_solo: launch (unconditional)
vetoes.ground: Hurdle and unselected downside. Expected -3.94 (base) and -2.18 (sel 0.2) against the +$2B bar. Worst -8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9, with no selection on the record. It is no better than launch_if_selected in any column (-5.31 expected against it). I withhold my co-signature.

vetoes.plan: jv_with_pw: commit (this round)

vetoes.ground: Advice only: defer. It loses in every column (-0.98 S1-S7, -0.29 S8-S9; -0.88 expected), earns nothing before 2042 without a Re-engine, and would put a permanent $5B strain on any later narrowbody entry. No binding veto.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Delivered numbers and an announced customer. (1) If an airframer names UltraFan on the public record (P about 0.6), an unconditional Solo could clear the +$2B bar: for example, 0.6 x 12.53 + 0.4 x (-3.26) = +6.21 on this grid's columns, re-tested on that round's grid. (2) If P&W's commitment is on the public record and the 'commit to JV' row beats hold with the same other orders, I co-sign the commit. That is also the fold test, judged on the 2035 grid with $5.71B of Solo spend to date. (3) If a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record and the UltraFan WB row beats hold, or its gap is within $1B, I co-sign it. (4) If a Re-engine EIS brings the upgrade's earning date forward so that its row beats hold, or its gap fits a declared premium within $3B, with no UltraFan in development or ordered, I co-sign the upgrade (re-test in 2035). (5) If Watson says a 2037 EIS cannot be met without compressing maturity, I defer to his veto on launch_if_selected against a 7-year airframe. (6) If FY free cash flow fell well below the GBP3.6-3.8bn guidance, so that GBP0.84bn a year put the payout or investment grade at risk, I would revisit even a triggered Solo.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet, then distributions, then investment. Tested in that order, this round is straightforward.

launch_if_selected is the one order I co-sign. It is zero in six columns and +9.5 to +23.1 in the three where an airframer picks us: +1.37 on Tufan's weights, +2.89 at a selection weight of 0.2, worst column zero against an $8B bill. I confirm his figures. On a stylised profile the selected columns clear our mid-to-high-teens hurdle, roughly 21-28%. But the board values lifecycle revenue, not margin, and engine-launch economics is not where my record is deep. Hold that as direction, not a number.

Triggered, it is about £0.84bn a year for seven years, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance. No equity, no new borrowing, no balance-sheet veto; the 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn buyback are untouched in every column. It does break our own $4B narrowbody line: $8B, or $5.7B if folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. I accept that only because it is selection-backed, and the money is redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, not added.

I would withhold my signature on an unconditional Solo (−3.94, worst −8.00), a Joint Venture commit before P&W's (worst −4.00), UltraFan WB (−3.54), and the upgrade beside any UltraFan (−5.98 against its $2B bill). The upgrade alone loses in every column; choosing it over launch_if_selected costs $2.25B. Defer it.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready (launch + 7) no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin against NGSA or a 7-year fps is a pass with a note. A later trigger, or a Joint Venture formed later with no folded Solo ready in time, fails. A fail is advice, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: launch_if_selected in 2030: ready in 2030+7 = 2037. NGSA launched 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0, pass, noted. A 7-year fps launched 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0, pass, noted. A 10-year or Embraer fps launched 2030 has EIS 2040: margin 3 years, pass. The order fires only if the engine is ready by the EIS, so it cannot fit a late engine. One window only: if we hold now, a 2035 trigger is ready in 2042, after both 2037 and 2040, so a 2030-launched airframe is lost to UltraFan NB (advice). Joint Venture: formed 2030, ready 2036; formed 2035, ready 2041, which misses 2037 and 2040 unless a folded 2030 Solo (ready 2037) carries it, as the bulletin would show. UltraFan WB launched 2030 is ready in 2036 and counts only from a Re-engine EIS (2035 at the earliest). The upgrade counts no earlier than the first Re-engine EIS, or 2042 if there is none.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB, 2037 for 2030), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB, 2036 for 2030) or formation + 6 (Joint Venture, 2036 if formed 2030, 2041 if formed 2035), unless a folded Solo gives an earlier date shown in the bulletin.
tests.numbers: CEO's draft statement: 'Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch', which is 2037 for 2030. It gives no Joint Venture or UltraFan WB date and no airframer dates. Pass. Advice, not a veto ground: qualify 'any new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us' with 'where seven years of development fit before its entry into service'. A 2035 selection by a 2030 airframe could not be met (2042 against 2037 or 2040), and the line should not read as a promise to meet that airframer's date.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale. A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (2037, or 2040 on a 10-year or Embraer fps), and must be in the package for any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit.
tests.numbers: Pass on the plan set out here, provided the package carries it. Partner-shop MRO network on the Singapore joint-venture model, with repair technology invested in those shops. Spares and lease-engine pool. An EIS field team able to respond quickly in the early years. All of it built inside the 7 development years and in place before EIS. The V2500 aftermarket support into the 2030s is the narrowbody base we build on (inference). With a Joint Venture, P&W's network could share the load (inference). If the package carries no support plan at the veto check, this becomes Civil veto ground (c).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Flag the $5B strain and the years of overlap whenever an NB project (Solo or Joint Venture) and a WB project (UltraFan WB or upgrade) are both on record. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or ordered.
tests.numbers: Recommended orders: one conditional NB project and no WB project, so the strain is $0 and there is no overlap. Option D (launch_if_selected + upgrade): Solo development 2030-2037 against upgrade 2030-2033 gives 2030-2033 of overlap. $5B strain in S2/S4/S5 (+6.55/+3.54/+17.15 against +12.53/+9.52/+23.13, i.e. -5.98 each). It breaks the red line. The strain is permanent once both are on record. A 2030 upgrade is ready in 2033, so on my reading it cannot be cancelled in the 2035 round, and any later Solo or Joint Venture carries $5B for good (S7 with upgrade + Joint Venture: -9.98). Option G (UltraFan WB beside launch_if_selected): $5B in S2/S4/S5, red line unless both are selected.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so this is not applicable. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and capacity at high-performing suppliers (advice).
tests.numbers: Hold: 197 WB engines a year, 2026-2060; 0 NB. If triggered, NB engine share in 2050 is 28.8% (S2), 31.6% (S4) or 51.2% (S5). My approximation, applying those shares to 2050 demand of 1,852 aircraft x 2 (not a board output), gives about 1,070, 1,170 or 1,900 NB engines a year by 2050. That is 3-6x my midterm widebody OE ramp of 300-350 a year. Advice: move castings and forgings to high-performing suppliers; size the gearbox early (a briefing constraint; P&W's gearbox could answer it through a Joint Venture, inference). Protect Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work while the NB line ramps.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection.
tests.numbers: Hold: 58.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (brief year table; worst year 58.0%), and 58.0% in 2050 in every column, S8 and S9 included. Upgrade: 63.0% in 2050. UltraFan WB: 68.0% in S8/S9 only. Even if CFM takes its single +5 pp GEnx move (public rules), RR is 53%, above the line. Note: in S8 Airbus's widebody airframe share falls from 41.2% to 25.2%, which shrinks the A350 fleet we power alone even though the board's engine share does not move. A 787 Re-engine on the record is the trigger to retest UltraFan WB. Time on wing is the lever.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: A cancelled or idle UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively only; grid values are never adjusted.
tests.numbers: No grid adjustment. The UltraFan demonstrator (run at full power) and its technology keep flowing into today's Trent fleet for time on wing whether or not the trigger fires. The in-service HP turbine blade work on the Trent 1000 and 7000 continues without the board's $2B upgrade order.

vetoes.plan: Not invoked this round. This is the standing condition for the veto check: any public statement or public other move that discloses an UltraFan NB EIS or ready date before 2037 (for a 2030 launch), a Joint Venture ready date before formation + 6, or an UltraFan WB date before launch + 6; any rationale that counts on an engine entering service before its ready year; or a launch_if_selected with no partner-shop support plan before EIS in the package.
vetoes.ground: Civil maturity, early date or no support plan. It would be binding under the team rule if I invoke it at the veto check. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). The CEO's draft statement and lean pass today, so I invoke nothing now.

vetoes.plan: Option D: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected + t1000_upgrade launch
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or ordered) and engineering load: 2030-2033 overlap and a permanent $5B strain in S2/S4/S5 (-5.98 against B). This is not my Civil veto ground. The CEO strikes it, and the Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: Option E: ultrafan_nb_solo launch (unconditional)
vetoes.ground: It is not a Civil ground: a 2030 launch is ready in 2037, uncompressed. It is advice only. No airframe is on the record, and we would build support and supplier capacity for an engine no one may fly (-8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9). The Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: Zero margin: UltraFan NB ready 2037 against an NGSA or 7-year fps EIS of 2037
vetoes.ground: A note, not a fail and not a veto. If we are triggered, the test programme is paced to 2037 and is never compressed to meet an airframer's date. If maturity slips, the engine is simply not fitted, and McCabe prices that downside.

vetoes.plan: Any later-round trigger or Joint Venture for an airframe launched in 2030
vetoes.ground: Ready by EIS fail, as advice. A 2035 UltraFan NB launch is ready in 2042 and a 2035 Joint Venture in 2041, both after the 2037 and 2040 EIS dates, unless a 2030 Solo folds in. This is not a veto ground.

vetoes.plan: Options F (jv_with_pw commit) and G (ultrafan_wb launch) this round
vetoes.ground: These are advice, not Civil grounds. F: no P&W commitment, and a Joint Venture with no airframe costs -4.00 in S7. G: no Re-engine on the record, -4.00 in S1-S7, and an overlap with launch_if_selected (red line unless both are selected). Partnership remains my preferred structure once P&W commits (inference).

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- The UltraFan test programme shows that seven years does not fit a properly paced maturity schedule. Then I would recommend hold over launch_if_selected, because the trigger cannot pick between a 2037 airframe and a 2040 one, and I will not take an engine to a date it cannot mature for.
- The package carries no partner-shop support plan before EIS. I would invoke the Civil veto on ground (c).
- The statement or other moves disclose a date earlier than 2037 (UltraFan NB), formation + 6 (Joint Venture) or launch + 6 (UltraFan WB). I would invoke the Civil veto.
- P&W's commitment appears on the record. Then I would support jv_with_pw commit, ready formation + 6 (earlier only if a folded Solo is further along).
- A 787 or A350 Re-engine appears on the record. UltraFan WB would reopen, but only if no NB Solo is in development, or both are selected.
- Named airline demand for a third narrowbody engine maker would strengthen the case for staying in.
ops.memo:
So, plainly, from the operating seat: launch_if_selected alone, with the Joint Venture, UltraFan WB and the upgrade at hold.

Readiness. Launched in 2030, UltraFan NB is ready in 2037: launch plus seven, not compressed. That's zero margin against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2040. It passes; I note the margin. If we're selected, we pace that programme properly and hold 2037, not a day earlier. If testing says it needs longer, we say so. A Joint Venture formed in 2030 is ready in 2036; formed in 2035, 2041.

Support. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so support comes through partner shops on the Singapore model: repair technology, a spares pool and an EIS field team, all in place before entry into service. That plan has to be in the package; it's the condition of my concurrence.

Load. No widebody project sits beside it, so no strain. The upgrade beside it breaks our red line and books $5B for good.

Capacity. Today we build 197 widebody engines a year. Selected, narrowbody runs to roughly 1,100-1,900 a year by 2050, three to six times our 300-350 widebody OE ramp. We need our high-performing suppliers and the gearbox sized early.

Widebody. 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column, 63% with the upgrade. The 50% line isn't at risk. Trent 1000 durability work carries on without the board order.

No Civil veto this round.

other_moves.move: Public invitation to Pratt & Whitney on the Joint Venture
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce invites P&W to commit to a narrowbody Joint Venture. Rolls-Royce commits in the round P&W's commitment is on the public record, on terms that credit the technology each side brings [RX-0118, RX-0072]. No Rolls-Royce commitment is made this round. Gating is partner first, and the Board vetoes a first commit.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan before EIS (condition of Watson's concurrence)
other_moves.detail: This sits in the package and becomes live only if launch_if_selected triggers. It sets up a partner-shop MRO network on the Singapore joint-venture model with repair technology invested in those shops, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team. All of it is built inside the seven development years and in place before any narrowbody EIS: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. It builds on the V2500 aftermarket base (inference). With a Joint Venture, P&W's network shares the load (inference) [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Supplier and engineering capacity readiness (no spend unless triggered)
other_moves.detail: Contingency plan if selected. Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, and gearbox capacity is sized early. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work is ring-fenced while a narrowbody line ramps. The narrowbody runs to roughly 1,100-1,900 engines a year by 2050 if selected (Watson's approximation, not a board output). Money is redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not added [RX-0214, RX-0284, RX-0286].

other_moves.move: Commercial discipline: standard terms through the Investment Committee
other_moves.detail: No price concessions to buy share. Any airframer or airline campaign is priced 'win-win' with value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

other_moves.move: UltraFan technology and Trent durability continue inside existing R&D
other_moves.detail: The UltraFan demonstrator programme and its technology keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing. In-service Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine durability work continues inside the existing durability budget. This is not the board's $2B t1000_upgrade order and makes no grid adjustment [RX-0123, RX-0094].

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us, where seven years of development fit before its entry into service. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't compress maturity for anyone. Partnership is our preference, not our need: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit the round they do. UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION (team rule: the CEO proposes and decides; tie-break CEO). Orders: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected; jv_with_pw hold; ultrafan_wb hold; t1000_upgrade hold. This is my framing proposal unchanged. McCabe co-signs launch_if_selected. Watson concurs, with no Civil veto, provided the support plan is in the package, and it is (other moves). Overrides: none.

GRID, ROW WITH AND WITHOUT EACH BOARD ITEM. The only Board item is ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected.
- 'UltraFan NB if selected', S1-S9: 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold', S1-S9: 0 in all nine columns.
- The gain over hold is never negative, so the row weakly dominates hold under any weights.
- Weights. Base S1-S9: 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.20 / 0.03 / 0.02 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05. The selection weight (S2+S4+S5) is 0.10 because nothing is announced. Sensitivity case, selection 0.20: 0.25 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.05 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.05.
- Expected gain: +1.37 (base) and +2.89 (sensitivity). Worst column 0, against an $8B bill. Premium 0.
- Every other order is at the hold default.

ROWS STRUCK, with the binding ground for each.
- Unconditional Solo. Expected -3.94 (base) and -2.18 (sensitivity); worst -8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9. It is no better than launch_if_selected in any column and is -5.31 against it. If an NGSA or a 7-year fps selects us, Watson should bring the test pacing to 2037 and the partner-shop support, spares and EIS field-team plan to the committee as a live programme within the first year. If an airframer selects us, bring a margin-based investment case against the mid-to-high-teens hurdle to the Audit Committee before the first full year of spend. If triggered, ring-fence Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support. Bring a supplier plan (castings, forgings, gearbox) with the first-year programme review.

Next round. Watson's 'one window' point is noted: a 2035 trigger cannot serve a 2030-launched airframe, so a 2035 launch_if_selected matters only for an airframe whose EIS is at least seven years out. Read the 2035 bulletin first. If an airframer has named another engine, do not chase it; narrowbody remains an option the company does not need. Partner first on the Joint Venture, and cancel nothing that a live airframe flies.

board_review.note: The Board approves `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. Safety comes first, and the package respects it. The engine would be ready in 2037, at launch plus seven and never compressed, with support in place before entry into service and no early date disclosed. The airframe goes first and we follow. The row is never below hold: 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is worth +1.37 on McCabe's confirmed weights, with a worst column of 0 against an $8B bill and no premium. It carries her co-signature and Watson's concurrence, and overrides is empty. We note, and accept, that a trigger breaks our own $4B narrowbody line in the very columns where it pays most; a 2035 fold cannot repair that. The upgrade rightly waits. "We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles." And we do not want to underestimate the risks: discipline now, and the growth story if an airframer chooses us.

public_statements.boeing:
Five years ago I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I'll give you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable, the 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 are flying with customers, and the balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is moving too. There will be good new engines out there. The market case for us isn't there yet. So we are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners. We won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

We turned the big ship. The job now is to keep it steady, not to swing the wheel to chase a headline.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. Our customers want more airplanes than we're building, and I understand that. I'd rather give a customer an honest delivery date than run an unstable line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep growing Charleston.

The financials will follow our production performance. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. We are taking it through certification on the clock of maturity: no test will be compressed to hold a date, and no engine will enter service before it is mature. Our engine partners CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are maturing their engines for the aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp-up. That ramp-up will be disciplined and controlled. Through the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we are securing the engines, structures and materials our own ramp-up needs. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Five years ago we said we'd commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus has committed, and so have we. Together with our partners at Safran, CFM is launching a new single-aisle engine. It builds on the hot section and the durability lessons of the LEAP fleet, and it enters service when the testing says it's ready, not before. The dates and rates for that aircraft are Airbus's to give, not ours.

We're also teaming up with Embraer. It's open, it's not exclusive, and there are no terms to talk about today. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it.

Here's what we know. Our first job is still the LEAP fleet flying today. We'll keep shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits ahead of the new-engine delivery rate, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn. Airbus has asked for long-term engine supply, and we'll work that through with them, jointly with Safran.

Here's what we don't know: how the next decade's market plays out, or when the airframers will want the next architecture. RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set the date for it.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Control what you can control. The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms, and we will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

Our next-generation geared turbofan, launched in 2030 for the new Airbus single-aisle, is planned to be ready in 2036. Its durability will be proven before it enters service: time on wing ahead of fuel burn, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. If the test data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

Today Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. This adds to our engine on the new Airbus aircraft; it is not a hedge against it. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not done so. The terms are these: risk, investment and revenue shared, and both partners on one new engine. Each partner keeps its own technology. Our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property. What each side brings counts in the share split and is not licensed. Nothing changes in the engine we are certifying.

Our next-generation engine is available to any other new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody is in development for NGSA, ready in 2037, seven years from launch. We pace it to maturity and we don't compress it for anyone. If maturity needs longer, we will say so. Support through partner shops is being built now, in place before entry into service. Partnership is our preference, not our need. NGSA already carries Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, so our Joint Venture commitment is now on the record. It forms when Pratt & Whitney joins, on terms that credit the technology each side brings. There is no change of strategy. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 MAX at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed KPI gates
boeing.detail: That is Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. No Rate Increase is on the order sheet this round. Pope's KPI check passes: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. The waiting backlog under Do Nothing reaches 540 in 2041. We tell customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line. That is stability over share, and its trigger is present [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

boeing.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; work with GE to bring the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers
boeing.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is CFM/GE's own programme, ready since 2033. This is not a 787 Re-engine order. The board does not price it.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for the NGSA ramp-up and the A320 transition
airbus.detail: Long-term agreements for NGSA engine delivery slots, anchored on CFM, with the Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce engines added as each one matures. A320neo engine slots with CFM and Pratt & Whitney, matched to the transition so that no airframe waits for an engine. NGSA wing and structures at rate, including the work packages we brought in-house. Titanium and rare earths for the combined peak, following on from the 2025 de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. All of this is for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

airbus.move: Engineering recruitment for NGSA certification and ramp-up
airbus.detail: Normal hiring and internal redeployment to staff NGSA certification and the ramp-up. It is sized so that the A320 sustaining teams and the A350 teams are not stripped [A-0366, A-0485]. It does not target any competitor's programme or staff, and it is not a Delay Tactics move.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

cfm.move: CFM answers Airbus's public request for long-term engine supply (A320neo tail and NGSA), jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: Made as CFM, jointly with Safran. Price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, on standard terms [CX-0184]. Nothing goes out in public: no price, no concession, no volume, no rate and no delivery year. Ghai's condition applies: the NGSA volume assumptions are worked with Airbus inside this answer before any number goes out. Unpriced on the board.

cfm.move: Embraer partnership announced as open and not exclusive
cfm.detail: Announced without terms: no volume, price, start year or exclusivity. No airframer is locked out (H1). It rides on the new CFM engine and adds no board R&D. Any real spend (integration or support) comes back to Ghai's capex test and to the Board before it is committed. Doctrine (profile section 6) drives this call, not my record.

cfm.move: CFM engines stay on offer to both airframers
cfm.detail: The LEAP derivative is fitted on the NGSA from its entry into service, and CFM offers its engines on any new single-aisle Boeing launches (H1). No price, terms or dates in public. Any pricing goes to Safran first.

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
cfm.detail: Funded as technology and not cancelled for cost (H5). No product launch, and no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public (H6, Ali's advice). The airframers set the date for the architecture.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit across the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing: no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. We give no dated AOG recovery, because my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0098][PX-0104]. We publish no fleet figure we do not have (Eddy's advice). The kit's hot-section parts are pacing parts and are ranked fleet first. It changes no payoff on the board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture commitment terms, published with the commitment
pratt_whitney.detail: Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Terms: risk, investment and revenue are shared. Both partners work on one new engine [P-1875]. Each partner keeps its own technology. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property [P-1233]. What each side brings is recognised only as a valuation in the share split. No licence or rights over our gear or core pass to the partner. No cash payment goes to the partner. Formation changes nothing in the configuration being certified for the new Airbus aircraft; partner content can enter only after entry into service, as an engineering change with its own test evidence. Pratt & Whitney signs durability only on an engine it has tested. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not committed. The commitment stands until withdrawn. We claim no formation date, Joint Venture ready date or share gain.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture commitment on the record, and a correction of the round-1 note
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce's commitment to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney is on the record from this round. It forms when Pratt & Whitney joins, on terms that credit the technology each side brings [RX-0118, RX-0072]. Correction of our round-1 note ('the Board vetoes a first commit'): our partner test asks for P&W's commitment on the record or a live airframe whose engine selection already includes P&W. NGSA's selection now carries both P&W and Rolls-Royce, so the test is met. Under sealed orders, 'we commit the round they do' can only be honoured by standing committed. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098]. No Joint Venture date of any kind is given.

rolls_royce.move: Commercial discipline: standard terms through the Investment Committee
rolls_royce.detail: No price concessions, no earlier dates and no launch-style terms to buy share or an airframer's confidence. Campaigns are priced 'win-win' with value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097]. Our answer to doubts about readiness is maturity shown in tests.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan technology and Trent durability continue inside existing R&D
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan development and demonstrator technology keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing. Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine durability work continues inside the existing durability budget [RX-0123]. This is not the board's t1000_upgrade order and makes no grid adjustment.

boeing.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine study warm on the GEnx route; launch nothing
boeing.detail: Durability first [BX-1298]. It comes back in 2045 only if no A350 Re-engine is on the public record (H3, second half). It must also be H4-legal against any 2045 fps with Pope's slip slack shown: a 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years with no slack and cannot pair with a 2045 7-year. If it is ever launched: a public EIS with buffer (Malave: 2042 public, 2040 internal) and risk-share terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

boeing.move: Prepare the 2045 fps case; do not announce it
boeing.detail: The 10-year ramp, at Renton, with Pope's MAX wind-down plan. She signs it only once the fps ramp covers MAX demand above Everett's 180 a year. Code 7 (CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB) is under test. It replaces my Code 3 inference, which was Low. Three installations are paced so certification never runs concurrent with production [BX-1263]. Development terms are cost-plus or risk-share. The package carries Malave's eight items: the row against Do Nothing in every column with the buffer test; the Do Nothing erosion year by year to 2060; the bill and its cash by year against base and stress FCF; the stress net-debt peak; the long-run split each EIS implies (35/65 for 2052, 32/68 for 2055); the full cost of a slip at +3 years; the value of waiting to 2050; and every premium. No date before launch [B-2315].

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot; keep the LEAP-1B allocation reviews running
boeing.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. CFM supplies the MAX as sole source, plus Airbus's longer A320 tail and NGSA from 2037, so we measure allocation [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure (company doctrine [B-1923]).

airbus.move: Board paper: cash line, sizing of the supply agreements and Audit Committee tracking
airbus.detail:
NGSA cost to complete is 2 x $5.074B = $10.148B over 2035-36, against the $5.2B line.
- Alt pre-EIS spend: at most $0.10B a year.
- Alt pre-EIS spend plus all long-term-agreement prepayments: at most $0.126B in total in each of 2035 and 2036.
- If the agreements need more than $0.026B of prepayment, the Alt spend moves after EIS, or the slots are signed without prepayment, rather than breach the line.
- Alt $0.75B: phased over 2037-44.

Sizing, for the ECSC check:
- NGSA engines: 56 (2038), 1,170 (2041), 2,402 (2044).
- With the A320 tail: 2,770 engines in 2044, 36% above today's 2,040.
- Titanium and rare earths: sized to the 1,385-aircraft peak.

The Audit Committee reviews cost to complete at each scheduled top-risk review. Any overrun goes to the Board with re-phasing options and the payout set within 30-50%, never an equity raise. State support counts as upside only. No new buyback authority before NGSA spend rolls off in 2036.

airbus.move: NGSA certification sequencing and the safety-review watch list
Prepare the 2045 A350 Re-engine case (internal only)
Consolidate the A320 tail on the fewest lines (continuing)
airbus.detail: Wagner's quality watch. The tail runs at about 14-15 a month in 2043-44 while staff move to NGSA. We concentrate it on the fewest lines to keep skills and quality. We publish no 2040s A320 rates.

cfm.move: Ducted hot-and-harsh durability gate, run as an entry-into-service gate
LEAP fleet first on the constrained suppliers, plus a supplier-clearance review
cfm.detail: Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate and ahead of Ducted development hardware on the constrained suppliers. They are durability work, not spares [CX-0529]. Any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team. Ali reviews the 9 suppliers at 15 sites on field data [CX-0613, CX-0633] and reports to the Board in the 2045 round. Tripwire: if OE deliveries fall below airframer rate, or kits fall behind OE rate, on field data, the Ducted's development hardware is sequenced behind them.

cfm.move: Board watch list

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet first on pacing parts through the A320neo tail and the GTF2 ramp
pratt_whitney.detail: On the roughly 30 pacing parts, AOG fleet spares and MRO material rank first, then OE: the A320neo long-term-agreement slots under Airbus's Alt plan and GTF2 installs. Allocation is decided daily and reviewed weekly. A GTF2 install never takes a pacing part from an AOG engine [PX-0080][PX-0123]. Supplier quality gates come before each GTF2 rate step, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. The squeeze to watch is 2040-44, when P&W narrowbody engines go from 699 to 1,068 (+53%) while about 7,300 GTF engines delivered in 2026-36 come into the shops.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 durability gate to the Board's Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first
pratt_whitney.detail: Before entry into service, Eddy reports to the committee: severe-environment endurance data (three quarters of the GTF fleet flew in cool climates, which hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122]), all LLPs at full life at entry into service [PX-0128], and maturity gates against the planned 2036 ready date on a weekly drumbeat [PX-0131]. The bad number first: today the committee has no endurance hours, LLP-life figures or gate status, and we will not invent any. The margin to NGSA's entry into service is one year. Eddy's slip prior of +1.5 to 2 years would land past it. No testing is compressed to hold a date. If the data put 2036 at risk, Airbus and the Board hear it from us first.

pratt_whitney.move: Finance reviews the Joint Venture commitment every round; 2045 withdraw test written in
pratt_whitney.detail: The commitment is reviewed by Finance every round. Before Rolls-Royce can match in 2045, Mitchill runs the 2045 grid's withdraw row against hold. We withdraw before formation if hold beats withdraw in any column he weights at 0.2 or more, or on weighted value. We also withdraw if Eddy finds that formation would touch the in-service GTF2's gear, core or certified configuration, or would start a second development while the fleet is short of parts. GTF2 is ready in 2036, so a 2045 formation may not fold it in and could mean $2B of new Joint Venture R&D. Orders are simultaneous, so a 2045 withdrawal stops formation even if Rolls-Royce commits that round. None of this is booked.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 whole-life case to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: ΔPV −0.97 = +1.03 engine value − $2.00B R&D (charged undiscounted), against Do Nothing (0.00) and a buyback (about 0 at fair value, and debt returns to pre-ASR levels before any buyback). Two columns lift it to 0 or above: S4, a formed Joint Venture (+1.38), and S3, an fps 10-yr on code 7 (+1.36). Neither is booked. The marginal case passes: the last $0.33B of spend keeps 2.01 to 19.98 of PV against a cancel. Mitchill's discounted view (about −0.06) is shown as Finance information only. We report −0.97.

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan, live against the 2037 EIS (condition of Watson's concurrence)
rolls_royce.detail: Three parts, all in place before EIS. (i) Partner-shop MRO on the Singapore Joint Venture model, with repair technology invested in those shops [RX-0287]. (ii) A spares and lease-engine pool. (iii) An EIS field team able to intervene quickly in the early years [RX-0283]. Sized for 7 engines in 2037 and 115 installed by 2039, with partner-shop capacity scaling past about 1,600 engines by 2042 and 4,700 by 2045 (Watson's cumulative sums from the brief). If the Joint Venture forms, P&W's network adds to the plan but does not replace it. Reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

rolls_royce.move: Certification-readiness gate one year before EIS, with no compression
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan NB test pacing runs to 2037 on schedule, with the remaining 2035-36 work uncompressed. Durability standard at EIS: a time-on-wing target in the specification, endurance and durability testing complete, and life-limited parts cleared to full life. Watson holds an internal certification-readiness review in 2036 and reports it to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If the evidence is not at standard, we say publicly that maturity needs longer and the engine is not fitted at 2037. It is not rushed [RX-0296, RX-0284].

rolls_royce.move: Fold engineering rule, if the Joint Venture forms
rolls_royce.detail: One chief engineer and one test plan to EIS. The UltraFan NB configuration and certification basis stay frozen to EIS. Shared gearbox technology comes after EIS, tested on its own. No engineers are pulled off the test programme. Rolls-Royce never states 2036 for UltraFan NB. Any Joint Venture date we ever give is the bulletin's date with its folded basis, or formation + 6.

rolls_royce.move: Supplier and capacity plan for the narrowbody ramp
rolls_royce.detail: The ramp is 267 NB engines in 2040, 742 in 2042 and 1,132 in 2045, about six times the widebody line. Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers. Gearbox capacity is sized early; a formed Joint Venture could share the gearbox load (inference). Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support are ring-fenced while the narrowbody line ramps from 2037 [RX-0284, RX-0286].

rolls_royce.move: Margin-based hurdle case to the Audit Committee (McCabe)

Expected NPV at 15% is +2.07 to +4.17. Full-life lookback on the 2030 $8B: 8-11%, below the mid-to-high-teens hurdle, stated plainly as a miss on this board's lifecycle multiple. Funding stays inside the broadly flat gross R&D envelope. Payout and buyback cadence are unchanged [RX-0213, R-1579].

rolls_royce.move: Maturity evidence for Airbus, without dates or price
rolls_royce.detail: Through the NGSA programme, share endurance and durability test results and the support-plan build with Airbus. No dates beyond the public 'ready 2037', no price, no launch-style terms.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture commitment re-test in 2045
rolls_royce.detail: The commitment is time-boxed to NGSA's fold window. In 2045 it is re-tested on that round's grid. If P&W has not joined and the commit row is below hold (for example, a ready Solo charged a fresh $4B share, or a Joint Venture that would be ready in 2051 and meets no airframe), we order jv_with_pw: withdraw. A standing commitment no airframe can use is options management [RX-0051].

other_moves.move: Hold the 737 MAX at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed KPI gates
other_moves.detail: That is Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. No Rate Increase is on the order sheet this round. Pope's KPI check passes: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. The waiting backlog under Do Nothing reaches 540 in 2041. We tell customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line. That is stability over share, and its trigger is present [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

other_moves.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; work with GE to bring the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is CFM/GE's own programme, ready since 2033. This is not a 787 Re-engine order. The board does not price it.

other_moves.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine study warm on the GEnx route; launch nothing
other_moves.detail: Durability first [BX-1298]. It comes back in 2045 only if no A350 Re-engine is on the public record (H3, second half). It must also be H4-legal against any 2045 fps with Pope's slip slack shown: a 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years with no slack and cannot pair with a 2045 7-year. If it is ever launched: a public EIS with buffer (Malave: 2042 public, 2040 internal) and risk-share terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].
