public_statements.boeing:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and you'll get the same straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane isn't there yet. On paper it looks closer than it was. I've looked hard at why, and I'm not going to tell you something has turned when it hasn't. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it. In the meantime we're keeping our engineering teams and our suppliers ready, because readiness doesn't keep by itself.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We'll keep giving customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in service, and its ramp-up is completing in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and we will keep running it on that clock. This is how we prepared the Airbus of the 2030s, and it is how we will serve our customers into the next decade. To the end of the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the ramp, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus asked for long-term engine supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. The GTF fleet on the A320neo is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. A large fleet is coming through the shops, so the fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We will report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA. Our job now is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, is in place and scaling with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 MAX at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed KPI gates
boeing.detail: That is Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. No Rate Increase is on the order sheet. Pope's KPI check passes: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. The waiting backlog under Do Nothing is 432 in 2045, 265 in 2047 and 0 by 2050. We give customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

boeing.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; keep bringing the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers with GE
boeing.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is CFM/GE's own programme, ready since 2033. This is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board does not price it.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for NGSA's last ramp step and the end of the A320 transition
airbus.detail: We are extending the long-term agreements for NGSA engine delivery slots with CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, at 2,612-2,732 engines a year, which is below the 2,770 we carried in 2044. A320neo engine slots are matched to the last aircraft, and the surplus slots go back to CFM and Pratt & Whitney as the lines close. NGSA wing and structures run at rate, including the work packages we brought in-house. Titanium and rare earths stay at or below the 2044 peak, following on from the 2025 de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. All of this is for our own production. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

airbus.move: Engineering staffing for NGSA in-service support and sustaining
airbus.detail: We fill these roles by internal redeployment first, with A320 line staff moving only after the last aircraft is delivered, and then by normal hiring. A320 sustaining engineering for the in-service fleet and the A350 teams stay fully staffed [A-0366, A-0485]. The staffing does not target any competitor's programme or staff, and it is not a Delay Tactics move.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
cfm.detail: Funded as technology and not cancelled for cost (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0398]. We launch no product. In public there is no ground-test, flight-test or entry year (H6, Ali's date test) [CX-0009]. The airframers set the date for the architecture [CX-0205]. We bring RISE test results from after October 2025 to the Board once they are on the record. No product claim is made, so my 20% line is not engaged [CX-0217].

cfm.move: CFM keeps answering Airbus's long-term supply request (A320neo tail and NGSA), jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: Made as CFM, jointly with Safran. Price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, on standard terms [CX-0184]. Nothing goes out in public: no price, concession, volume, rate or delivery year. Ghai's volumes-first condition stands: the NGSA volume assumptions are worked with Airbus inside this answer before any number goes out [CX-0944]. The board does not price this move.

cfm.move: CFM engines stay on offer to every airframer
cfm.detail: CFM offers its engines on any new single-aisle Boeing launches, and the Embraer partnership stays open and not exclusive. No airframer is locked out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. There are no price, terms or dates in public, and any pricing goes to Safran first.

cfm.move: GEnx upgrade brought to 787 customers with Boeing (GE alone)
cfm.detail: This answers Boeing's public request. The upgrade is GE's own programme, ready since 2033 and counting since 2042 (WB share 44.8%). It is won on product, not price [CX-0599, CX-0615]. There is no Safran gate and no price in public. It is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board does not price it.

cfm.move: LEAP fleet first: kits and shop-visit material ahead of the OE delivery rate
cfm.detail: Time-on-wing kits and shop-visit material stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the A320 Alt-plan tail and the NGSA ramp [CX-0529]. Any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team, never one person [CX-0012]. Kits and shop visits stay at standard terms with no free upgrade (Ghai's advice). The wording follows the Board's 2035 advice: 'OE delivery rate', not 'new-engine delivery rate'.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit to the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0088][PX-0106]. There is no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100]. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. We publish no 2045 share figure, because we do not have one: Eddy's last figure is 60% in June 2023, with a 90% target [PX-0116], and the evidence has no outcome for that target. We give no dated AOG recovery, because my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Kit parts rank third on the pacing parts, behind AOG spares and shop material. The move changes no payoff on the board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture held to its published terms
pratt_whitney.detail: The terms are those published with the 2035 commitment [P-1233][P-1875]. Risk, investment and revenue are shared, with both partners on one engine. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property. Partner contributions are recognised only as a valuation in the share split, with no licence and no cash payment to the partner. Partner content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and P&W signs durability only on an engine it has tested. Any departure in the definitive agreement is a significant transaction and goes through Finance to the full Board before signature.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture engine offered, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet
pratt_whitney.detail: The offer is on standard terms, priced for value [PX-0055]. No concession, discount, free upgrade or launch-style term goes to Boeing, Airbus or a fleet customer to win a selection or defend NGSA share. Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto applies, and on the grid an fps code-7 selection is worth −0.03. Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise. We give no airframer date [PX-0062].

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture engine in service, paced on durability; engineering-change rule
rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never to hold a date or win a campaign. P&W's published terms say the same. rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard 'win-win' terms through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no earlier dates, no launch-style terms. rolls_royce.move: Trent durability and UltraFan technology pull-through inside the existing budget
rolls_royce.detail: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine and life-limited-part durability work continues inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). - Formation was worth +2.35. CFM's two moves took −3.03. His rough split, which is inference: the ducted engine about −2.3, the Embraer partnership about −0.75.
- Holding GTF2 in 2035 still kept 17.65 against a cancel. From 2045 forward the engine adds +0.94 of PV at 2026.

- A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule −35 pp, or −20 pp with lobbying, for CFM. Favourable to us; size not on the brief.
- An fps without us: below S2.
- An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
- Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.

boeing.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and you'll get the same straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane isn't there yet. On paper it looks closer than it was. I've looked hard at why, and I'm not going to tell you something has turned when it hasn't. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it. In the meantime we're keeping our engineering teams and our suppliers ready, because readiness doesn't keep by itself.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We'll keep giving customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: DO NOTHING IN EVERY FIELD
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody call: the three work streams [BX-1296], debt first read on the grid [BX-1305], Airbus's timing does not set ours [B-2313], and doing less [BX-1239].
- On the 787 Re-engine, my record breaks the tie: doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. The odds of an A350 Re-engine are Malave's (Low), and the Board's Business case test points the same way.
- Every cell below was checked against the brief in work/r3_ceo_decide_calc.py.

1. TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding veto covers nine rows: every 7-year row, every via Embraer row, and the 10-year at the new site alone (S3 -2.87, short by $0.04B). I accept it and have no override.
- Three 10-year rows pass his buffer test, so the fps call on those is mine.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on: no Rate Increase is offered and no problem is live.
- Her H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is moot because I don't order it.
- No red line is breached, and both memos recommend these orders.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. Nothing is live, and LEAP-1B is a watch item that is easing (Pope).
(2) Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready?
- Boeing: yes. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029, and the 10-year rows are fundable.
- Technology: yes. CFM and the Joint Venture are both mature by any EIS from 2052.
- Market: no. Every fps row trails Do Nothing by more than ε in every column.
- Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I read S3 as Malave's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83. His results are in section 4.
(4) Is this doing less, better? Yes. Nothing beats Do Nothing by more than ε in my expected column [BX-1239].

3. TESTED CASE (S1 / S2 / S3)
- Submitted, Do Nothing: -0.83 / -1.16 / -0.83. Expected -0.95 at 35% odds of an A350 Re-engine.
- Rejected rows, shown against Do Nothing:
  - Re-engine alone: -0.10 / -1.97 / -0.10 (+0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73); expected -0.75.
  - 10-year at Renton: -2.61 / -2.94 / -2.71 (-1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88).
  - 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -2.12 / -3.99 / -2.22 (-1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39).
  - 7-year at Renton: -3.82 / -4.15 / -3.97 (-2.99 / -2.99 / -3.14).
  - Best via Embraer: -6.34 / -8.22 / -6.44.

4. MALAVE: BINDING ON NINE ROWS, ADVICE ON THE REST
Buffer test (S3 no lower than -2.83):
- Pass: Do Nothing ($2.00B clear); the Re-engine ($2.73B); 10-year at Renton ($0.12B); 10-year + Re-engine ($0.45B); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine ($0.61B).
- Fail: 10-year at the new site (by $0.04B); 7-year (by $0.85-1.36B); via Embraer (by $3.61-4.08B).
Fundable:
- Pass: every 10-year row, the Re-engine and Do Nothing, each at $0.0B stress net debt.
- Fail: 7-year ($0.5-4.7B) and via Embraer ($3.8-10.1B).
For scale only, never netted twice: the undiscounted penalties are $19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B. A 10-year fps would take $47.7B after the 79% factor over 2045-54: 36% of base surplus and 55% of stress, all of it surplus the Board reserves.

5. fps: HOLD, EVEN THOUGH THE BUFFER PASSES AND A PREMIUM WOULD FIT
- The market leg fails, and so does my debt-first test: the best fps trails Do Nothing by $1.29B (S1) and the 10-year at Renton by $1.78B.
- My frame said most of the narrowing was the discount clock. Jay says it is all the clock, and I take his number.
  - Net of the clock, the market moved $0.20B against us.
  - In decision-year dollars the gap went -$7.8B (2030), -$10.5B (2035), -$11.9B (2045).
  - The case is getting worse, not better. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" doesn't even apply here [BX-1300].
- Headroom: $0.12B of buffer absorbs 2-3 months of slip, against doctrine's +3 years costing $1.4-2.0B once, all in. That's not a plan with room for hiccups [BX-1275, BX-1318].
- Pope fails every fps on predictable delivery, after 18 years with no major development.
- The Board would veto every launch on Business case and Downside, so the order would revert to hold anyway.
- Objective premium declined. The 10-year at Renton needs $1.78B (with the Re-engine hold, $1.97B in total, at the edge of the cap).
  - The 50/50 split is the company's mission, not a reason to launch an airplane the grid says loses value.
  - My tests read the grid, and a launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
- Ramp and form for the record: the 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.21-1.53B in every column. Via Embraer trails Solo by $4.03-4.23B and adds no IP we lack (Pope).

6. THE VALUE OF WAITING, SAID PLAINLY
- On the board, waiting costs nothing. Jay projects the 2050 10-year at -1.08 to -1.28 against Do Nothing, $2.1-2.3B short of the Board's bar, and he finds no 2050 path that clears ε.
- So a hold in 2050 likely means never, on this board. I'd rather say that now than discover it then.
- I won't launch to avoid saying it: "It is so much more important that we do this right than fast" [BX-1241].
- Waiting does cost things the grid doesn't price: workforce, supplier health, a 737 base falling to 16% by 2060, and MAX volume down 64%. I answer those with the non-public moves: a risk-reduction team, a hiring plan and funded suppliers.

7. 787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD
- I correct my frame (30% odds, $0.27B premium) to Jay's odds: 35%, worth +0.19, or about +0.01 after his 2050 haircut.
- Even at zero odds it is +0.73, inside ε.
- Tie-breaks, all toward hold: doing less, the higher worst column (-1.16 against -1.97), the higher-confidence plan, and no added penalty.
- The Board vetoes it on Business case.
- Pope's workforce-bridge point is real but unpriced. It bridges to a 2050 fps that Jay finds no case for, and a warm risk-reduction team does that job for less.
- I accept that this likely closes the option: 2050 is worth about +0.44 at best.

8. STANDING RULINGS
- H1: stays lifted. The condition was met, not waived.
- H2: cannot bind.
- H3: first half lifted. Second half open: no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4: a 2045 Re-engine with a 2045 10-year overlaps 2 years, legal with no slack. With a 7-year it overlaps 5 years and is barred.
- H5: never cancel a launched programme.
- H6: not engaged.
- H7: no trigger on this board.
- H8: $0.19B.

9. BIASES SHOWN, TRIGGER PRESENT
- Stability over share: the backlog is 432, fading by 2050.
- Under-disclosure: no fps date.
- Cash for readiness: suppliers kept funded.
- Inward focus.
- Certification optimism: no trigger, since nothing is in certification.

frame.situation:
Decision year 2045, round 3 of dash-2050-cons.

WHERE WE STAND
- We have launched nothing and are on today's products.
- The 737 MAX holds at 57 a month: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate order offered.
- Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in stress) and holds to 2050 in base and stress.
- The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are done. My conditions for the next airplane (debt repaired, developments finished) are met [BX-1305, B-2326].

PUBLIC RECORD
- NGSA: in service since 2037, fitted with CFM + PW + RR. Airbus is on its A320 Alt plan.
- P&W and Rolls-Royce: both committed to the Joint Venture in 2035. GTF2 and UltraFan NB were folded into it, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.
- CFM: ducted engine ready since 2041. Its Embraer partnership has been live since 2042 (open and not exclusive).
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says the A350 "remains our widebody focus".
- Observed narrowbody delivery share: 33.1% in 2044 (684 against Airbus's 1,385).

DO NOTHING
- Scores -0.83 / -1.16 / -0.83. The labels have changed this round: S1 = rivals hold; S2 = Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine; S3 = risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics (covert). With no fps launched, Delay Tactics would be naked, so S3 equals S1.
- Narrowbody preference: 34.0% (2045), 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- MAX deliveries: 684 (2045), 513 (2050), 346 (2055), 248 (2060).
- Waiting backlog: 432 (2045), 265 (2047), 0 by 2050.
- Operating profit runs $0.5-1.4B a year below the status quo from 2048. FCF stays at $12.66B or more and net debt at $0.0B. Value erodes; the balance sheet does not.

OBJECTIVES UNDER DO NOTHING
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 27.7%).
- Met: repairing the balance sheet and keeping it repaired, in base and stress.
- Engine enabler: dual or triple sources not met (the MAX flies CFM only); three narrowbody makers met. No fps launched in 2045 or later is in production by 2050, so no order this round can meet the dual-source line for 2050.

THE GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3)
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73. Best plan in S1 and S3.
- 10-year at Renton: -1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88. At the new site: -1.94 / -1.94 / -2.04.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39. The best fps row in S1 and S3.
- 7-year: -2.70 to -4.48. It trails the 10-year by $1.21-1.53B in every column.
- Via Embraer: -5.51 to -7.23. It trails the Solo 10-year by $4.03-4.23B.
- Renton adds +0.16 to +0.17 on a 10-year fps and +0.22 to +0.23 on a 7-year. It adds nothing while the fps holds.
- On top of a 10-year fps, the Re-engine adds +0.49 / -1.05 / +0.49.

TREND OF THE 10-YEAR AT RENTON AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2030: -4.39 to -5.26 (-5.26 in the column that came true, NGSA on the Alt plan).
- 2035: -4.24 to -4.35.
- 2045: -1.78 to -1.88.
- Ten years of discounting at 10.5% multiplies by 0.37. That alone would take 2035's -4.29 to -1.58. So most of the narrowing is the discount clock, not the market turning (inference; Jay to check).

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes, on the brief. Pope's seat to confirm.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
   - Boeing: yes. Net debt is $0.0B, and every 10-year row holds it in stress.
   - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give CFM plus the Joint Venture.
   - Market: no. Every fps row trails Do Nothing by more than ε in every column.
   - Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
3. What if certification takes longer than we think? S3 is Jay's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83. Three fps rows now pass:
   - 10-year at Renton, by $0.12B;
   - 10-year + Re-engine, by $0.45B;
   - 10-year at Renton + Re-engine, by $0.61B.
   So on those rows the fps call is mine, not his veto.
4. Is this doing less, better? Do Nothing beats every fps row by more than ε in every column. The Re-engine is within ε of Do Nothing at any odds [BX-1239].

BOARD RISKS (guidance, not red lines)
The Board says it would veto:
- launch_10yr at any site, in any combination. It fails Business case (needs more than +$1B), Downside (below -$1B in every column) and the market leg. At the new site alone it also fails Rating first (S3 -2.87).
- launch_7yr: S3 is $0.85-1.36B short of the limit, and stress net debt is not held ($0.5-4.7B).
- launch_via_embraer.
- re787: launch in any combination. Its best column (+0.73) is below +$1B. Paired with a 10-year fps it breaks the Downside limit (-1.05 to -1.06 in S2).
- A launch carried by a premium. Its tests read the grid.

It would approve:
- every hold;
- Renton, with Pope's wind-down result;
- a 10-year Solo in a round whose grid supports it.

It wants in the package:
- the Do Nothing erosion to 2060;
- the value of waiting until 2050;
- the trend since 2030;
- Jay's buffer and Fundable results, with numbers;
- Pope's results;
- my standing rulings on H1, H3, H4 and H5;
- every premium logged, with any hold its own tests require shown apart;
- no fps date.

  - the 50/50 split is the company's mission, not a reason to launch an airplane the grid says loses value;
  - my own tests read the grid;
  - the Board has told us a launch carried by a premium is vetoed, and a launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.

- Doing less [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the higher worst column (-1.16 against -1.97) all break the tie toward hold. The Board vetoes it on Business case.
- Doctrine premium: about $0.27B at 30% odds. Jay sets the odds.
- Board-required forgone value, logged apart: +0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73.
- I accept the cost plainly: this is probably the last useful window. 2050 is worth about x0.61 (about +0.44 at best) and overlaps a 2050 10-year fps by 2 years.
- Odds alone can't change my mind. Even at zero odds it stays inside ε. Only a change on the grid can.

ALONGSIDE, NOT ANNOUNCED
- The 2050 case: 10-year ramp at Renton with Pope's wind-down, Code 7 (CFM + Joint Venture) under test, cost-plus or risk-share terms, and Jay's package items.
- Engineering and workforce readiness kept warm.
- Fragile suppliers funded; LEAP-1B allocation reviews running.

PUBLIC

- In decision-year dollars: -$7.8B (2030), -$10.5B (2035), -$11.9B (2045). The case is getting worse, not better.
- Net of the clock, the gain fell 13% over 2030-35 but only 7% over 2035-45.

2050 PROJECTION (EIS 2060, split 27/73)
- Bill plus penalty: $2.66B PV. Gain stream: $1.38-1.58B.
- Item value: -1.08 with no further market loss, -1.14 at the 2035-45 rate, -1.28 at the 2030-35 rate. Your -1.1 is the optimistic end.

(a) The window moves with EIS and catches more of the post-2060 replacement wave (544 in 2060, 1,244 in 2065). That is why the slide slows, but it doesn't turn it:
- the board doesn't escalate prices;

- the 737 customer base: 16% preference by 2060, still falling 1 pp a year;
- MAX volume down 64% (684 to 248) while the board holds the 8% margin, so fixed-cost under-absorption goes unpriced;
- supplier health.
What waiting buys: about $47.7B of after-factor cash stays in the Board's surplus for five more years, and we see Airbus's 2045 widebody move first. 2050 is the last round, so a hold then means never, on this board.

FOR THE fps (2050 is the last round)
- I would back a launch on a grid where the best 10-year row beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon in the expected column and holds stress net debt.
- As advice, I would also want it to clear the slip leg by enough to absorb doctrine's +3-year slip at full cost: about $1.5B or more of S3 margin, against $0.12B today.

CONDITIONS ON MY NUMBERS
These numbers hold barring:
- an A350 Re-engine on the public record;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- any change to the stress-case cash path the brief shows.
My 35% odds are Low confidence; they move the Re-engine premium between $0 and $0.73B, never past the cap.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.83 in S3, so the limit is -2.83. Three fps rows pass: the 10-year at Renton (-2.71, by $0.12B), the 10-year with the Re-engine (-2.38) and the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine (-2.22). Nine fail, and under the team rule I veto them: every 7-year row ($0.85-1.36B short), every via Embraer row ($3.61-4.08B) and the 10-year at the new site alone ($0.04B).

A pass is not a case. Your inference holds, and more: the discount clock explains all of the narrowing. Net of the clock, the gain has lost about $0.2B since 2035. In 2045 dollars the 10-year at Renton trails Do Nothing by $11.9B, against $10.5B in 2035 dollars. Doctrine's three-year slip costs $1.4-2.0B, all in, once; $0.12B absorbs two or three months of it. That's not a baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

On the board, waiting to 2050 costs nothing. I project -1.1 to -1.3, still $2.1-2.3B short of the Board's bar. The later window and the 2060s replacement wave slow the slide but don't turn it. What waiting costs is off the board: workforce, suppliers, a 737 base at 16% by 2060.

The Re-engine is a tie. At my 35% odds it's worth +0.19, near zero after a 2050 haircut, and Do Nothing has the higher worst column. Hold it; I log $0.19B.

Hold everything, barring an A350 Re-engine on the record. The balance sheet stays fully restored.

The brief gives no KPI series, so this result rests on its no-live-problem record. rate_737: hold is the only value offered, so no Rate Increase is on the order sheet. My veto has nothing to act on, and H6 cannot engage. Confirmed.

tests.name: Supplier readiness: LEAP-1B and fragile suppliers [doctrine]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, and engine supply that covers the current rate.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 1. 684 MAX a year needs 1,368 LEAP-1B a year, unchanged since 2030.
From the observed tables (narrowbody engines = 2 x deliveries x share), CFM delivered about:
- 2,593 narrowbody engines in 2035 (76.1% of 3,408);
- 2,284 in 2041;
- 2,239 in 2044 (54.1% of 4,138).
Our call rose from 53% to 61% of CFM's narrowbody output only because CFM's total fell by about 354 engines as the Joint Venture ramped on NGSA. P&W + RR went from about 815 engines (2035) to about 1,899 (2044). CFM's Airbus load fell from about 1,225 to 871 engines. The ducted engine (since 2041) and the Embraer partnership (since 2042) are new-engine lines, not LEAP-1B.
Verdict: a watch item, and easing, not a problem. Keep the allocation reviews running [BX-1264, BX-1325], measure allocation, and attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure [B-1923].
Doctrine context: beyond 47 a month the supply chain binds [B-2340], and the step to 52 once strained CFM supply [B-1449]. No step is asked.
Fragile suppliers: the brief is silent. Keep them funded and producing ahead of our rate [B-2330, BX-1243].

Answer to ask 3. Item against hold: S3 +0.73 equals S1 +0.73. Delay Tactics act only from fps EIS, so the risk case does not touch the Re-engine.
S2 (-0.81) is Airbus's move, not a delivery risk. An A350 Re-engine launched this round also enters service in 2050. When both enter service in the same year nothing changes, so we would carry the $5B for no share.
The board prices no Re-engine slip. The doctrine prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). Shifting the whole S1 item at 10.5% (inference) gives:
- +0.66 at a 1-year slip;
- +0.60 at 2 years (x0.819);
- +0.49 at 4 years (x0.671).
It stays positive in S1 and S3 across the range, so at most about a third of its S1 value rides on the nominal date.
Engine route: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, giving 17 years of fleet time by a 2050 EIS. Durability comes first [BX-1298, B-2304].

The board's risk case costs the fps rows little. S3 against S1 is -$0.10B on every 10-year and via Embraer row, and -$0.15B on every 7-year row. Almost none of the value rides on the nominal date, because there is no positive value to protect. Against Do Nothing:

- best fps row (10-year at Renton + Re-engine): -1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39;
- worst row: -7.23.
The board does not price the doctrine clean-sheet slip of +3 years central (range +2 to +5). On that slip, a 2055 EIS becomes 2058:
- the long-run split against NGSA 2037 moves from 32/68 to 29/71 (rules.md, 1 pp per year of lead);
- rate 50 moves from about 2059 to 2062.
Certification is the pacing item [B-2343]. Our last clean sheet entered service in 2011, and by 2045 we will have run no major development for 18 years (MAX 7/10 in 2026, 777X in 2027).
Technology passes: by a 2055 EIS, the Joint Venture engine (ready 2036) has 19 years of readiness and the CFM ducted engine (ready 2041) 14.
The test fails on value at the nominal date and on unpriced predictability, not on engines or site. This is my flag against any launch this round (ask 8).

Answer to ask 6. Via Embraer trails the Solo 10-year by $4.03-4.04B in every column, and by $4.22-4.23B with the Re-engine.

CFM's Embraer partnership (live since 2042) is CFM's own, open and not exclusive. It gives Boeing no capital, capacity or IP. Capacity is not what we lack, since Renton covers our long-run demand (see the Renton test). Solo passes; via Embraer fails.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand [one remark; inference]
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column.
tests.numbers:
No Rate Increase row is on this round's grid (it was a 2030-only lever), so there is nothing to score.
For the record, demand has turned. Under Do Nothing:
- the waiting backlog falls from 432 (2045) to 265 (2047) and 0 by 2050;
- MAX deliveries fall to 543 (2048), 513 (2050), 346 (2055) and 248 (2060) against 684 of capacity. Utilisation is 79%, 75%, 51% and 36%, with 141-436 a year idle.
No capacity addition on the MAX is warranted. The stability-over-share trigger fades by 2050.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and trained workforce (unpriced enabler) [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: One major development at a time, with capacity free to start it. A trained workforce in place, or a funded plan to rebuild it, before any launch.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 2. Capacity passes: nothing is in development, so one major development fits [B-0341].
Skills are a watch item that grows while we hold. With the 777X (2027) and MAX 7/10 (2026) done, by 2045 we will have run no major development for 18 years, and by 2050 for 23. Our last clean sheet (787) entered service in 2011.
Doctrine answers scarcity with hiring, transfers and retention:
- about 10,000 engineers hired [B-1941];
- about 8,000 people transferred from Defense to Commercial Airplanes [B-0729];
- talent is a 'ruthless competition' [B-1835].
New-airplane R&D starts 5-6 years before first delivery and peaks 1-2 years before it [B-0373]. For a 2060 EIS that start is about 2054-55, so a 2050 launch leaves time to rebuild.
Mitigation (inference): keep a dedicated fps risk-reduction team warm, as on the NMA [B-1593].
A 2045-50 Re-engine would keep a development team in work and feather into a 2050 fps with zero overlap [B-1393]. That is an unpriced point in its favour, but not enough to clear ε.
Condition of any launch: a funded hiring and transfer plan.

tests.name: Re-engine readiness: Charleston, engine route, fragile suppliers [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, an engine route ready by EIS, and capacity for the share gain.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 3.
Charleston: the 787 builds 100 a year (58.8% of 170, or 8.3 a month). A lone re-engined 787 gains 1 pp a year from a 2050 EIS, reaching:
- 108.5 a year (9.0 a month) in 2055;
- 117 (9.8) in 2060;
- 134 (11.2) in 2070.
That fits inside a footprint being grown for rates in the teens [B-2336, BX-1317]. If an A350 Re-engine enters service the same year, nothing changes and Charleston needs no step.
Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 17 years by EIS. Durability comes first [BX-1298].
Workforce: nothing is in development, so one derivative fits one-at-a-time [B-0341].
Fragile suppliers: the brief is silent. Keep them funded and hot [B-2330, BX-1243].

tests.name: Renton wind-down readiness, for any launch (signed, conditional) [rules arithmetic plus doctrine]
tests.threshold: The Renton MAX wind-down follows the fps ramp and never leads it. The Everett North Line carries on at up to 15 a month (180 a year). Renton is chosen at least 3 years before EIS for the full $3.0B.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 4.
Under Do Nothing, MAX demand above Everett's 180 is 504 (2045), 333 (2050), 166 (2055), 147 (2056), 125 (2057) and 68 (2060) a year. On a linear reading of the rules' ramp (0 at EIS to 50 a month 4 years on; inference), the fps builds about 150 a year at EIS+1 and 300 at EIS+2.
When the ramp covers it:
- EIS 2055 (2045 launch): about EIS+2, 2057, allowing for preference climbing 1 pp a year from EIS. On the doctrine's +3-year slip, about 2060.
- EIS 2060 (2050 launch): within about the first year, 2061.
At the long-run split our whole narrowbody demand is:
- about 495-666 a year (41-56 a month; 32% of 1,548-2,082) for a 2055 EIS;
- 418-562 a year (35-47 a month) at 27/73 for 2060.
One Renton-scale build (47 a month) plus Everett carries that, inside the 100-a-month cap, so a new site buys capacity the market won't fill.
The board already has the MAX top up what the fps cannot build after 2050, and Renton adds +0.16 to +0.17 on every 10-year row, so it shows no net delivery loss.
I sign the result for any launch on three conditions:
1. The trigger is the ramp, not a date: on a slip, Renton's MAX lines run on.
2. No airplane is built at rate before certification [BX-1263, B-2228].
3. Renton is chosen at least 3 years before EIS (a 2050 10-year launch gives 10).
The site has no effect while the fps holds, so new_site stays this round. Under Do Nothing the MAX lines run at 75% (2050) to 36% (2060) of 684 regardless.

tests.name: Engine code for the 2050 case (prepare, do not order) [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: Engines named are ready and durable by EIS. Two sources where available. Certification never runs concurrent with production.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 5. The code is null this round because nothing launches. My read for the case:
- Joint Venture engine: ready since 2036 and in NGSA service since 2037. P&W and RR delivered about 1,899 narrowbody engines in 2044 (45.9%), RR from 0% before 2037. That gives 18 years in service by a 2055 EIS and 23 by 2060.
- CFM ducted engine: ready since 2041, giving 14 and 19 years.
Both meet durability-first by any EIS from 2052 [BX-1298, B-2304].
Supply stability: Code 3 keeps sole-source exposure, which is today's LEAP-1B position on the MAX [B-1449]. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give two sources, CFM + the Joint Venture, and all are allowed pairs with NGSA's Code 7. Code 7 over Code 3.
Pacing: certify one lead installation for EIS and the second as a follow-on before its production slots, so certification never runs concurrent with production [BX-1263]. Two installations is unpriced certification load, and certification paces [B-2343].
No order from 2045 on meets the 2050 dual-source line. Engine choice is not my veto ground.

On this board the cash goes out and the value does not come back.

(1) KPI veto: a brief reporting a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem would make it bind against any Rate Increase. None is offered or reported. A CFM allocation shortfall on LEAP-1B at 684 a year would turn my watch item into a fail [B-2308, BX-1264].

(3) 787 Re-engine: operations passes it on every test, so my hold rests on doctrine's ε rule (+0.73 at best, 0.73 - 1.54p at odds p), not on an operations finding. Only a grid putting it above +$1B would move me. If the CEO weighs the unpriced workforce bridge (a 2045-50 derivative that feathers into a 2050 fps with zero overlap), operations can deliver it.
(4) Renton: I would withdraw my sign-off if a launch plan wound Renton's MAX lines down ahead of the fps ramp covering MAX demand above Everett's 180 a year, or tied the wind-down to a date rather than the ramp.
(5) Engine code: a reported durability problem on the Joint Venture engine in NGSA service would move me to a CFM-led installation, with the second source added only after its own test evidence.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes; the KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and hold is the only rate order, so my KPI veto has nothing to act on. 57 a month holds. LEAP-1B stays a watch item, and an easing one: CFM delivered about 2,239 narrowbody engines in 2044 against 2,593 in 2035, while our call is unchanged at 1,368.

Second, engineering capacity. Strain confirmed: a 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) with no slack, since a 1-year Re-engine slip breaches H4. It overlaps a 7-year by 5 years ($3.0B), which is barred, and any 2050 fps by zero. The unpriced item is people. By 2050 we will have run no major development for 23 years. Any launch needs a funded hiring and transfer plan first [B-1941, B-0729].

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. Operations backs the 10-year ramp at Renton, $1.21-1.53B ahead of the 7-year. I sign the Renton wind-down, conditionally: it follows the ramp, never leads it. At a 32/68 split our whole narrowbody demand is about 41-56 a month, so a new site buys capacity the market won't fill. Embraer trails Solo by $4.03-4.23B and adds nothing we lack [BX-1330]. Code 7 gives two mature sources.

But no fps beats Do Nothing; the best trails by $1.29B. I recommend hold on every lever.

other_moves.detail: That is Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. No Rate Increase is on the order sheet. Pope's KPI check passes: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. The waiting backlog under Do Nothing is 432 in 2045, 265 in 2047 and 0 by 2050. We give customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

Keep a dedicated fps risk-reduction team warm and fund a hiring and transfer plan for engineering

decision.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and you'll get the same straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane isn't there yet. On paper it looks closer than it was. I've looked hard at why, and I'm not going to tell you something has turned when it hasn't. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it. In the meantime we're keeping our engineering teams and our suppliers ready, because readiness doesn't keep by itself.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We'll keep giving customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: DO NOTHING IN EVERY FIELD
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody call: the three work streams [BX-1296], debt first read on the grid [BX-1305], Airbus's timing does not set ours [B-2313], and doing less [BX-1239].
- On the 787 Re-engine, my record breaks the tie: doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. The odds of an A350 Re-engine are Malave's (Low), and the Board's Business case test points the same way.
- Every cell below was checked against the brief in work/r3_ceo_decide_calc.py.

1. TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding veto covers nine rows: every 7-year row, every via Embraer row, and the 10-year at the new site alone (S3 -2.87, short by $0.04B). I accept it and have no override.
- Three 10-year rows pass his buffer test, so the fps call on those is mine.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on: no Rate Increase is offered and no problem is live.
- Her H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is moot because I don't order it.
- No red line is breached, and both memos recommend these orders.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. Nothing is live, and LEAP-1B is a watch item that is easing (Pope).
(2) Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready?
- Boeing: yes. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029, and the 10-year rows are fundable.
- Technology: yes. CFM and the Joint Venture are both mature by any EIS from 2052.
- Market: no. Every fps row trails Do Nothing by more than ε in every column.
- Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I read S3 as Malave's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83. His results are in section 4.
(4) Is this doing less, better? Yes. Nothing beats Do Nothing by more than ε in my expected column [BX-1239].

3. TESTED CASE (S1 / S2 / S3)
- Submitted, Do Nothing: -0.83 / -1.16 / -0.83. Expected -0.95 at 35% odds of an A350 Re-engine.
- Rejected rows, shown against Do Nothing:
  - Re-engine alone: -0.10 / -1.97 / -0.10 (+0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73); expected -0.75.
  - 10-year at Renton: -2.61 / -2.94 / -2.71 (-1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88).
  - 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -2.12 / -3.99 / -2.22 (-1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39).
  - 7-year at Renton: -3.82 / -4.15 / -3.97 (-2.99 / -2.99 / -3.14).
  - Best via Embraer: -6.34 / -8.22 / -6.44.

4. MALAVE: BINDING ON NINE ROWS, ADVICE ON THE REST
Buffer test (S3 no lower than -2.83):
- Pass: Do Nothing ($2.00B clear); the Re-engine ($2.73B); 10-year at Renton ($0.12B); 10-year + Re-engine ($0.45B); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine ($0.61B).
- Fail: 10-year at the new site (by $0.04B); 7-year (by $0.85-1.36B); via Embraer (by $3.61-4.08B).
Fundable:
- Pass: every 10-year row, the Re-engine and Do Nothing, each at $0.0B stress net debt.
- Fail: 7-year ($0.5-4.7B) and via Embraer ($3.8-10.1B).
For scale only, never netted twice: the undiscounted penalties are $19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B. A 10-year fps would take $47.7B after the 79% factor over 2045-54: 36% of base surplus and 55% of stress, all of it surplus the Board reserves.

5. fps: HOLD, EVEN THOUGH THE BUFFER PASSES AND A PREMIUM WOULD FIT
- The market leg fails, and so does my debt-first test: the best fps trails Do Nothing by $1.29B (S1) and the 10-year at Renton by $1.78B.
- My frame said most of the narrowing was the discount clock. Jay says it is all the clock, and I take his number.
  - Net of the clock, the market moved $0.20B against us.
  - In decision-year dollars the gap went -$7.8B (2030), -$10.5B (2035), -$11.9B (2045).
  - The case is getting worse, not better. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" doesn't even apply here [BX-1300].
- Headroom: $0.12B of buffer absorbs 2-3 months of slip, against doctrine's +3 years costing $1.4-2.0B once, all in. That's not a plan with room for hiccups [BX-1275, BX-1318].
- Pope fails every fps on predictable delivery, after 18 years with no major development.
- The Board would veto every launch on Business case and Downside, so the order would revert to hold anyway.
- Objective premium declined. The 10-year at Renton needs $1.78B (with the Re-engine hold, $1.97B in total, at the edge of the cap).
  - The 50/50 split is the company's mission, not a reason to launch an airplane the grid says loses value.
  - My tests read the grid, and a launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
- Ramp and form for the record: the 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.21-1.53B in every column. Via Embraer trails Solo by $4.03-4.23B and adds no IP we lack (Pope).

6. THE VALUE OF WAITING, SAID PLAINLY
- On the board, waiting costs nothing. Jay projects the 2050 10-year at -1.08 to -1.28 against Do Nothing, $2.1-2.3B short of the Board's bar, and he finds no 2050 path that clears ε.
- So a hold in 2050 likely means never, on this board. I'd rather say that now than discover it then.
- I won't launch to avoid saying it: "It is so much more important that we do this right than fast" [BX-1241].
- Waiting does cost things the grid doesn't price: workforce, supplier health, a 737 base falling to 16% by 2060, and MAX volume down 64%. I answer those with the non-public moves: a risk-reduction team, a hiring plan and funded suppliers.

7. 787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD
- I correct my frame (30% odds, $0.27B premium) to Jay's odds: 35%, worth +0.19, or about +0.01 after his 2050 haircut.
- Even at zero odds it is +0.73, inside ε.
- Tie-breaks, all toward hold: doing less, the higher worst column (-1.16 against -1.97), the higher-confidence plan, and no added penalty.
- The Board vetoes it on Business case.
- Pope's workforce-bridge point is real but unpriced. It bridges to a 2050 fps that Jay finds no case for, and a warm risk-reduction team does that job for less.
- I accept that this likely closes the option: 2050 is worth about +0.44 at best.

8. STANDING RULINGS
- H1: stays lifted. The condition was met, not waived.
- H2: cannot bind.
- H3: first half lifted. Second half open: no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4: a 2045 Re-engine with a 2045 10-year overlaps 2 years, legal with no slack. With a 7-year it overlaps 5 years and is barred.
- H5: never cancel a launched programme.
- H6: not engaged.
- H7: no trigger on this board.
- H8: $0.19B.

9. BIASES SHOWN, TRIGGER PRESENT
- Stability over share: the backlog is 432, fading by 2050.
- Under-disclosure: no fps date.
- Cash for readiness: suppliers kept funded.
- Inward focus.
- Certification optimism: no trigger, since nothing is in certification.

memo_weighing.cfo:

- His figures match the brief cell for cell.
- Buffer veto on every 7-year row, every via Embraer row and the 10-year at the new site alone: accepted. I have no override.
- His passes on the three 10-year rows left the fps call to me. His advice decided it:
  - the discount clock explains all of the narrowing, and the market moved $0.20B against us;
  - in decision-year dollars the gap went -$10.5B (2035) to -$11.9B (2045);
  - a $0.12B margin covers 2-3 months of slip.
- 35% odds adopted, replacing my 30%. Also adopted: the $0.28B haircut, the 2050 projection (-1.08 to -1.28) and his finding that no 2050 path clears ε.
- Fundable results and cash path adopted. A 10-year fps takes 36% of base and 55% of stress surplus over 2045-54.
- Thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and his Airbus odds are Low. Beyond the buffer test I weighed him as advice. His slip reconstruction and trend arithmetic are inference, but they are consistent with the brief.
memo_weighing.ops:
Full weight on KPIs, strain and readiness, the [NOW] doctrine the seat is built on.
- KPI veto: not invoked. Nothing is live and no Rate Increase is offered.
- LEAP-1B: a watch item, and easing (2,239 CFM narrowbody engines in 2044 against our 1,368 call).
- Strain arithmetic confirmed: 2 years against a 10-year with no slack (a 1-year Re-engine slip breaches H4); 5 years against a 7-year, barred; zero against any 2050 fps.
- Her advice flag against any fps this round (predictable delivery, 18 years with no major development) supports the hold.
- She backs the 10-year ramp, Solo over via Embraer, and Code 7 with the lead installation first and the second as a follow-on. All three go into the 2050 case.
- Her conditional Renton wind-down result is carried forward. Renton is not ordered this round because it has no effect while the fps holds.
- Her unpriced workforce-bridge point on the Re-engine: weighed, but it does not clear ε. I answered the workforce gap with a risk-reduction team and a hiring and transfer plan, which she makes a condition of any launch.
- Thin seat: Very low on airplanes. I used her numbers and gates, not her market views.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1 (rivals hold) for the narrowbody. S3 equals S1 on rows with no fps and sits $0.10-0.15B below it on fps rows.

For the 787 Re-engine: S1 blended with S2 (an A350 Re-engine) at Malave's 35% odds (Low confidence). On that blend Do Nothing scores -0.95.

S3, the risk case, stays the buffer baseline and is not blended in.
decision.premium_reason:
Doctrine premium under H8: $0.19B, for holding the 787 Re-engine.
- At Malave's 35% odds of an A350 Re-engine its expected gain is 0.73 - 1.54 x 0.35 = +0.19. I give that up for doing less, the higher-confidence plan, the higher worst column and no added penalty.
- After Malave's haircut for a 2050 A350 Re-engine, it is about $0.01B.
- The odds move it between $0 and $0.73B, so it cannot breach the cap. An A350 Re-engine on the record sets it to zero (H3).

Objective premium: $0.
- The 10-year fps at Renton would need $1.78B (S1 and expected) to $1.88B (S3). Added to the $0.19B above, that is $1.97B, inside the cap. I decline it.
- My debt-first and three-work-streams tests read the grid. The Board's Business case and Downside tests would veto a launch carried by a premium.
- Holding the fps gives up nothing on the grid.

Total H8: $0.19B, within $2B.

Logged apart and not added: the forgone value of the Board-required Re-engine hold, +0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73 by column ($0.73B at most).
decision.objective_note:
The briefing objective under Do Nothing:
- Hold the 50/50 split: not met. 34.0% in 2045, 27.7% in 2050.
- Defend incumbency: not met. The worst year is 27.7%.
- Repair the balance sheet and keep it repaired: met in base and stress. Net debt is $0.0B from 2029 (2030 in stress) and held to 2050.
- Dual or triple engine sources on our narrowbody: not met. The MAX flies CFM only, and no 2045 order can meet it for 2050.
- Three narrowbody engine makers in the market: met.

Only an fps moves the split. The cheapest fps gives up $1.78B against Do Nothing, and its case is worsening in decision-year dollars. The objective never changes the payoff, so I take no objective premium.

The long cycle is on the record:

airbus.rationale:
DECISION: the all-default package. ngsa hold, engine code fixed (none), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
1. Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081]. Two transitions run this round: NGSA's last ramp step (1,306, then 1,339, then 1,366) and the closure of the last A320 lines (28 in 2045, none from 2047). Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch on both rows, and no event is reported. One condition applies: no engine enters service before it is mature. No widebody engine for the A350 is on the record as mature for a 2050 EIS, so a Re-engine EIS would have to move rather than take an immature engine. On the pillars that is a re-timing note, not a breach (Wagner).
2. Ramp. It stays disciplined and controlled to the last step [AX-0010]. Nothing new goes on top of the closure that Lars cannot pass.
3. Prepare the next decade on its technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006]. I would welcome a late, cheap A350 derivative [AX-0082, A-0090], but not ahead of its engine.
4. What I can take to the Board. Nothing beyond the default, on this round's tests.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Rule 5: nothing is in development.
  - Integrity applies to bottleneck and both.
  - Every row breaks the -$2B line: one move -11.46 / +0.06 / +0.06 / +0.44 / +0.06 / -11.46 / +0.05; both moves -11.72 / -0.13 / -0.13 / +0.22 / -0.13 / -11.72 / -0.14.
  - The Board vetoes all of them.
- The team's stricter condition stands; I have not set it aside in any round. On the Board's reading, Delay Tactics are closed for the rest of the game [A-0299, A-0474].
- No other red line binds. Rule 3 is open (no 787 Re-engine is on the record) and rule 6 is clean (zero overlap).

STEP 2: SURVIVORS
- The default passes every test of Toepfer and Wagner.
- The A350 Re-engine row fails two binding soft vetoes, each on an independent ground:
  - Toepfer: the added-move test. The item is +0.89 in S1-S5 and -0.50 / -0.51 in S6 / S7. It is negative in two plausible columns and never reaches $1B, so it fails the doctrine's $1B launch condition (profile section 6).
  - Wagner: engine readiness. No A350 widebody engine has been launched or committed. UltraFan widebody would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, and in 2056 on Rolls-Royce's own sequence. The GEnx upgrade is a 787 engine. Doctrine's sequencing (profile section 11.3) is not met.
- So the only survivor is the default.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The raw best in S1 is the Re-engine at +14.98 against the default's +14.09, a gap of +0.89 (+0.75 at my weights). That is inside the $1B band where my rule takes the default anyway (profile section 9, step 6).
- The tie-breaks all point to hold:
  - less concurrency during the last ramp step and the A320 closure;
  - a later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2045);
  - fewer Board items (0 against 1 Qualified Majority item).
- Three grounds lead to hold, each on its own: Toepfer's veto, Wagner's veto and my default rule. Toepfer notes that his failure rests on the added-move reading, while the teams.md row test passes (Re-engine worst column S7 +13.33, default worst S4 +13.29). Even setting his veto aside, Wagner's engine finding and my $1B rule each decide it.

OVERRIDE CHECK
None is used. An override needs at least $1B over the best passing option. The margin is +0.89 at best, +0.75 weighted and -0.51 in S7. The Board would also veto a Re-engine that reached it through an override. The override budget (one per game) remains unused.

WHAT I ACCEPT, KNOWINGLY
- About $0.89B forgone in S1 ($0.75B weighted). This sits inside the $1B band, so it is not a doctrine premium.
- Waiting is worth little. A 2050 launch (EIS 2055) is not on today's grid. The pure-discount pre-read is about +0.61, below $1B (an inference; Toepfer confirms it).
- Rolls-Royce commits a widebody engine only once a Re-engine is on the record, so the doctrine's engine sequencing may never be met. Holding now is therefore close to keeping the A350 at Do Nothing for good.
- I decide that on the record. Do Nothing is a legitimate choice where the $1B test binds (profile section 6). The A350 stays our widebody focus at 70 a year and 41.2% share, flat on the grid.

BOARD-GATE LINES
- Package: no Board item. Every field is at its default, so there is nothing for the Board to approve or veto.
- For the record, the Re-engine not submitted:
  - Pillars: pass, with a re-timing note on the engine.
  - Toepfer: fail on the added-move test (binding soft veto). Cash passes: $1.0B a year, with $4.2B of headroom under $5.2B.
  - Wagner: fail on engine readiness (binding soft veto). Safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass.
  - Grid item: +0.89 x5 / -0.50 / -0.51.
  - Not taken to the Board.

REACTION DISCIPLINE (our own clock, rules 2 and 7)
- An fps launch re-times nothing.
- NGSA is never cancelled.
- A 787 Re-engine made public closes the A350 Re-engine under rule 3 and triggers no other move.

DELAY TACTICS
Off all game. They are never named in public.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
- Five pillars first [AX-0073, AX-0081]. Two transitions run at once, NGSA's last ramp step and the closing of the last A320 lines. Nothing goes on top of them that Lars cannot pass.
- Ramp: disciplined and controlled to the end of the transition [AX-0010].
- Prepare the next decade on its technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006].
  - A late, cheap A350 Re-engine, second in line to NGSA, is a derivative I would welcome (profile section 4) [AX-0082, AX-0019].
  - But no widebody engine for a 2050 EIS is yet on the record as mature, and doctrine's own engine sequencing (UltraFan widebody committed a year before our launch) is not met.
- What I can take to the Board.
  - My rule is to propose the company default unless the best option beats it by more than $1B (teams.md step 1; profile section 9, step 6).
  - Doctrine launches the A350 Re-engine only on a gain of at least $1B (profile section 6).
  - The Re-engine adds +0.89 in S1-S5 (about +0.75 weighted) and loses 0.50 / 0.51 in S6 / S7, so it clears neither bar.
  - The tie-breaks within $1B (later capex start, less concurrency during the last ramp step and the A320 closure, fewer Board items) all point to hold.

WHAT I ACCEPT ON THE RECORD
- About +0.89 forgone in S1 (+0.75 weighted). This sits inside the $1B band and is not a doctrine premium.
- Waiting is worth little. A 2050 launch is not on today's grid, my pre-read is about +0.61, and rule 3 may close it. A hold now is close to keeping the A350 at Do Nothing for good, and I want the ExCo to decide that knowingly.

HOW FIRMLY I HOLD THE LEAN
This is a preference inside the $1B band, not a red line, and the Board has asked for this case two rounds running. Test the Re-engine in full, as if it were going to the Board:
- cash and the net-cash path;
- robustness;
- a mature engine for 2050;
- absorption shown by a milestone.
If both of you pass it cleanly, and either of you gives a reason on the brief's numbers why the $1B rule should not decide here, I will weigh that at the decide step against the rule and the Board's request, and record which way I go and why. If either test fails, the hold stands: +0.89 cannot carry an override, and the Board has said it would accept the hold.

NOT IN PLAY
- Delay Tactics stay off and are closed for the game. No fps is public; one move is worth -11.46 in S1 and S6 and at best +0.44. They fail rules 4 and 5 and integrity, and the team's stricter condition stands [A-0299, A-0474].
- NGSA, the engine code and the Alt plan carry no choice this round.

REACTION DISCIPLINE, DECIDED NOW
- An fps launch or a 787 Re-engine re-times nothing.
- If we did launch the Re-engine, a 787 Re-engine launched this round would be no ground to cancel it in 2050.

EXPECTED SCENARIO
- S1, rivals hold. Working weights: S1 50%, S2 15%, S3 5%, S4 15%, S5 5%, S6 5%, S7 5%.
- The default is worth about +13.9 weighted and the Re-engine row about +14.7.
- The choice does not turn on the scenario call: the item keeps its sign unless a 787 Re-engine is more than about 64% likely.

PUBLIC LINE
- Five pillars first.
- NGSA in service, with the ramp completing in a disciplined and controlled way.
- The A320 family served on our proven lines to the last aircraft.
- The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. No engine is named before it is mature.
- Only if the Board approves a Re-engine: 'the next step for the A350 family, entering service around the turn of the decade'.
- Zero-for-zero trade [AX-0088].
- No dates, no payout figures, no Delay Tactics.

cfo.memo:
Round 3 (2045), brief's grid. Recommended: ngsa hold, engine code none (fixed in service; I defer to Lars), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

Peak cash. NGSA spend ended in 2036 ($35.52B / 7 over 2030-36). The Alt plan's $0.75B ran at $0.094B a year to 2044. A350 Re-engine: $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year in 2045-49, with zero overlap and zero strain. Peak $1.0B against $5.2B leaves $4.2B of headroom for all prepayments combined. Pass.

Net cash at end-2049, before any new buyback (an inference, round-2 method): 48% payout $80.5B, or $75.5B with the Re-engine; 30% $123.7B / $118.7B; 50% $75.7B / $70.7B. The Re-engine takes 6% of 2045-49 FCF. A new buyback sized to the yearly surplus (about $6.5B at 48%, after the Re-engine) fits the 10% authority. No equity raise.

Robustness. Both rows stay positive in their worst column: default S4 +13.29, Re-engine S7 +13.33. The item is +0.89 in S1-S5 and -0.50 / -0.51 in S6 / S7: inside the -$2B line, +0.75 weighted. It turns negative in two plausible columns and never reaches $1B, so it fails the company's added-move test: a binding soft veto. At a best margin of +0.89, no override can carry it. For the record, the failure is on value, not cash.

Waiting: a 2050 launch is worth about +0.61, also below $1B; rule 3 closes it if the 787 is re-engined.

Deleted: all Delay Tactics (naked $48.32B fine, rules 4-5).

tests.name: Safety: NGSA's last ramp step and the closure of the last A320 lines [Faury ask 1]

- A320: 184 in 2044, 28 in 2045 (about 2-3 a month) and 0 from 2047. The lines are running down on certified processes, never ramping.
- Condition: sustaining engineering for the in-service A320 fleet stays fully staffed after the lines close.
Passes on the default row and on the Re-engine row.

tests.name: Production readiness: a mature engine for the A350 Re-engine at EIS 2050 [Faury ask 4]
tests.threshold: Readiness is proven before launch. Team Step 3: the Re-engine's engine adds 0 EIS years, and any other engine needs at least $1B. Doctrine (profile section 11.3) wants the UltraFan widebody committed a year before our A350 launch, and treats a commitment in our launch year as a wait that fails the $1B test (section 11.2). The A350 Re-engine defaults to Rolls-Royce (rule 8 note). A failure is a soft veto.
tests.numbers:
What is on the record:
- No widebody engine for the A350 has been launched or committed.
- UltraFan widebody is ready 6 years after launch:
  - 2051 if Rolls-Royce launched it blind this round, 1 year after a 2050 EIS;
  - 2056 on Rolls-Royce's own stated sequence (to its board only once a Re-engine is on the record, i.e. a 2050 launch), 6 years after EIS.
- No Trent upgrade for the A350 is on the record. The board's Trent 1000 upgrade is a 787 engine. Rolls-Royce's Trent durability work stays inside existing R&D, which is not a re-engine.
- The GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033, is a 787 engine. It has never flown on the A350, which flies only the Trent XWB, and CFM/GE has not offered it for the A350.
- The doctrine's sequencing (committed by 2044) is not met.

Value:
- The grid's +0.89 (S1-S5) assumes EIS 2050, which no mature new engine can meet.
- My pure-discount pre-read (an inference) at the engine's earliest EIS: about +0.82 (2051) and about +0.56 (2056).
- An engine that adds EIS years needs at least $1B under Step 3, and none of these values reaches it.

Result: fail, a soft veto, binding. The grid margin against the best passing option (the all-default row) is +0.89 in S1-S5 and -0.50 / -0.51 in S6 / S7, about +0.75 weighted. That is below $1B, so no override can carry it.

This is not a failure of safety, quality, the ramp shield or supply crunch.

tests.threshold: No engine enters service before it is mature. If no mature widebody engine exists for 2050, the EIS moves; an immature engine never goes in, and none is named in public.
tests.numbers: On the five pillars this is a re-timing note, not a breach. Launching would not by itself put an immature engine into service, and the company's commitment (EIS moves, no immature engine named) holds on either row. So the hold rests on my readiness soft veto above, not on a pillars breach. If the ExCo ever launched, any public line must name no engine and give only a window.

tests.threshold: Supply and recruitment moves are sized to our own ramp and aimed at no rival; otherwise they read as bottleneck or poaching.

ops.memo:
My tests come from my role, not my record. Confidence: Very low.

Both changes running this round pass. NGSA's last step is small: 1,306 to 1,339 a year, then 1,366. That needs 2,612-2,732 engines a year, below the 2,770 we carried in 2044 with no crunch. The A320 tail is 28 aircraft in 2045 and none from 2047. Build them on the fewest lines, keep certified staff to the last aircraft, and release the surplus A320neo engine slots. Safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass on both rows.

The A350 Re-engine passes engineering capacity: NGSA development ended in 2037, so there is no overlap and no strain. It passes absorption too. The A350 line has delivered its planned 70 a year since 2026, with no event reported.

It fails readiness on the engine. No widebody engine for the A350 has been launched. UltraFan widebody is ready six years after launch: 2051 at the earliest, and 2056 on Rolls-Royce's own sequence. The GEnx upgrade is a 787 engine that has never flown on the A350. Doctrine wanted the engine committed a year before our launch; it has not been. Engine supply reset our 2027 rate. I will not launch an airframe into an engine gap.

On the five pillars this is a re-timing note. On my readiness test it is a binding soft veto, and at +0.89 no override can carry it.

Hold. Delay Tactics are deleted (rule 4, integrity). Secure the engine, then test again in 2050.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in service, and its ramp-up is completing in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and we will keep running it on that clock. This is how we prepared the Airbus of the 2030s, and it is how we will serve our customers into the next decade. To the end of the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the all-default package. ngsa hold, engine code fixed (none), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
1. Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081]. Two transitions run this round: NGSA's last ramp step (1,306, then 1,339, then 1,366) and the closure of the last A320 lines (28 in 2045, none from 2047). Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch on both rows, and no event is reported. One condition applies: no engine enters service before it is mature. No widebody engine for the A350 is on the record as mature for a 2050 EIS, so a Re-engine EIS would have to move rather than take an immature engine. On the pillars that is a re-timing note, not a breach (Wagner).
2. Ramp. It stays disciplined and controlled to the last step [AX-0010]. Nothing new goes on top of the closure that Lars cannot pass.
3. Prepare the next decade on its technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006]. I would welcome a late, cheap A350 derivative [AX-0082, A-0090], but not ahead of its engine.
4. What I can take to the Board. Nothing beyond the default, on this round's tests.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Rule 5: nothing is in development.
  - Integrity applies to bottleneck and both.
  - Every row breaks the -$2B line: one move -11.46 / +0.06 / +0.06 / +0.44 / +0.06 / -11.46 / +0.05; both moves -11.72 / -0.13 / -0.13 / +0.22 / -0.13 / -11.72 / -0.14.
  - The Board vetoes all of them.
- The team's stricter condition stands; I have not set it aside in any round. On the Board's reading, Delay Tactics are closed for the rest of the game [A-0299, A-0474].
- No other red line binds. Rule 3 is open (no 787 Re-engine is on the record) and rule 6 is clean (zero overlap).

STEP 2: SURVIVORS
- The default passes every test of Toepfer and Wagner.
- The A350 Re-engine row fails two binding soft vetoes, each on an independent ground:
  - Toepfer: the added-move test. The item is +0.89 in S1-S5 and -0.50 / -0.51 in S6 / S7. It is negative in two plausible columns and never reaches $1B, so it fails the doctrine's $1B launch condition (profile section 6).
  - Wagner: engine readiness. No A350 widebody engine has been launched or committed. UltraFan widebody would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, and in 2056 on Rolls-Royce's own sequence. The GEnx upgrade is a 787 engine. Doctrine's sequencing (profile section 11.3) is not met.
- So the only survivor is the default.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The raw best in S1 is the Re-engine at +14.98 against the default's +14.09, a gap of +0.89 (+0.75 at my weights). That is inside the $1B band where my rule takes the default anyway (profile section 9, step 6).
- The tie-breaks all point to hold:
  - less concurrency during the last ramp step and the A320 closure;
  - a later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2045);
  - fewer Board items (0 against 1 Qualified Majority item).
- Three grounds lead to hold, each on its own: Toepfer's veto, Wagner's veto and my default rule. Toepfer notes that his failure rests on the added-move reading, while the teams.md row test passes (Re-engine worst column S7 +13.33, default worst S4 +13.29). Even setting his veto aside, Wagner's engine finding and my $1B rule each decide it.

OVERRIDE CHECK
None is used. An override needs at least $1B over the best passing option. The margin is +0.89 at best, +0.75 weighted and -0.51 in S7. The Board would also veto a Re-engine that reached it through an override. The override budget (one per game) remains unused.

WHAT I ACCEPT, KNOWINGLY
- About $0.89B forgone in S1 ($0.75B weighted). This sits inside the $1B band, so it is not a doctrine premium.
- Waiting is worth little. A 2050 launch (EIS 2055) is not on today's grid. The pure-discount pre-read is about +0.61, below $1B (an inference; Toepfer confirms it).
- Rolls-Royce commits a widebody engine only once a Re-engine is on the record, so the doctrine's engine sequencing may never be met. Holding now is therefore close to keeping the A350 at Do Nothing for good.
- I decide that on the record. Do Nothing is a legitimate choice where the $1B test binds (profile section 6). The A350 stays our widebody focus at 70 a year and 41.2% share, flat on the grid.

BOARD-GATE LINES
- Package: no Board item. Every field is at its default, so there is nothing for the Board to approve or veto.
- For the record, the Re-engine not submitted:
  - Pillars: pass, with a re-timing note on the engine.
  - Toepfer: fail on the added-move test (binding soft veto). Cash passes: $1.0B a year, with $4.2B of headroom under $5.2B.
  - Wagner: fail on engine readiness (binding soft veto). Safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass.
  - Grid item: +0.89 x5 / -0.50 / -0.51.
  - Not taken to the Board.

REACTION DISCIPLINE (our own clock, rules 2 and 7)
- An fps launch re-times nothing.
- NGSA is never cancelled.
- A 787 Re-engine made public closes the A350 Re-engine under rule 3 and triggers no other move.

DELAY TACTICS
Off all game. They are never named in public.

- **Stable engine supply: met on every row.** NGSA has had CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine (2 sources) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, with three narrowbody makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) in 2045 and 2050.

- No Delay Tactics.

**2050 round**
