cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the ramp, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus asked for long-term engine supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item. The hold row is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and -27.95 in S2. Premium $0. No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer has already set that date: the NGSA has been in service since 2037. We win this round by running the fleet, keeping RISE whole, keeping CFM on offer to every airframer, and being straight about what we got wrong and what we don't know.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Hold: -28.04 / -27.95.
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
- Items against hold (Ghai and Ali both verified to the cent):
  - Open Fan alone: -20.01 / -19.97;
  - Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52;
  - Lobby alone: about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Weighted at .75 / .25: hold -28.02; Open Fan -20.00; Open Fan + Lobby -17.47. No call turns on the weights.

MY TESTS
1. No birthright [CX-0564]: neither column has a rival taking our slot. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers. The cases that could take a slot (a 7-year fps with a code that drops CFM) sit outside both columns, so they go on the watch list.
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody is on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -20.01 alone and -17.48 with Lobby.
   - Each loses more than its bill: $12.01B beyond $8B; $8.48B beyond $9B on Ghai's strain reading.
   - Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is not launching this year and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]:
   - An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after the NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056.
   - So no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. I'm saying that plainly rather than stretch the test.
   - The RISE allowance cannot cover $17.48B or $20.01B. Both are above $15B, and above $15B plus the $2.0B round cap.
   - I know my installed-base lens could dress this up as 'seeding the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. It doesn't apply when no airframer can take the engine inside the window.
5. Ducted as a defence (H3): it is ready, it has earned +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041, and there is nothing to decide.
6. Can the suppliers carry it: holding adds no project and no strain. The open supplier items are below.
7. Next generation: no fuel-burn claim and no 'next generation' wording. The 20% line binds RISE and is not engaged.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next row by $17.48B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap: $0, with the game total at $0 of $4.0B.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend before a volume is agreed;
  - price or terms talk without Safran.
  His terms test passes my statement as drafted.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times, and the statement carries no date. He raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and the overrides field is empty.

STRAIN READING (correction to the Board's inference)
Ghai's model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent with no new strain. Ali confirms that Lobby loads no supplier. So the bills are $8B (Open Fan alone) and $9B (Open Fan + Lobby), not $11B. This is inference, and no call turns on it.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 2's S1 forecast was -25.03. I booked -27.00 (Embraer's +1.97 left out), and today's row is -28.04.
- R&D (-4.00) and strain (-2.00) came in as forecast, so the whole -3.01 is engine value.
- On Ghai's derivation from the observed shares (inference: the bulletin doesn't state the folding rule):
  - The Joint Venture's rule effect is CFM -10 pp on the NGSA. Against the solo engines we priced, the GTF2's -5 gave way but the UltraFan's -10 effectively stayed, so CFM ran 5 pp lower on the NGSA at every step.
  - That 5 pp is worth -3.15. Embraer is worth +0.14 more on the lower base. Net -3.01, nothing left over: the Joint Venture is all of the gap.
  - Against the book, the -1.04 is -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11, which is in the row but was not booked.
- My 2045 and 2050 share calls ran about 3 pp high (5 pp times the NGSA's 65-72% of NB deliveries). The arithmetic was right on the column; the column was wrong.
- I called a Joint Venture commitment 'more likely than not' to stay off the record. Both partners had public conditional commitments and the airframe test was met. I listed it and didn't price it. That one's on me. From now on, a rival's standing public commitment is a live column.
- The programmes delivered: the Ducted took CFM from 13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA in 2041 on schedule, and Embraer took it to about 27% in 2042.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T (field data)
- What we know: deliveries. In every year from 2035 to 2044 each aircraft got two engines at our share (2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044), and no aircraft waited on a CFM engine.
- What we don't know: in 2035 we told the Board it would get field numbers in 2045, and we don't have them. The brief carries no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data. Ali certifies no gate result and raises no flag on analysis.
- I take this as an open item, not a pass. The cross-functional team owes the five items listed in other moves, and any failure comes to the Board at once. None of this changes a hold; it sets the agenda.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record doesn't address Embraer handling, Lobby or the game's Open Fan window, so company doctrine (profile section 6; dashboard_game section 2) drove those calls. Money follows Ghai's tests. Dates and readiness follow Ali's.

NEXT ROUND (2050)
No lever on this board lifts NB share. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window. I expect to hold again unless a Boeing fps, a Re-engine or a field finding changes the facts.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? It's the same game: the installed base, not share for its own sake. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages."

This round the board leaves us one real choice, and it isn't a hard one. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only levers left are an Open Fan and lobbying on emissions, and the airframer has already set that date. The NGSA has flown since 2037. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2055. One launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, after the board's narrowbody window closes in 2056. So no Open Fan reaches an airframer in this game. Both Open Fan rows lose more than their bill in both columns.

So the question isn't what to launch. It's three things.
1. Is the fleet flying today safe and durable on field data? That covers the LEAP fleet and the new single-aisle engine counting since 2041. Any flag ranks ahead of everything else on this page.
2. Do we keep delivering through the NGSA ramp and the longer A320 tail, with time-on-wing kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate?
3. Are we candid about what we got wrong? The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035. Last round I called it "more likely than not" to stay off the record, and I was wrong. Today's hold row is -28.04, against -25.03 forecast and -27.00 booked. We tie that out in numbers. In private, we say plainly that both objectives will be reported as not met.

How we win: hold every field, run the business, keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, and keep CFM on offer to every airframer. Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order, decide any tie.

(4) The LEAP-1B kit's certification outcome. It was due in early 2026, and my evidence ends in October 2025. If you have it, bring it. If not, say so, and say what that means for the installed fleet.

(5) The supplier-clearance review of the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613], and the tripwire status.
- The brief's field data: our NB engines run at two per aircraft delivered, at our share, every year. That was 2,144 engines on 1,570 aircraft in 2040, and 2,237 on 2,069 in 2044. Airbus is ramping the NGSA on the Alt plan, and Boeing is at 684 a year. No aircraft waited on a CFM engine.
- The tripwire was written to sequence Ducted development hardware behind the fleet, and that development is done. The fleet-first rule stays: kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate through the A320 tail and the NGSA ramp, and any rationing call made cross-functionally. Is that met on field data?

(6) Dates.
- An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055 (launch + 10). One launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, after the window closes in 2056.
- The NGSA has been in service since 2037, so the penalty applies in both columns. That includes S2, where a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055.
- Confirm that no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game.

(7) RISE: test results on the record, and any open durability item. RISE stays whole, and there is no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public.

(8) Supply load: holding adds none. Confirm or correct that an Open Fan + Lobby would stack two projects on the same constrained suppliers.

(9) Wording. Check my draft line for dates, for any Ducted figure, and for "next generation" (never for the Ducted). Check also "our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers": is that a fact you can stand behind?

BOARD GUIDANCE (labelled, non-binding).
- It vetoes any launch carrying a safety or durability flag of yours without a cross-functional answer on evidence, and any value resting on a ready year earlier than launch plus development years.
- It asks for every item in (2) to (5), and for any flag "at once".

Your record is thin here: your own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering. On supply, your record is my description of your job [CX-0633], so I'll check those parts against doctrine.
frame.initial_lean:
Lean: hold on every field. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx offer only hold. open_fan and lobby_emissions stay at hold. RISE stays whole as 50-50 technology with Safran.

Why:
- Hold is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and -27.95 in S2. The premium is $0, the game total stays at $0 of $4.0B, and the RISE allowance is unused.
- The Open Fan fails every test I have.
  - Not additive: -20.01 in S1 alone, $12.01B worse than its own bill. With Lobby it is -17.48.
  - The airframer set the date (H2). The NGSA has flown since 2037, and a 2045 launch is ready in 2055.
  - Allowance: the cost is $17.48B with Lobby and $20.01B alone. Both are above the $15B allowance, and above the allowance plus the round cap.
  - It buys no objective, because it can't be ready by 2050.
  I won't stretch the allowance.
- I know my installed-base lens could dress an Open Fan up as "seeding the next 30 years". Not here: no airframer can take it inside the window. "It's really not for us to say" when that architecture enters service [CX-0205], and the airframer has said.
- Lobby does nothing without an Open Fan.

Safran gate:
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We are not asking Safran to fund a product no airframer can take, and there is no reason on the record why it would.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE, and it is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- Embraer: no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first.
- Airbus long-term supply: the answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first and no public terms.
- genx: GE alone.

Expected column: S1, weighted provisionally at .60 against .40 on S2. Book low: the S1 hold row less Embraer's value until a volume is agreed. Rahul gives the number.

Candour, kept in private:
- I missed the Joint Venture. From here, a rival's standing public commitment gets weighted as a live column.
- Both objectives will be reported as not met: NB share is 47.2% in 2050, and the Open Fan can't be ready by 2050. No PV is given up for either.

What would change the lean: nothing on the grid. A safety or durability flag from Mohamed wouldn't change the holds, but it would go to the Board at once and go to the top of our statement. "We don't want to be rash, but we need to get after this straight away."

Draft public line (no rival, no Joint Venture comment, no dates, no Ducted figure, no price):
"Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate through the ramp. Airbus asked for long-term supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers. RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date. It's that simple. Ain't that hard."

tests.name: Item values verified (ask 1)
tests.threshold: Culp's item values match the round-3 grid rows to within $0.01B; Lobby alone, which has no row, is checked by inference
tests.numbers:
All match to the cent (S1 / S2).
- Open Fan row -48.05 / -47.92 minus hold -28.04 / -27.95: -20.01 / -19.97.
- Open Fan + Lobby row -45.52 / -45.40 minus hold: -17.48 / -17.45.

- Lobby alone: no row. About -1.00 in both columns (inference). It costs $1B, takes effect at once and has no board effect without an Open Fan. In round 2, Lobby on an Open Fan that was already floored at zero share came out at exactly -1.00 in every column.
- Culp's weights (.60 / .40): hold -28.00, Open Fan item -19.99, Open Fan + Lobby item -17.47.

tests.name: Strain reading (ask 2)
tests.threshold: The reading of the bill that ties the grid rows to the cent is the one the rows support (inference: my price/cost rule needs the bill right before the item is judged against it)
tests.numbers:
The rows support no new strain for either Open Fan row. This is an inference from my rough share model, which ties both rows to the cent.
- The model: all pp moves on the NGSA are summed, then floored at zero and renormalised. CFM sits at 26.98% on the NGSA in the hold row. One pp of CFM NGSA share from 2045 to 2056 is worth about $0.445B of PV (about $5.98M per NB engine in 2026 money, 2.2% inflation, 8.5% WACC).
- Open Fan alone: CFM goes from 26.98% to 0%, a share loss of $12.01B. Add $8B and the item is -20.01 (model -20.02) with no strain. With $2B of strain it would be -22.02.
- Open Fan + Lobby: CFM goes to 7.94% ((23.33 - 20 + 5) / 105), a loss of $8.48B. Add $8B + $1B and the item is -17.48 with no strain, to the cent. With strain it would be -19.48.
- Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 ties only with no strain. With strain it would be +0.53.
So the bills are $8B for the Open Fan alone (one project, and nothing is in development now) and $9B for Open Fan + Lobby. Lobby takes effect at once and is not a development project. The Board's $11B reading (Lobby making the Open Fan a second project) does not tie: the row would be $2B lower. The hold row's -2.00 of strain is the 2035 Ducted's, and it is sunk.
Either reading, each item loses more than its bill: the Open Fan alone by $12.01B / $11.97B beyond $8B; Open Fan + Lobby by $8.48B / $8.45B beyond $9B ($6.48B / $6.45B on the Board's $11B).

tests.numbers:
- Hold is -28.04 in S1 (yield 82.47%) and -27.95 in S2: the best row in both columns.
- It beats the next-best row (Open Fan + Lobby) by $17.48B in S1 and $17.45B in S2.

tests.name: Pays for itself: Open Fan alone, Open Fan + Lobby, Lobby alone (ask 3: value, cost, worst column, premium)
tests.threshold: Each launch's row beats hold in the expected column with its bill charged in full; no item loses more than its bill in any plausible column (inference: my price/cost rule in PV form, with the Board's bounded-downside reading)

For each option: value in S1 (expected column), cost in S1, worst column, and premium.

Your read of $20.01B / $19.97B and $17.48B / $17.45B checks. None of these buys an objective, because no Open Fan can be ready by 2050.

It ties to the cent. R&D (-4.00) and strain (-2.00) came in as forecast, so all of the -3.01 is engine value.
The observed NGSA split, derived from the bulletin (inference): the MAX is all CFM, the A320neo is CFM 60 / P&W 40, and P&W equals RR under the Joint Venture.

Value: 1 pp of NGSA share from 2038 is worth $0.63B. The model reproduces round 2's +1.97 and +6.07.

Share calls: the 5 pp on the NGSA times the NGSA's share of NB deliveries (65% in 2045, 72% in 2050) is 3.1 pp and 3.4 pp. On round 2's column, 2045 would have been 55.3% and 2050 50.6%. Culp's arithmetic was right on the column; the column was wrong.

cfo.memo:
Larry, the money ties out.

Your item values match to the cent: Open Fan -20.01 / -19.97; with Lobby -17.48 / -17.45; Lobby on top +2.53 / +2.52. On strain, the rows carry none: my rough model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent without it and is $2B off with it. So the bills are $8B and $9B, not the Board's $11B (inference). Either way each loses more than its bill, costs above $17.0B, and no airframer can take it inside the window. Hold is best in both columns. Premium $0, game total $0 of $4.0B, RISE allowance unused.

Reconciliation. The Joint Venture is the whole -3.01. On the observed shares we ran about 13% on the NGSA before our engines counted, against the 18% round 2 priced: five points lower at every step. That's -3.15, less +0.14 because Embraer is worth more on a lower base. Against my book, -1.04 is that -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11 I left out. Your share calls were right on the column; the column was wrong. I listed the Joint Venture and never priced it. We've been proven wrong on that one before.

But the good news is the programmes delivered: the Ducted took us from 13.5% to 23.2% in 2041, Embraer to 27% in 2042.

Floor: no new R&D, payout whole, no rating risk. Weights: I'd run .75 / .25; nothing turns on it.

Book -30.15: S1 less Embraer until a volume is agreed.

tests.numbers:
Culp's ask (6), recomputed from rules.md and the brief.

- Embraer (hold): 2035 + 7 = 2042, counting since 2042.
- GEnx (hold): 2030 + 3 = 2033. It counts from 2042, with no re-engine on the record. WB share 44.8% since 2042.
- Open Fan, options B and C: max(2045 + 10, 2045) = 2055. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060.

Grid (S1 / S2):
- hold: -28.04 / -27.95;
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
Items against hold, which I recomputed to the cent:
- Open Fan: -20.01 / -19.97;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
- Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52.
Both Open Fan rows carry the wait penalty, so they are valued on 2055, not on an earlier year. Hold adds no date.

The 'ready by 2050' objective cannot be met, because 2045 + 10 = 2055. Any premium or claim resting on it would rest on a year five years earlier than the board allows, and it would fail. Culp's frame claims none.

What test stands behind 2041? None on ducted hardware in my evidence. It is the board's development time, and it is now a date on the public record. I report no slip, because I have no evidence of one. I certify no gate result, because I have none.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my date veto): Culp's draft public line and other moves (Culp's ask 9)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, no ready year before launch plus development years, and no RISE ground-test, flight-test or entry year (hard rule 6).
tests.numbers:
Line by line:
- 'Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order': no date.
- 'the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers': no year. I can stand behind it on the record. The Ducted has been ready since 2041 (public table), and CFM is fitted on the NGSA, in service since 2037. The board counts the Ducted's share on NGSA deliveries from 2041. That it is flying is my reading of those two facts (inference): the record says 'ready', not 'in service'. Add nothing to it: no cycles, no time on wing, no 'durable', no year. We have no field numbers.
- 'We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and what we don't know yet': a commitment with no date. Today we have delivery data and nothing on durability.
- 'kits stay ahead of OE rate through the ramp': no date.
- The Airbus answer 'jointly with Safran': no rate, no year.
- 'RISE stays a technology programme ... the airframers will set its date': no ground-test, flight-test or entry year. My 2022 fly demo, 'by the middle of this decade', became 'this decade'. Promise none.
- No 'next generation', no Ducted figure, no rival named.

Other moves F(i) to (vii) carry no public dates. 2055, 2060 and 2056, and the objective note, stay in the rationale and with the Board.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service avoids the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
The first new narrowbody is the NGSA, in service since 2037.
- Launch in 2045: ready 2055, 18 years after the NGSA. In S2 a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055, the same year, but the NGSA came first, so the penalty applies in both columns.
- Launch in 2050: ready 2060, 23 years after the NGSA and 4 years after the board's narrowbody window closes in 2056.

Grid: Open Fan alone -20.01 / -19.97; with Lobby -17.48 / -17.45.

Confirmed: no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. The 2055 date itself is correct, so this is not my veto. Hard rule 2 bars the launch.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted and Embraer (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new narrowbody is in service, so lateness does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: ready 2041, 4 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry. It has earned its +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041.
- Embraer: counts from 2042, 5 years after the NGSA.
- In S2 a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055. The Ducted is ready 14 years ahead of it and Embraer counts 13 years ahead, if Boeing keeps code 7.
Hold carries both. There is nothing to launch.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Without a fuel-burn claim this is a wording check on the statement (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Neither the brief nor the draft line makes a fuel-burn claim.
- 'Next generation' does not appear. 'Our new single-aisle engine' is not a next-generation claim.
- Culp's H3 holds: the Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain. It is a defence, never the next generation.
- Culp's 20% line binds RISE. No RISE product is proposed, so the line is not engaged.

RISE facts for the Board: designed for 'more than 20%', ready for sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-capable. In tests with Airbus, open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's.

tests.name: Durability first: no plan trades durability for fuel burn or schedule
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers:
The test applies because Culp's frame puts durability first.
- Hold everything trades nothing: no new programme, no fuel-burn target, no schedule to compress.
- The plan keeps kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate.
- The Open Fan options would start a new hot-section development on the constrained suppliers while the installed fleet's durability data is still open. See the supply-load test.

tests.name: The Ducted's hot-and-harsh gate and enhanced inspection, on field data (Culp's asks 2 and 3; the Board's first ask)
tests.threshold:
- Harsh time on wing against the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 cycles, not the LEAP's about 4,800. The company target is 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral.
- The gate passed on turn-on, turn-off testing before entry into service.
- Enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts, in new make and MRO, from the first engine.
Field or test data only.
tests.numbers:
Not applicable because the test cannot be run. This is not a pass.
- The brief's only field data is deliveries. It has no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data, and the frame says the same. My own evidence ends in November 2025, before any ducted hardware existed.
- The engine has been in service four years (2041-2045). The fleet leader's cycles against 7,000-8,000 are not in the data.
- Did the gate pass before 2041? There is no evidence either way. The record shows ready in 2041 on the board's development time. No slip was reported, and no pass is certified.
- Enhanced inspection is institutionalised in new-make shops and MRO (my 2024 words). Findings from the first Ducted engine: none in the data.

Is missing data a flag? No. A flag is a finding: a failure turned on in test, or found in the field or in inspection. I have none, and I will not raise one on analysis. But missing data is not a clean bill either. It goes to the Board as an open item, and the cross-functional team owes the numbers. Until they exist, nothing in public or in private may claim the Ducted meets the yardstick.

tests.name: Installed LEAP fleet: the LEAP-1B kit (Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: A durability fix counts only when it is certified and the failure is turned off in test. A kit that does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of any new programme.

tests.name: LEAP supply review on field data, and the tripwire (Culp's ask 5; the Board's ask)
tests.numbers:
Pass on the delivery leg only.
- Every year from 2035 to 2044, CFM NB engines equal 2 x aircraft delivered x our share, to within 2 engines of share rounding: 2,592 engines on 1,704 aircraft (2035); 2,604 on 1,714 (2036, the peak); 2,144 on 1,570 (2040); 2,283 on 1,804 (2041); 2,237 on 2,069 (2044).

- Load: 2044 ran 367 engines below the 2036 peak of 2,604. On hold, volume is 2,106 in 2045 and 1,749 in 2050.
- The 9 suppliers at 15 sites: there is no supplier-level data. They are not certified, and I will not certify them on analysis.
- Kits and shop-visit material against OE rate: there is no kit data, so I cannot say this leg is met on field data.

Tripwire: not tripped on the OE leg, and the kit leg cannot be read. It was written to sequence Ducted development hardware behind the fleet. That development ended in 2041, so it has nothing left to sequence. The fleet-first rule stands through the A320 Alt-plan tail (CFM has 60% of A320neo engines) and the NGSA ramp, and any rationing call is cross-functional.

Supply in my record is only Culp's description of my job. No evidence: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 8)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. Inference: my supply role is in Culp's words only (the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers:
Hold adds no project and no strain. R&D stays at -4.00 (the 2035 Ducted) and strain at -2.00, both already in the row.

Open Fan + Lobby: the board's rule counts Lobby as a project, so the pair is two projects and carries the $2B strain. That is the board's count, for Ghai to verify. On the shop floor I correct it:
- Lobby loads no supplier; the Open Fan is the one hardware project.

So the stack is real, and the grid does not pay for it: -17.48 / -17.45 with Lobby, -20.01 / -19.97 alone. I recommend against.

No evidence: following doctrine (the board's strain rule).

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into the in-service engines while RISE matures (inference).
tests.numbers:
- GEnx: hold is the only option. The upgrade is on a proven architecture, ready since 2033 and counting since 2042 at 44.8% WB. Taking it to 787 customers puts the same proven engine on more aircraft. It is not a new engine.
- Narrowbody: RISE technology keeps flowing into the in-service LEAP and the Ducted while RISE matures. Hot-section cycles are the moat.

tests.name: Safety call (Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Any problem or order that touches safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, never to one person. Any flag goes to the Board at once.
tests.numbers:
No safety or durability flag is open on the evidence: the gate and LEAP-1B tests found no data and no finding. All orders are holds.

The frame sends any rationing call and the safety report (other move vi) to a cross-functional team. Any flag goes to the Board at once and to the top of the agenda and the statement. That meets the test. A flag, if one comes, arrives with the cross-functional answer on evidence.

tests.name: RISE test record (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: RISE test progress reported, and no open durability failure, before any Open Fan launch. No RISE date in public.

vetoes.ground:
Dates not backed by real testing, binding grounds 1 and 2: 'if it's not turn on and turn off, I will not believe the outcomes'; 'it's not on the back of a theory. It's not on the back of analysis.'

Inference note: my words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern whether to believe durability-fix results. That they give me a veto over programme dates is an inference. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with test evidence.

Every value on the grid rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2055), so nothing is vetoed now. I will re-check the final orders and the statement at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in 2045, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto: 2055 is the correct ready year.

Hard rule 2 bars it. Keep RISE whole as technology. We failed twice. We got it done.

Technical facts, if ever needed: RISE is designed to be ready for sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-capable, and open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's in tests with Airbus.

vetoes.plan: Wording in the public statement
vetoes.ground:
Advice.
- Keep 'now flying with our customers' and add nothing to it. No cycles, no time on wing, no 'durable' or 'mature' for the new engine or the LEAP-1B: we have no field numbers.

vetoes.plan: Open evidence items for the Board (not a flag)

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data would change my mind, never analysis.
(1) A flag. A Ducted or LEAP finding in the field or in inspection would be one: a harsh-environment failure turned on that the design does not turn off, a finding on a safety-critical part, or a fleet leader removed short of the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 harsh cycles. I raise it at once, with the cross-functional answer. The holds stay; the agenda and the statement change.
(2) The LEAP-1B kit. A certification result showing the kit does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of everything.
(3) Supply. Field data showing kits or shop-visit material behind OE rate, OE deliveries below airframer rate, or a supplier site not cleared. Then kits come first, and the rationing call goes to a cross-functional team.
(4) The Open Fan. Nothing on this board moves it. I would need an airframer whose first new narrowbody enters service no earlier than the Open Fan's ready year, plus RISE ground-test, flight-test and compact-core durability results turned on and turned off. With the NGSA flying since 2037, that cannot happen in this game.
(5) A Boeing fps on the record. It changes the column, not my dates: a 7-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2052, and a 10-year one in 2055. The Ducted is ready for either.
ops.memo:
In 2035 I told this Board that a failed gate moves the date, not the gate, and that you would get field numbers in 2045. Here is what I have.

Dates. Ducted: 2035 plus 6, 2041. Embraer and the GEnx count from 2042. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2055, eighteen years after the NGSA entered service. Launched in 2050, it is ready in 2060, past the 2056 window. No Open Fan reaches an airframe in this game. No option is valued on an earlier year. My date test passes. No veto.

Deliveries. From 2035 to 2044 every aircraft got two engines at our share: 2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044. No aircraft waited on us.

Durability. The brief has no time on wing, no harsh cycles, no inspection findings and no kit data. The yardstick stays the CFM56 in harsh service, 7,000 to 8,000 cycles, not 4,800. I cannot tell you the Ducted meets it. I cannot tell you it misses it. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in my evidence. The 9 suppliers are not certified.

Missing data is not a flag: a flag is a failure turned on. It is not a pass either. I sign off nothing on results. The cross-functional team owes you the numbers.

Public line: "now flying" stands on the record. Add nothing to it. No cycles, no "durable", no year, no "next generation".

Hold everything. Kits ahead of OE rate. RISE whole. Embraer, lobbying: No evidence: following Culp.

We bring RISE test results from after October 2025 to the Board once they are on the record. No product claim is made, so my 20% line is not engaged [CX-0217].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the ramp, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus asked for long-term engine supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item. The hold row is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and -27.95 in S2. Premium $0. No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer has already set that date: the NGSA has been in service since 2037. We win this round by running the fleet, keeping RISE whole, keeping CFM on offer to every airframer, and being straight about what we got wrong and what we don't know.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Hold: -28.04 / -27.95.
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
- Items against hold (Ghai and Ali both verified to the cent):
  - Open Fan alone: -20.01 / -19.97;
  - Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52;
  - Lobby alone: about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Weighted at .75 / .25: hold -28.02; Open Fan -20.00; Open Fan + Lobby -17.47. No call turns on the weights.

MY TESTS
1. No birthright [CX-0564]: neither column has a rival taking our slot. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers. The cases that could take a slot (a 7-year fps with a code that drops CFM) sit outside both columns, so they go on the watch list.
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody is on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -20.01 alone and -17.48 with Lobby.
   - Each loses more than its bill: $12.01B beyond $8B; $8.48B beyond $9B on Ghai's strain reading.
   - Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is not launching this year and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]:
   - An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after the NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056.
   - So no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. I'm saying that plainly rather than stretch the test.
   - The RISE allowance cannot cover $17.48B or $20.01B. Both are above $15B, and above $15B plus the $2.0B round cap.
   - I know my installed-base lens could dress this up as 'seeding the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. It doesn't apply when no airframer can take the engine inside the window.
5. Ducted as a defence (H3): it is ready, it has earned +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041, and there is nothing to decide.
6. Can the suppliers carry it: holding adds no project and no strain. The open supplier items are below.
7. Next generation: no fuel-burn claim and no 'next generation' wording. The 20% line binds RISE and is not engaged.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next row by $17.48B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap: $0, with the game total at $0 of $4.0B.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend before a volume is agreed;
  - price or terms talk without Safran.
  His terms test passes my statement as drafted.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times, and the statement carries no date. He raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and the overrides field is empty.

STRAIN READING (correction to the Board's inference)
Ghai's model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent with no new strain. Ali confirms that Lobby loads no supplier. So the bills are $8B (Open Fan alone) and $9B (Open Fan + Lobby), not $11B. This is inference, and no call turns on it.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 2's S1 forecast was -25.03. I booked -27.00 (Embraer's +1.97 left out), and today's row is -28.04.
- R&D (-4.00) and strain (-2.00) came in as forecast, so the whole -3.01 is engine value.
- On Ghai's derivation from the observed shares (inference: the bulletin doesn't state the folding rule):
  - The Joint Venture's rule effect is CFM -10 pp on the NGSA. Against the solo engines we priced, the GTF2's -5 gave way but the UltraFan's -10 effectively stayed, so CFM ran 5 pp lower on the NGSA at every step.
  - That 5 pp is worth -3.15. Embraer is worth +0.14 more on the lower base. Net -3.01, nothing left over: the Joint Venture is all of the gap.
  - Against the book, the -1.04 is -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11, which is in the row but was not booked.
- My 2045 and 2050 share calls ran about 3 pp high (5 pp times the NGSA's 65-72% of NB deliveries). The arithmetic was right on the column; the column was wrong.
- I called a Joint Venture commitment 'more likely than not' to stay off the record. Both partners had public conditional commitments and the airframe test was met. I listed it and didn't price it. That one's on me. From now on, a rival's standing public commitment is a live column.
- The programmes delivered: the Ducted took CFM from 13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA in 2041 on schedule, and Embraer took it to about 27% in 2042.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T (field data)
- What we know: deliveries. In every year from 2035 to 2044 each aircraft got two engines at our share (2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044), and no aircraft waited on a CFM engine.
- What we don't know: in 2035 we told the Board it would get field numbers in 2045, and we don't have them. The brief carries no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data. Ali certifies no gate result and raises no flag on analysis.
- I take this as an open item, not a pass. The cross-functional team owes the five items listed in other moves, and any failure comes to the Board at once. None of this changes a hold; it sets the agenda.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record doesn't address Embraer handling, Lobby or the game's Open Fan window, so company doctrine (profile section 6; dashboard_game section 2) drove those calls. Money follows Ghai's tests. Dates and readiness follow Ali's.

NEXT ROUND (2050)
No lever on this board lifts NB share. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window. I expect to hold again unless a Boeing fps, a Re-engine or a field finding changes the facts.

memo_weighing.ops:
Ali's record is thin. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering. On supply, his record is only my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts against doctrine.
- Date test: passes on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2055, 2060), and it binds nothing here.
- His Open Fan advice matches hard rule 2 and the grid.
- His supply-load view (Lobby loads no supplier; an Open Fan would stack a new hot section on the constrained suppliers) is consistent with the board's strain rule and with Ghai's tie, so I accept it.
- On durability, I took his line exactly: no flag, because a flag is a finding, but missing data is not a pass. He certifies nothing on analysis. The five open items go to the Board as owed by the cross-functional team.
- I adopted his wording advice in full. 'Now flying with our customers' stands, with nothing added: no cycles, no 'durable', no year, no 'next generation'.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. The GTF fleet on the A320neo is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. A large fleet is coming through the shops, so the fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We will report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service on NGSA since 2037 on code 7. It meets an fps 10-yr EIS of 2055 (S2) with a 19-year margin, and a 7-yr EIS of 2052. No second development is running.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are the only values the brief lists (round3.md §3). The grid has one row: -1.65 in S1 and -1.68 in S2.

WHY `gtf2_solo: hold`. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture when it formed in 2035. It is no longer a separate programme: its engine is the Joint Venture engine, ready since 2036. Hold keeps that in-service engine and its durability work whole.

WHY `jv_with_rr: hold`. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a commitment can be withdrawn only before formation (rules.md). Hold keeps it on the published terms: one engine, the gear and core P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233], and partner content only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

ANSWERS TO CALIO

(1) Proposal: as above. Holding both fields costs us nothing technically.

(2) Readiness: confirmed.
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2. GTF2 launched in 2030 and was ready in 2036 (launch + 6). Formation + 6 would have been 2041 and UltraFan NB 2037, so ready = 2036.
- NGSA entered service in 2037 on code 7, with CFM + PW + RR fitted. The one-year margin held, and the code cannot change now.
- S2, an fps 10-yr launched in 2045, enters service in 2055: a 19-year margin. An fps 7-yr would enter service in 2052 (16 years), and an fps via Embraer in 2055. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2057 or 2060.
- No second development is running: no new programme on the record, and $0 of new R&D. Programme R&D is $2.00B in total, booked in 2035 (brief §1).
- Caution (bias check on my own reassurance): the board sets ready at launch + 6 and models no slip. That the 2036 date held on the record is the rule's outcome, not evidence that our dates no longer slip. The company's +1.5 to 2 year derivative-entry prior is not refuted by it.
- Condition on the fps offer: we offer the engine as certified. Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise.

(3) In-service durability: the bad number first.
- The brief and our files hold no time-on-wing, LLP life against plan, shop-visit findings, removal causes or hot-and-sandy data for the Joint Venture engine. That is eight years into service, 2037-45.
- They also do not hold the 2036 gate data (endurance hours, LLP life at EIS, maturity-gate status) that the Board asked for in round 2.
- I invent none. That is what we report to Governance and Public Policy.
- Process for the report (doctrine and my record):
  - Report by operating environment, never as a fleet average. In 2023, three quarters of the GTF fleet flew in cool climates and that hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122].
  - Track fleet leaders in hot-and-sandy operation separately.
  - Report LLP life by part family against the life declared at EIS [PX-0128].
  - Report shop-visit findings by cause.
- On the public record, Airbus took the engine into service in 2037 on its 'clock of maturity' ('no engine will enter service before it is mature'). That is Airbus's word, not our data.

(4) Parts and capacity: ground 2 PASS.
- Load (brief §1):
  - 730 engines in 2040, 1,024 in 2044 (the peak; +40%, about the size of the 2023 castings step [PX-0125]; the 2043-44 step alone was +13%).
  - Then 976 in 2045 (-4.7%) and 928 to 987 a year to 2056.
  - The highest year after the peak is 987 (2051), 3.6% below it. The largest yearly step after it is +2.8% (2049).
  - Round 2 projected +53% to 1,068. The squeeze came in smaller.
- Installed base on the brief's counts: 7,339 engines delivered in 2026-36 and 13,937 P&W NB engines in 2026-44 are coming into the shops. The board does not model shop visits, so I give no shop-visit peak date or interval. '2044-47' is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak.
- As the A320neo OE tail ends under the Alt plan, GTF OE demand on pacing parts falls away and those parts go to MRO.
- Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123], decided daily and reviewed by the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]:
  1. AOG spares.
  2. MRO material for engines in the shop. Shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124].
  3. GTF Advantage kit parts, fitted to engines already in the shop.
  4. OE installs: NGSA long-term-agreement slots and the A320neo tail.
- This can leave Airbus short of engines on some days. That trade is Calio's to balance with Airbus [PX-0099][PX-0110], and the tie-break says the fleet beats a new engine.
- Supplier quality gates come before each rate step, including the small post-2048 steps, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040].
- The brief shows no live P&W quality escape or supply problem, and no order launches anything.

(5) Configuration control.
- On the record, nothing has changed: the engine is the one ready since 2036, with no new programme and $0 of new R&D.
- The published rule stands:
  - Partner content enters only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence.
  - We instrument any new feature in our own application rather than take a partner's design at face value [PX-0168][P-1215].
  - P&W signs durability only on what it tested.
  - The gear and core stay P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233].
- The engineering-change log itself is not in my brief. It goes to the committee with the durability report.

(6) Product answer to CFM's ducted engine: YES, as an internal other move, on four conditions.
- (a) Time on wing ahead of fuel burn [P-1360]. No new programme, no derivative, no board R&D.
- (b) Each change goes in as an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence.
- (c) Kit parts rank behind AOG and shop material.
- (d) The same in-service engineering team that works the shop findings does the work.
On those conditions it is fleet work, not a second engine: it cuts shop visits and therefore pacing-part demand. It changes no payoff, and it is not a price answer.

(7) GTF Advantage kit.
- It continues at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0117] (pass-through for the kit is inference).
- My last fleet-configuration figure is 60% in June 2023, with a target of 90% within 2-3 years [PX-0116]. The evidence has no outcome for that target and no 2045 figure, so we publish none.

(8) Two-ground ruling on hold/hold: both pass. No veto.

ROUND-2 BOARD RECOMMENDATIONS IN MY LANE
- Withdraw test (rec 1): overtaken. My technical trigger was not hit. Formation came in 2035, two years before EIS. It folded GTF2 in as the one engine, with no second development and no change to the configuration being certified.
- Durability gate (rec 3): the gate data are not in my brief (see 3). The +1.5 to 2 year prior is the company's, not mine.
- Fleet first (rec 7): adopted as above. The brief shows no escape through the +40% step, but the board models no quality, so that is not proof that there was none.

STATEMENT CHECK (Calio's draft): PASS. 'Ready since 2036' and 'flown on NGSA since 2037' are facts on the bulletin. 'Claim the durability the fleet data show' is right, and the draft gives no forward date and no share projection.
Advice, not binding: 'more time on wing from every engine ... our new engine ... alike, and that work is not done' reads as a known shortfall on the Joint Venture engine. We have no data either way. Keep the known GTF shortfall, and for the new engine say we will report what the fleet data show, bad news first.

vetoes.plan: Orders `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (my proposal)
vetoes.ground: None invoked. Ground 1 passes: no order puts an engine on an airframe, the engine was ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS, and hold compresses nothing. Ground 2 passes: no launch, and no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem in the brief.

Ground 1 would bind at the veto check if the statement claimed proven durability, time-on-wing or LLP figures not in the fleet data, or promised an fps-specific rating or configuration before it is tested. ops.would_change_mind_if:
(1) In-service data show a durability shortfall on the Joint Venture engine: hot-and-sandy time on wing below plan, LLP life short of plan, or an unplanned shop-visit finding. It then goes first in the statement and the committee report. The incremental work refocuses on that fix, and the fps offer carries the fixed configuration only once it has its own test evidence.
(2) A brief shows a live quality escape, rising AOG or a supply break. I contain first, give a dated recovery, and OE gives way to the fleet.
(3) The incremental durability work starts pulling engineers or pacing parts from the shops. We drop it.
(4) Partner content enters the certified configuration without its own test evidence, or rights over the gear or core pass. I invoke ground 1 and flag the red line.
(5) In 2050, a new engine item appears on the sheet. It must serve a committed airframe and be ready by its EIS. The in-service engine already meets any fps EIS, so I would ask what a second development buys during the shop-visit tail.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. Our Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA for eight years, and I can't put one time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figure in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee. They're not in my brief, the board doesn't model them, and I won't make them up. A caution on us: the 2036 ready date held because the board sets ready at launch plus six. That's a rule, not proof our dates stopped slipping.

What I can confirm. The engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service 2037. One engine, no second development, $0 of new R&D. It meets any fps EIS: 2052 on a 7-year, 2055 on a 10-year. Gear and core stay ours; partner content goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

Parts. OE peaked at 1,024 engines in 2044, up 40% from 730 in 2040, then 976 in 2045 and 928 to 987 a year to 2056. No step above the peak. About 13,900 P&W engines delivered since 2026 are coming through the shops as the A320neo tail ends. On the 30 pacing parts: AOG first, shop material second, kits third, OE last, daily. No live escape in the brief. Ground 2 passes.

I propose hold and hold, the only legal values. No veto. Durability work inside existing R&D: yes, as fleet work that cuts shop visits.

My record is one event, June 2023. The Joint Venture, configuration and in-service views are seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit to the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0088][PX-0106]. There is no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100]. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. We publish no 2045 share figure, because we do not have one: Eddy's last figure is 60% in June 2023, with a 90% target [PX-0116], and the evidence has no outcome for that target. We give no dated AOG recovery, because my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Kit parts rank third on the pacing parts, behind AOG spares and shop material. The move changes no payoff on the board.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on pacing parts through the OE plateau and the shop-visit tail
other_moves.detail: On the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123] the ranking is: (1) AOG spares; (2) MRO material for engines in the shop, since shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124]; (3) GTF Advantage kit parts for engines already in the shop; (4) OE installs, meaning NGSA long-term-agreement slots and the A320neo tail. Allocation is decided daily and reviewed by the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]. Supplier quality gates come before every rate step, including the small steps after 2048, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. The load is 1,024 NB engines at the 2044 peak, 976 in 2045, and 928 to 987 a year to 2056. About 13,900 P&W NB engines delivered in 2026-44 are coming into the shops. Eddy's correction stands: 2044-47 is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak, because the board does not model shop visits. Some days this leaves Airbus short of engines. I balance that with Airbus jointly [PX-0099][PX-0110], and the fleet comes first [PX-0080].

other_moves.move: In-service durability report on the Joint Venture engine to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first
other_moves.detail: Eddy reports. The bad number first: after eight years in service (2037-45), we have no time-on-wing, LLP-life, removal or shop-visit figures for the Joint Venture engine, and no 2036 gate data, in front of the committee. We invent none. Going forward the report gives: time on wing by operating environment, never as a fleet average, with hot-and-sandy fleet leaders tracked separately [PX-0122]; LLP life by part family against the life declared at EIS [PX-0128]; shop-visit findings by cause; and the engineering-change log, confirming that no partner content entered the certified configuration except as an engineering change with its own test evidence. If the data show a shortfall, it goes first in the next statement and the next report.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture held to its published terms
other_moves.detail: The terms are those published with the 2035 commitment [P-1233][P-1875]. Risk, investment and revenue are shared, with both partners on one engine. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property. Partner contributions are recognised only as a valuation in the share split, with no licence and no cash payment to the partner. Partner content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and P&W signs durability only on an engine it has tested. Any departure in the definitive agreement is a significant transaction and goes through Finance to the full Board before signature.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture engine offered, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet
other_moves.detail: The offer is on standard terms, priced for value [PX-0055]. No concession, discount, free upgrade or launch-style term goes to Boeing, Airbus or a fleet customer to win a selection or defend NGSA share. Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto applies, and on the grid an fps code-7 selection is worth −0.03. Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise. We give no airframer date [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: Whole-life NPV review and round-2 bridge to the Finance Committee; off-grid rival exposure named, not booked
other_moves.detail:
Mitchill presents the review, as UTC's board reviewed the GTF every year [P-1191].

Whole life:
- ΔPV is −1.65: +0.35 of engine value less $2.00B of R&D, charged undiscounted. That is $0.18 of PV per $1 of R&D.
- It is −1.65 against Do Nothing and against a $2B buyback.
- Capitalise is NOT MET, and no order on the grid closes the 1.65 gap.
- His discounted view, about −0.74, is Finance information only.

Bridge to round 2:
- −0.68 against round 2's hold row in S1, and −3.03 against S4 (+1.38).
- Formation was worth +2.35. CFM's two moves took −3.03. His rough split, which is inference: the ducted engine about −2.3, the Embraer partnership about −0.75.
- Holding GTF2 in 2035 still kept 17.65 against a cancel. From 2045 forward the engine adds +0.94 of PV at 2026.

Exposures named and not booked:
- A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule −35 pp, or −20 pp with lobbying, for CFM. Favourable to us; size not on the brief.
- An fps without us: below S2.
- An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
- Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.
- Rolls-Royce widebody moves: no effect on us.

This is the baseline for the 2050 bridge.

other_moves.move: Incremental time-on-wing work on the Joint Venture engine and the GTF Advantage kit inside the existing durability budget
other_moves.detail: This is the product answer to CFM's ducted engine, not a price answer [P-0768][PX-0093]. It goes ahead on Eddy's four conditions: (a) time on wing ahead of fuel burn [P-1360], with no new programme, no derivative and no board R&D; (b) each change goes in as an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence; (c) its parts rank behind AOG spares and shop material; (d) the in-service engineering team that works the shop findings does the work. Mitchill's condition also applies: it is funded inside the existing durability budget, and any money above that comes to his gate first. If it starts pulling engineers or pacing parts from the shops, we drop it. It changes no payoff on the board.

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. The GTF fleet on the A320neo is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. A large fleet is coming through the shops, so the fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We will report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
Decision: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and the only values the brief lists. Premium is $0.00B and `overrides` is empty. The round never reaches the Board's review, so this rationale is the record.

1. The bad number first. ΔPV is −1.65 (yield 98.5%): +0.35 of engine value against $2.00B of R&D. Capitalise is NOT MET, a gap of 1.65. No order, premium or concession on this sheet closes it. The grid has one row: −1.65 in S1 and −1.68 in S2.

2. Starting point and vetoes.
- Eddy proposed hold/hold and passes both of his grounds. Mitchill recommends the same and finds no veto on the orders.
- Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto falls on any concession for the fps code or NGSA share (other-move test 1). I framed that move only to reject it. It is not submitted, and the veto is recorded.
- His conditional ground-4 veto on booking upside is not triggered. The final statement books no fps selection, share projection, Open Fan gain, airframer date or durability figure.
- Eddy has no binding veto. I took his statement advice: the Joint Venture engine has no time-on-wing data either way, so the statement no longer implies a shortfall on it and keeps only the known GTF one.

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service on NGSA since 2037 on code 7. It meets an fps 10-yr EIS of 2055 (S2) with a 19-year margin, and a 7-yr EIS of 2052. No second development is running.
- The binding readiness test passes.
- Eddy's caution is accepted: the 2036 date held because the board sets ready at launch + 6. That is the rule's outcome, not proof that my dates stopped slipping. I keep discounting my own operating dates [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- The in-service evidence is the bad number. After eight years we have no time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figures in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and we invent none.
- Parts pass Eddy's ground 2. The ranking is AOG spares, then shop material, then kit parts, then OE, with quality gates before each rate step.

4. Optimise inside it. With one legal row there is nothing to choose on the grid, and the tie-breaks all point the same way:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is answered. We are on NGSA, and the engine can meet any fps EIS. Applying that RTX-wide line to engines is inference.
- A rival's discount, or CFM's new engine, never moves our price [PX-0055].

5. Weights. I take Mitchill's weights, S1 0.75 and S2 0.25, over my framing draft of 0.70/0.30.
- Against an fps launch: Boeing's latest words on the record are 'not launching a new airplane this year', 'the market case for us isn't there yet' and 'a month late rather than a month early', and it has passed two rounds.
- For one: its NB share fell from 45.1% to 33.1% with the MAX at its cap. That is pressure, not a launch.
- My own incrementalism bias leans the same way, so I do not push S2 above his figure.
- Expected PV: −1.6575, rounded to −1.66. It is −1.659 on my draft and −1.665 on equal weights. Worst column: S2, −1.68.

6. Why S2 is −0.03 (Mitchill, inference on the rules). An fps launched now enters service in 2055 against an NB count that ends in 2056. Code 7 splits that slice three ways. Boeing's gain comes off Airbus, where we already sit. A selection is worth nothing to us on the grid, so we pay nothing for it.

7. Bridge to round 2 (Mitchill confirms; the attribution is the Board's inference and his).
- Against round 2's hold row in S1: −0.68. Against S4: −3.03. Formation was worth +2.35, and CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership took −3.03.
- His rough split is about −2.3 for the ducted engine and about −0.75 for Embraer.
- Year profile (nominal): 2037 −0.1; 2038-40 −1.2/−1.1/−0.9 during the A320 wind-down; then +0.1 to +1.4 to 2054, +1.5 in 2055 and +2.0 in 2056.
- Correction to the Board's text: from 2041 the range is +0.1 to +2.0, not +0.3 to +1.5.
- My PV check gives +0.37 (−0.57 before 2045, +0.94 from 2045), against the brief's +0.35.
- Lesson: in round 2 we held CFM at hold, and it cost 3.03. Off-grid rival exposure is now named beside each column and not booked:
  - A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule CFM loses 35 pp, or 20 pp if it lobbies. Favourable to us; not booked.
  - An fps without us: below S2.
  - An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
  - Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.
  - Rolls-Royce widebody moves: no effect on us.

8. Dividend and debt (Mitchill).
- $0 of new R&D. Programme R&D is $2.00B in total, with no fold-in write-off.
- The published terms carry no Joint Venture cash to the partner.
- The dividend is covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. The stretch is unused.
- −1.65 is 1.5% of EV; it is a PV, not a cash call.

9. Veto checks.
- Mitchill's four grounds:
  - Dividend and debt: not reached, because the envelope passes.
  - Unselected engine: not applicable. The engine is selected and in service.
  - Aggressive terms: pass. No concession is offered, and the concession move is vetoed.
  - Booked upside: pass. The booked number is S1 −1.65.
- Eddy's two grounds:
  - Durability by EIS: pass.
  - Parts and capacity: pass. No live escape is in the brief, though the board models no quality.
- No red-line flag is open.

10. Bias check.
- Optimism on dates: discounted, per point 3.
- Architecture loyalty: the Joint Venture engine is our GTF2 architecture, but I claim no durability for it that the fleet data do not show.
- Value capture: the grid backs it here, since a selection is worth −0.03.

11. Red lines in force, none breached:
- durability first;
- fleet first;
- Joint Venture terms (never the gear or core [P-1233]);
- dividend, then debt, then buybacks;
- value, not share;
- proof before commitment [P-1367];
- no airframer dates [PX-0062];
- narrowbody only [PX-0027].
Shared source on code 7 and equal Joint Venture shares are declared as doctrine relief at $0.00B (franchise defence, inference [PX-0058][P-1292]).

12. Disclosure changes, per the Board.
- Dropped: 'planned to be ready in 2036', 'Today Pratt & Whitney commits' and 'Rolls-Royce has not done so'.
- Now stated as facts on the bulletin: ready since 2036, and flown on NGSA since 2037 alongside CFM.
- Durability: we claim only what the fleet data show. We give no share projection and no airframer date, and we repeat that our gear and core stay ours.

13. Look-ahead to 2050.
- I expect `hold` only on the sheet, with no cancel or withdraw right left.
- Any engine item would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, the last year of the NB count. It must clear the grid alone (≥ 0 against hold, worst column no more than $2B below it) and serve a committed airframe on the record. No premium is available against credibility, which is already met. Mitchill expects any such item to fail.
- Set up now: the −1.65 baseline and the exposure list, so the 2050 bridge needs one line per rival move.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighted heavily. I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own operating dates, and he owned his round-2 miss plainly.
- I adopted his weights (S1 0.75, S2 0.25) in place of my 0.70/0.30. Boeing's latest record and its two passed rounds outweigh the share-pressure indicator. The change is 0.0015 of expected PV.
- I adopted his row arithmetic (−1.6575; worst column S2 −1.68) and his envelope check: $0 new R&D, no Joint Venture cash, dividend covered, debt on its pre-ASR path, stretch unused.
- I adopted his whole-life review: −1.65 against Do Nothing and a buyback; about −0.74 discounted, as information only; +0.94 forward from 2045; 17.65 kept against the 2035 cancel.
- I adopted his bridge. Attribution confirmed: formation +2.35, CFM −3.03, split about −2.3 for the ducted engine and −0.75 for Embraer as inference. That includes his correction of the Board's +0.3 to +1.5 range to +0.1 to +2.0, and his PV check (+0.37).
- I adopted his reading of why S2 is −0.03, and his off-grid exposure list beside each column, named and not booked.
- His binding ground-3 veto on any concession is recorded and respected; the move is not submitted. His conditional ground-4 veto is not triggered by the final statement.
- I took his advice that any statement on time on wing rest on Eddy's data.
- I adopted his 2050 hurdle.
memo_weighing.ops:
His proposal is the starting point, taken as proposed: hold/hold.
- Readiness: confirmed and binding on me. The engine is the folded GTF2, ready 2036 and in service 2037, and it meets fps EIS 2052 or 2055. No second development is running.
- His bias caution is accepted. The held 2036 date is the board's launch + 6 rule, not evidence that our dates stopped slipping, so the company's +1.5 to 2 year derivative-entry prior stands.
- His bad number is accepted as given: no time-on-wing, LLP or shop-visit data after eight years, and no 2036 gate data. We report that and invent nothing. His reporting method goes to the committee: by operating environment, hot-and-sandy leaders separate, LLP life by part family, findings by cause.
- His ground-2 pass and pacing-part ranking are adopted, including his correction that 2044-47 is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak. His load figures are adopted: 730 to 1,024 (+40%), then 928 to 987 a year.
- His four conditions on the incremental durability work are adopted.
- His configuration-control confirmation is adopted, with the change log going to the committee.
- His statement advice is taken: the line implying a known shortfall on the Joint Venture engine is dropped, and the known GTF shortfall is kept.
- I publish no kit-configuration figure, since his last is 60% in June 2023.
- Weight caveat: Eddy's seat rests on one event, June 2023, so his record is Low. His Joint Venture, configuration and in-service views are seat doctrine. On readiness, parts and capacity I defer to him as the rule requires.

rolls_royce.rationale:
So, a delivery round. All four fields at hold. No Board item.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Start from my proposal: all hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.
2. Binding vetoes. McCabe withholds her co-signature on t1000_upgrade launch and on ultrafan_wb launch (binding). Respected: both stay at hold. Watson invokes no Civil veto. He checked the public statement sentence by sentence and it carries no year. I added his support line, which has no date. Overrides are empty.
3. Expected scenario S1. Weights shown (the brief gives none): mine 0.65 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10; the Board's 0.70 / 0.05 / 0.15 / 0.10; a Re-engine stress 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20.
4. Grid rows, with and without each item (ΔPV against the status quo):
- 'UltraFan NB: hold': +11.03 / +10.99 / +11.03 / +11.28. Expected +11.05 on mine, +11.05 on the Board's, +11.08 on the stress. Worst column +10.99 (S2). It is the best plan in every column.
- 'hold + T1000 upgrade': +4.55 / +4.51 / +4.55 / +4.82, so −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 against hold. Expected −6.48 on all three weight sets. Worst column −6.48, beyond its own −$2B bill. It buys $0.52-0.54B of engine value for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- 'hold + UltraFan WB': +2.03 / +1.99 / +2.75 / +3.26, so −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02 against hold. Expected −8.79 on mine and the Board's, −8.59 on the stress. Worst column −9.00, beyond its own −$4B bill. It buys $0 / $0 / $0.72B / $0.98B.
- Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights.
5. Premium 0. All hold is the best plan. Shortfalls declined: upgrade $6.48B against the $3B cap; UltraFan WB $8.79B (worst $9.00B) against the $1B sub-cap.
6. Red lines checked on the final orders:
- No UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it: UltraFan WB with no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record would breach it. Watson and McCabe both flagged this. Struck: it is held.
- No early dates: none in public.
- No new narrowbody value: both narrowbody fields hold, the only legal value.
- One big programme at a time: strain stays $0.
- Balance sheet: untouched.
- Commercial discipline: standard terms only.
No unresolved flag.

WHY HOLD, IN MY OWN TERMS
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]. The upgrade is differentiated on 787 time on wing, but fails 'viable business model' on the strain. UltraFan WB fails 'large market' (no Re-engine) and 'viable business model'.
- My instinct on the 787 is 'Why not?' [RX-0117], and I said we could regain share [RX-0101]. But 4.8 points of share for −$6.48B is share bought at a loss, and 'we are not after market share' [R-1582]. Widebody is safe without it: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column.
- No options management [RX-0051]: a widebody item with no Re-engine to fly is not launched as a hedge.
- The Joint Venture is formed and ready. The 2035 re-test is closed by formation, withdrawal is gone, and the money is booked.

CORRECTIONS TAKEN FROM THE MEMOS
- Watson: widebody share was 58.0% in 2040, not 55.2%. The GEnx upgrade counts from 2042.
- Watson: the upgrade would count from 2048 in every column, not from 2050 in S3-S4. The rules and the grid agree.
- McCabe: the right 2035 benchmark for the lookback is S4, P&W commits (+14.06), not S1. Against it the miss is −$3.03B of engine value, with the fold saving $2.29B.
I record them plainly.

WHAT I CANNOT CLAIM
- The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data. There is no time-on-wing or shop-visit figure, and I invent none. The written standard and the first report go to the Committee this round.
- The gear and core are P&W's. Our aftermarket cash rests on durability we do not design (Watson, inference).
- My record has no evidenced decision on running a formed Joint Venture. The governance, support and lookback moves follow company doctrine (profile.md §4, §9 steps 6-12) and the Board's guidance, not my own words.
- Widebody items in 2050: closed on this board unless that grid shows otherwise. McCabe's estimate is about −6.7 and −8.6 against hold, and Watson confirms the shorter windows (upgrade counting from 2053, UltraFan WB ready 2056).

'They are a milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062].

board_response.response:
Status:
- The Joint Venture commit was approved and formed in 2035, so the 2045 re-test is closed by formation.
- The engine was ready in 2036 and entered service on NGSA in 2037, with nothing compressed.
- Widebody items stayed at hold.
- Standard terms held.
