priorities: 1. Product safety in service comes first. Since the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine has been ready since 2036, the narrowbody question is no longer when we launch. It is whether we deliver what flies. On the brief's figures the Joint Venture engine has about 3,091 Rolls-Royce engines delivered by the end of 2044, about 4,044 by the end of 2045, and roughly 950-990 a year after that. Durability, time on wing, life-limited parts and support at that scale are now the absolute priority. Any Rolls-Royce content entering the in-service engine goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never compressed. P&W's published terms say the same [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283, R-1476].

2. Protect the widebody core without a board-level widebody programme. The $5B strain is now permanent for any widebody item: the Joint Venture is a narrowbody programme on the record, and it cannot be cancelled once ready. Against the hold row, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 and UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02 (S1-S4). Both lose more than their own bill in every column. Our widebody share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, 5.2 points above our line. Hold both, and keep Trent durability work inside the existing budget [R-1574, RX-0246, RG-0068, RX-0123, RX-0214, RG-0019].

3. Profit over share, with no narrowbody premium. Every narrowbody field can only be held this round. S2 (Boeing launches a 10-year fps and selects us on code 5) is −0.04 against S1 on the hold row, so a Boeing selection adds nothing to us on this grid. Chasing it with price, dates or launch-style terms would be buying share for its own sake. Keep standard terms through the Investment Committee [R-1561, R-1582, R-1011, RX-0081, RX-0097, RX-0213].

4. The balance sheet stays untouched, and cash goes back under the capital frame. No new programme spend is needed this round. The Joint Venture share ($4.00B) and the fold write-off ($1.71B) are already booked. We expect no balance-sheet trigger, an unchanged 30-40% payout, and a buyback cadence decided on fit, value and timing [RX-0242, R-0900, RG-0041, RG-0059, RG-0033].

5. Make the Joint Venture work. Alignment is what IAE lacked. P&W's terms are now public: gear and core stay P&W's, contributions are credited as a valuation in the share split, no licence passes, and partner content comes only after entry into service. We need a governed engineering interface, a shared support network and capacity that does not draw on Trent XWB and Trent 7000 [R-0318, R-1010, RX-0072, R-0916, R-0920, RX-0287, RX-0286].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4 of 5, unchanged. This is a delivery round, not a commitment round. Neither open item (t1000_upgrade or ultrafan_wb launch) stays within its own bill in any column. Both carry shortfalls far above our caps: $6.48B against $3B for the upgrade, and $8.02-9.00B against $1B for UltraFan WB. We therefore expect every field at hold, premium_b at 0 and no balance-sheet trigger. Our horizon (2.5) is honoured by keeping UltraFan technology and Trent durability inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, not by paying a premium on the grid.

recommendations.text:

Make the Joint Venture work on aligned terms. That is the IAE lesson.
- The 2045 re-test we asked for in round 2 is closed: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdrawal is no longer an option.
- What remains is governance. Agree with P&W one engineering interface and one durability standard. Run a joint support network, with our partner shops added to P&W's rather than replacing them. Have a clear process for crediting each side's technology in the share split.
- The equal-share rule now binds. The 2035 grid showed 31.3% for 2050; the brief now shows 26.4%, after CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership entered the record (inference). Bring any Joint Venture share or term question to the Board before it is public.

Hold both widebody items. We note what the hold costs, and what it does not.
- The $5B strain is permanent for any widebody item. On this board neither item can stay within its own bill in 2045, nor in 2050 unless that grid shows otherwise.
- The franchise is at 55.2%, 5.2 points above our line, in every column.
- Defend the Trent 1000 position on the 787 through time on wing, inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). Watch Boeing's 787 work with GE. A rival-engined 787 Re-engine on the record would trigger our franchise test, as a recommendation.
- Bring a widebody item in 2050 only if a Re-engine is then on the record, with the strain in its row and against the $3B cap and the $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB.

Commercial discipline. Narrowbody is an option, not a need, and it carries no premium.
- S2 is −0.04 against S1: a Boeing fps selection of Rolls-Royce adds nothing on this grid.
- Offer the Joint Venture engine to any new single-aisle on standard terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no earlier dates, no launch-style terms.
- Our answer to any doubt about readiness is in-service durability data.

Capital and audit. McCabe should confirm that this round needs no new programme spend, that no balance-sheet trigger applies, and that the 30-40% payout and the buyback cadence follow the capital frame. Narrowbody cash from the Joint Venture ramp should be shown in that frame.
- Bring to the Audit Committee an honest Joint Venture lookback: $5.71B of our own narrowbody money against delivered share, and the $4B narrowbody line missed beyond repair.
- The long-term technology position (UltraFan technology and the demonstrator) stays funded inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not by a grid premium.

Capacity and support for the ramp. Rolls-Royce narrowbody engines run at 953 in 2045 and about 930-990 a year to 2060, against 188 widebody engines.
- Bring the supplier plan: castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, and gearbox and shop capacity shared with P&W under the Joint Venture.
- Confirm that Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support stay ring-fenced. Engineering shared with widebody is the constraint our objective names.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: (1) A 787 or A350 Re-engine on the public record by 2050, and a 2050 grid in which a widebody row beats hold, or falls short by no more than the $3B cap ($1B for UltraFan WB) as a declared premium. On this board's arithmetic I do not expect it: the $5B strain alone is several times the most either item can earn. (2) Widebody share heading toward the 50% line, for example a rival-engined Re-engine. That is the CEO's franchise test; I would price the premium, not block it. (3) Joint Venture in-service data below the written standard on time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground. I would re-price the aftermarket, the lookback and any provision, safety first, and say so first. (4) Free cash flow well below guidance. I would revisit the pace of distributions, not support or safety spend. (5) Concessions, earlier dates or launch-style terms added as other moves: I would withhold my support. (6) Delivered numbers: actual NGSA pricing and shop-visit data, in place of the board's 1.6x lifecycle multiple, would move the lookback IRR either way.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. This is a delivery round, and the numbers say so plainly.

I confirm Tufan's grid. Hold is +11.03 / +10.99 / +11.03 / +11.28: +11.05 on his weights and the Board's, +11.08 on the Re-engine stress. Against hold, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.48 in S1-S3 and −6.46 in S4. UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02, or −8.79 expected. Each buys under $1B of engine value for $7B or $9B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain. To stay within its own bill, either would need $5B of engine value; this board gives at most about $1B. I withhold my signature on both. On this arithmetic both are closed for 2050 too, unless that grid shows otherwise.

No new programme spend. No equity, no new borrowing, leverage unchanged. Payout stays at 30-40%, and buybacks are set on fit, value and timing.

The lookback, plainly. We spent $5.71B of our own narrowbody money against a $4B line: missed, and beyond repair. Delivered share is 23.6% in 2045 and 26.4% in 2050, against 28.0% and 31.3% on the 2035 grid. The fold saved $2.29B; on my reading, CFM's moves took back $3.03B of engine value. On Civil margins of 17-25%, the $5.71B earns about 9-12%, below our mid-to-high teens. It adds value, but it does not yet clear the hurdle.

The job now is the quality of cash: time on wing, shop visits, support.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: A narrowbody engine is fitted only if it is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS. The Joint Venture engine is ready at the bulletin's date (2036, the schedule inherited from a folded Solo). Widebody: the Trent 1000 upgrade counts at launch + 3. UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. A late engine fails as advice: it is not fitted and McCabe prices the downside. It is not a veto ground.
tests.numbers:
Narrowbody:
- Joint Venture engine ready 2036, against NGSA EIS 2037 (2030 + 7). One year of margin. Fitted on code 7 (CFM + P&W + RR) and in service since 2037.
- 2036 is the folded GTF2 schedule shown in the bulletin (2030 + 6). UltraFan NB's own date was 2037, and we never stated anything earlier.
- No live airframe is waiting for an engine. NGSA is in service, and Boeing has launched nothing.
- S2: a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055 on code 5, and the Joint Venture engine is ready 19 years ahead. A 7-year fps would enter service in 2052, 16 years ahead.

Widebody (for the record; my orders hold both):
- The upgrade, launched 2045, counts from 2048 (2045 + 3) in every column.
- A correction to the Board's reading that it counts from 2050 in S3-S4. The rules count it at launch + 3 with no Re-engine condition, and the grid agrees: the S3 row (−6.48) equals S1, and S4 is −6.46. Counting from 2050 would remove about 2 of its 14 counting years to 2061 in S3 (inference).
- UltraFan WB, launched 2045, is ready in 2051. A 787 or A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050 (+5), so in S3-S4 UltraFan WB counts from 2051, a year after the Re-engine EIS. In S1-S2 it earns nothing.
- Engine value each buys (its row against hold, plus its bill and the $5B strain): upgrade $0.52B / $0.52B / $0.52B / $0.54B; UltraFan WB $0 / $0 / $0.72B / $0.98B.

tests.name: No early date
tests.numbers:
I checked the CEO's draft statement sentence by sentence. It contains no year at all.
- 'The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA': a fact on the record, with no date.
- 'Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone': no date. This is the right rule.
- 'If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first': keep it.
- 'Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes': conditional, with no date.
- Nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates, and no claim of a share gain.

Option E's public moves (i)-(iii) also carry no dates: the engine in service and paced on durability; on offer on standard terms with no dates; Trent durability inside budget.

Advice, not a condition: add one support line with no date, such as 'Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, is in place and scaling with the fleet.'

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: Before any narrowbody EIS, a support plan through partner shops must be in place, and it must scale with the fleet (inference). Both narrowbody fields are hold-only this round, so no launch, trigger or commit can create a new EIS. One arises only if a new single-aisle selects the Joint Venture engine.
tests.numbers:
NGSA (EIS 2037):
- The plan was carried live before EIS in the 2035 package: Singapore-model partner shops with repair technology, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team.
- That plan was sized on the round-2 brief for about 1,600 engines by 2042 and 4,700 by 2045.

The actual Rolls-Royce fleet (my cumulative sums of brief §1):
- 115 by 2039, 382 by 2040, 1,456 by 2042, 3,091 by 2044 and 4,044 by 2045.
- That is inside the round-2 sizing, with about 650 engines of headroom.

Forward:
- 4,804 more engines in 2046-50 (928-978 a year): about 8,848 by the end of 2050 and 13,652 by 2055.
- The network must roughly double by 2050.
- P&W holds an equal share of the Joint Venture engine, so the Joint Venture fleet on NGSA is larger than ours (inference). Our shops add to P&W's network; they do not replace it.
- The spares and lease pool and the field team scale with deliveries. Spares for aircraft on ground are ranked fleet first.

A new single-aisle: the earliest EIS is 2052 (a 7-year fps launched 2045). The same network is extended before that airframe's EIS.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Flag the $5B strain, with the years of overlap, whenever a narrowbody project and a widebody project are both on the record. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. These are seat and company rules, not my words (inference).
tests.numbers:
My recommended orders are all hold: strain $0 in S1-S4.
- The Joint Venture is on the record and has been ready since 2036. It cannot be cancelled, so any widebody item pays a one-off $5B, in 2045 or in 2050. I confirm the strain is permanent.
- Overlap if launched: upgrade development 2045-48, and UltraFan WB 2045-51, each beside a narrowbody line delivering 953-976 engines a year.
- On their letter, neither item breaks my two red lines. No UltraFan is in development: UltraFan NB folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036. No NB Solo is on the record. The numbers decide the case, not the red lines.
- Unpriced load I flag (inference): engineering changes for our content entering the Joint Venture engine use the same engineers as Trent fleet durability. One engineering programme at a time also means rationing those changes.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. The narrowbody ramp is flagged as advice: it needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity.
tests.numbers:
RR engines a year (brief §1), narrowbody + widebody = total:
- 2045: 953 + 188 = 1,141 (5.1 to 1).
- 2050: 978 + 188 = 1,166 (5.2 to 1).
- Narrowbody peak: 987 in 2051. Range 928-987 a year in 2046-60.

Supplier plan (advice):

- Gearbox and shop capacity shared with P&W under the Joint Venture. The gear is P&W's work-share under its published terms.

The brief reports no constraint.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
On hold, in every column:
- 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050.
- A correction to the frame: 2040 was 58.0%, because the GEnx upgrade counts only from 2042 (58/105 = 55.2%).
- Worst year 55.2%, 5.2 points clear.

Other plans:
- With the upgrade: 60.0% in 2050 (63/105).
- With UltraFan WB: 55.2% in 2050 in every column, because it is ready only in 2051.

Threats:
- Boeing's 787 work with GE is unpriced: 'not a 787 Re-engine order'.
- The board's widebody engine shares do not move with the 787/A350 airframe split. In S3-S4 we stay at 55.2%; Airbus's airframe share is 40.2% in S3.
- A hypothetical further 5 points to CFM would leave us at 52.7% (58/110; inference from the renormalisation rule). The line is not threatened anywhere on the board.

Trent 1000 on the 787 (the CEO's ask 7): on this board, time on wing inside the existing durability budget is enough. We keep improving HP turbine blades and extending the life of life-limited parts on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000. The board's upgrade adds 4.8 points of share, not durability, at −6.48.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: UltraFan technology keeps feeding the in-service fleets. Noted qualitatively only; never a grid adjustment.
tests.numbers:
No grid adjustment.
- UltraFan demonstrator and folded UltraFan NB technology keep flowing into the Trent fleet for time on wing, inside a broadly flat R&D envelope.
- Into the Joint Venture engine, they flow only as engineering changes with their own test evidence, after EIS.
- Technology flows both ways [RX-0272]: what we learn from the Joint Venture fleet comes back to the Trent fleet.

tests.name: In-service durability and engineering-change rule
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture fleet is reported against a written standard: time on wing in the specification, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, and aircraft on ground. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never to hold a date or win a selection. This is my maturity rule (attr.) applied to a formed Joint Venture (inference).
tests.numbers:
In-service record:
- The brief carries deliveries, not fleet data. I have no time-on-wing, shop-visit, life-limited-part or aircraft-on-ground figures, and I invent none.
- The fleet to report: 3,091 RR engines by the end of 2044 and 4,044 by the end of 2045.
- The first cohorts (7 in 2037, 115 by 2039, 382 by 2040) should be reaching early shop visits now, so this is the window for the first real durability read (inference).
- I cannot yet tell the Committee where we are below standard. The written standard and the first report go to it this round.

Exposure:
- Under P&W's published terms, the certified gear and core are P&W's.
- P&W says its GTF fleet 'is still not where our customers need it to be'.
- Our aftermarket cash on the fleet rests on durability we do not design (inference).

If the data are bad, in this order:
- tell operators and Airbus, with P&W, first;
- say it publicly, with the fix and no recovery date we cannot hold;
- spares and lease engines go to aircraft on ground first;
- no change is rushed in to cover it.

The engineering-change rule is confirmed. The CEO's draft and P&W's published terms both state it.

Governance I propose:
- one engineering interface;
- one durability standard and one fleet report;
- one chief engineer per change;
- each change carries its own test plan, certification basis and fleet-introduction gate, reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee;
- introduction in production and at shop visit once tested (inference).

Crediting:
- A joint technical valuation of each change is recorded at its gate and feeds the share split as a valuation only, with no licence and no cash, under P&W's terms.
- The share question is the CEO's, and it goes to the Board before it is public.
- On this board P&W and RR hold equal narrowbody shares whatever is credited, so crediting is unpriced.

vetoes.plan: All four fields at hold, with the CEO's draft public statement and the other moves in option E
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. No Civil ground is met: nothing compresses maturity, no public text carries a date, and no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is possible this round.

At the veto check I would invoke the veto if any of these appears:
(a) a public text gives a date for Rolls-Royce content entering the Joint Venture engine, an UltraFan WB date earlier than launch + 6, an upgrade count earlier than launch + 3, or any Joint Venture date other than the bulletin's;
(b) the rationale counts on our content in the certified engine before its own test evidence, or on UltraFan WB earning before 2051 or without a Re-engine in service;
(c) an engineering change, or the offer of the engine to a new single-aisle, is used to hold or win a date (compressed maturity).

If invoked, the team rule makes it binding. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

A request, not a veto ground this round: carry the scaled support plan in the package.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- **Fleet data below the written standard.** If the first in-service read on time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground is below standard, we say so first, in public with P&W. Engineers and spares go to the fleet ahead of any new item, and I would oppose any 2050 widebody item until the fleet recovers.
- **Content rushed into the engine.** Any proposal to put Rolls-Royce content into the certified engine to meet a date, or to win a selection, without its own test evidence: I would invoke the Civil veto for compressed maturity.
- **A date in public.** Any public date for our content entering the engine, any UltraFan WB date earlier than launch + 6, or an upgrade count earlier than launch + 3: I would invoke the veto.
- **A Re-engine on the record by 2050.** A 787 or A350 Re-engine launched, or announced in a public statement, would make me re-test UltraFan WB and the upgrade on the 2050 grid, with the $5B strain in the row. Each needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the strain.
- **A threat to the 50% line.** A brief projecting our widebody share near the line (a further CFM gain takes it to 52.7%), or a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, would trigger the franchise test, with time on wing as the first lever.
- **Support or capacity limits.** A brief reporting a capacity constraint would make the capacity test live. A new single-aisle selecting the Joint Venture engine would need the support network extended before its EIS.
- **Named airline wins.** Wins on the Joint Venture engine would firm up my confidence in the support ramp.
ops.memo:
All four fields at hold. No Civil veto.

The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and entered service on NGSA in 2037, a year of margin, nothing compressed. We have 4,044 Rolls-Royce engines delivered by the end of 2045 and about 8,850 by 2050.

The fleet. The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data, so I bring the Committee a written standard, not invented numbers: time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, aircraft on ground. The gear and core are P&W's, and P&W says its GTF fleet is "still not where our customers need it to be". So one durability standard and one voice: if the data are bad, we say so first.

The rule. Our content goes in only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence and one chief engineer per change, never to hold a date or win a campaign.

Support. The plan was sized for 4,700 engines by 2045, so it covers today's fleet. It must roughly double by 2050. Our partner shops add to P&W's network, not replace it.

Capacity. 953 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody in 2045, five to one. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 stay ring-fenced.

Widebody. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column. With the strain permanent, the upgrade is −6.48 and UltraFan WB −9.00. Time on wing inside the existing budget defends the 787.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA. Our job now is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, is in place and scaling with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, a delivery round. All four fields at hold. No Board item.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Start from my proposal: all hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.
2. Binding vetoes. McCabe withholds her co-signature on t1000_upgrade launch and on ultrafan_wb launch (binding). Respected: both stay at hold. Watson invokes no Civil veto. He checked the public statement sentence by sentence and it carries no year. I added his support line, which has no date. Overrides are empty.
3. Expected scenario S1. Weights shown (the brief gives none): mine 0.65 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10; the Board's 0.70 / 0.05 / 0.15 / 0.10; a Re-engine stress 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20.
4. Grid rows, with and without each item (ΔPV against the status quo):
- 'UltraFan NB: hold': +11.03 / +10.99 / +11.03 / +11.28. Expected +11.05 on mine, +11.05 on the Board's, +11.08 on the stress. Worst column +10.99 (S2). It is the best plan in every column.
- 'hold + T1000 upgrade': +4.55 / +4.51 / +4.55 / +4.82, so −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 against hold. Expected −6.48 on all three weight sets. Worst column −6.48, beyond its own −$2B bill. It buys $0.52-0.54B of engine value for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- 'hold + UltraFan WB': +2.03 / +1.99 / +2.75 / +3.26, so −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02 against hold. Expected −8.79 on mine and the Board's, −8.59 on the stress. Worst column −9.00, beyond its own −$4B bill. It buys $0 / $0 / $0.72B / $0.98B.
- Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights.
5. Premium 0. All hold is the best plan. Shortfalls declined: upgrade $6.48B against the $3B cap; UltraFan WB $8.79B (worst $9.00B) against the $1B sub-cap.
6. Red lines checked on the final orders:
- No UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it: UltraFan WB with no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record would breach it. Watson and McCabe both flagged this. Struck: it is held.
- No early dates: none in public.
- No new narrowbody value: both narrowbody fields hold, the only legal value.
- One big programme at a time: strain stays $0.
- Balance sheet: untouched.
- Commercial discipline: standard terms only.
No unresolved flag.

WHY HOLD, IN MY OWN TERMS
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]. The upgrade is differentiated on 787 time on wing, but fails 'viable business model' on the strain. UltraFan WB fails 'large market' (no Re-engine) and 'viable business model'.
- My instinct on the 787 is 'Why not?' [RX-0117], and I said we could regain share [RX-0101]. But 4.8 points of share for −$6.48B is share bought at a loss, and 'we are not after market share' [R-1582]. Widebody is safe without it: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column.
- No options management [RX-0051]: a widebody item with no Re-engine to fly is not launched as a hedge.
- The Joint Venture is formed and ready. The 2035 re-test is closed by formation, withdrawal is gone, and the money is booked.

CORRECTIONS TAKEN FROM THE MEMOS
- Watson: widebody share was 58.0% in 2040, not 55.2%. The GEnx upgrade counts from 2042.
- Watson: the upgrade would count from 2048 in every column, not from 2050 in S3-S4. The rules and the grid agree.
- McCabe: the right 2035 benchmark for the lookback is S4, P&W commits (+14.06), not S1. Against it the miss is −$3.03B of engine value, with the fold saving $2.29B.
I record them plainly.

WHAT I CANNOT CLAIM
- The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data. There is no time-on-wing or shop-visit figure, and I invent none. The written standard and the first report go to the Committee this round.
- The gear and core are P&W's. Our aftermarket cash rests on durability we do not design (Watson, inference).
- My record has no evidenced decision on running a formed Joint Venture. The governance, support and lookback moves follow company doctrine (profile.md §4, §9 steps 6-12) and the Board's guidance, not my own words.
- Widebody items in 2050: closed on this board unless that grid shows otherwise. McCabe's estimate is about −6.7 and −8.6 against hold, and Watson confirms the shorter windows (upgrade counting from 2053, UltraFan WB ready 2056).

'They are a milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062].

- Widebody never starved: MET, with $0 strain, but only while both widebody items stay at hold. Any widebody item now carries a permanent $5B strain.

3. The brief carries no fleet data. The written durability standard and the first fleet report go to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee this round, with no figure invented.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

public_statements.boeing:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I owe you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane moved our way this year, for the first time in a while. I think it's turning. I don't think it's turned. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. I'd rather tell you plainly that the case isn't there than launch an airplane to avoid saying so. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

One correction from me on the 737. I've been saying we're holding at 57 a month. That's our capacity, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We build to demand, and this year that's about 43 a month. As demand comes down, we'll bring the rate down in steps on those same gates, never off a cliff, and we'll keep our suppliers and our people ready through it. Customers will keep getting honest delivery dates.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is at full rate, and we run it in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and we will report its in-service performance as the fleet data show it. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and that is the clock we keep. A320 family production has completed, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported, with its sustaining engineering fully staffed. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs, on standard terms. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus and competes on product and value. We keep preparing the technologies for the generation after this one, on the clock of their maturity. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is still the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate as the fleet ages, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus is extending its long-term engine supply agreements, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. A large GTF fleet on the A320neo is coming through the shops, and until every one of those engines flies in the latest configuration, that fleet is not where our customers need it to be. We own that. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries, and we are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms. We will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration when we have the data to report it.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We claim no more for its durability than the fleet data show, and we will report those data by operating environment, hot and sandy included. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. Any change a new airframe needs goes in with its own test evidence. We are not in the early entry phase. Our capital order doesn't change: the dividend comes first. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Our job is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, scales with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core. Our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only once a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Build the 737 MAX to demand on the FAA-agreed KPI gates; 57 a month is capacity, not the build rate
boeing.detail: I'm correcting my own public line, on Pope's advice [BX-1284]. 57 a month is our capacity on the agreed gates: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. We have built to demand since 2048: 543 (2048), 483 (2049) and about 513 (2050), roughly 43 a month. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and hold is the only rate_737 order. Customers get honest delivery dates [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

boeing.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; keep bringing the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers with GE
boeing.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is GE's own programme, ready since 2033, and durability comes first [BX-1298]. This is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board doesn't price it.

airbus.move: Long-term supply for NGSA at full rate, sized to our own production
airbus.detail: We are extending the long-term agreements for NGSA engine delivery slots with CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, on standard terms. The slots, at 2,568-2,732 engines a year, are matched to our own deliveries and to a capacity of 1,366 aircraft. That is below the 2,770 engines we carried in 2044. No A320neo slots remain; the surplus went back to CFM and Pratt & Whitney when the lines closed. NGSA wing and structures run at rate, including the work packages we brought in-house. Titanium and rare earths stay at or below the 2044 peak, following on from the 2025 de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. All of this is for our own production, and no action is aimed at any rival's supply chain. The ECSC confirms the sizing formally before signature. All prepayments, together with any programme spend, stay inside the $5.228B annual line (Toepfer).

airbus.move: Engineering staffing for NGSA in-service support and sustaining
airbus.detail: We fill these roles by internal redeployment first, including former A320 line staff, and then by normal hiring. A320 sustaining engineering for the in-service fleet and the A350 teams stay fully staffed [A-0366, A-0485]. The staffing is sized to our own programmes and does not target any competitor's programme or staff. (This is Wagner's redraft. The clause the Board flagged in the 2045 text has been struck.)

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
airbus.detail: We continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

cfm.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
cfm.detail: RISE is funded as technology and is not cancelled for cost (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0398]. We launch no product. We give no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public (H6, Ali's date test) [CX-0009]. The airframers set the date for the architecture [CX-0205, CX-0469]. No product claim is made, so my 20% line is not engaged [CX-0217].

cfm.move: CFM keeps answering Airbus's long-term engine supply agreements (A320neo tail and NGSA), jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: We acknowledge that Airbus is extending its long-term engine supply agreements. We answer as CFM, jointly with Safran, and Safran agrees the wording first. Price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, on standard terms [CX-0184]. Nothing goes out in public: no price, concession, volume, rate, slot count or delivery year. The volume assumptions are worked with Airbus inside this answer before any number goes out [CX-0944]. The board does not price this move.

cfm.move: CFM engines stay on offer to every airframer
cfm.detail: CFM offers its engines on any new single-aisle Boeing launches. The Embraer partnership stays open and not exclusive. No airframer is locked out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. This is an offer of supply, not of terms: no price, terms or dates in public, and any pricing goes to Safran first.

cfm.move: GEnx upgrade brought to 787 customers with Boeing (GE alone)
cfm.detail: This answers Boeing's public request. The upgrade is GE's own programme, already in service, and it is won on product, not price [CX-0599, CX-0615]. There is no Safran gate and no price in public. It is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board does not price it.

cfm.move: LEAP fleet first: kits and shop-visit material ahead of the OE delivery rate
cfm.detail: Time-on-wing kits and shop-visit material stay ahead of the OE delivery rate as the A320 tail closes and the fleet ages [CX-0529]. Any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team, never one person [CX-0012]. This is CFM practice with Safran, at standard terms, with no free upgrade. It is a priority rule, not a measured result, and no number is attached to it.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit to the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing. There is no free upgrade and no launch-style discount. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration, and we publish that share only when we have the data to support it. We give no dated recovery. The fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of kit parts.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture held to its published terms
pratt_whitney.detail: The terms are the ones published with the 2035 commitment. Risk, investment and revenue are shared, and both partners are on one engine. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property. Partner contributions are recognised only in the share split, with no licence and no cash payment to the partner. Partner content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and Pratt & Whitney signs for durability only on an engine it has tested.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture engine offered, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet
pratt_whitney.detail: The engine is offered as certified, on standard terms, priced for value. We offer no concession, discount, free upgrade or launch-style term to win a selection or to hold a share. Any change specific to a new airframe, whether rating, installation or derivative, goes in as an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence. The airframer gives its own dates.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture engine in service, paced on durability; engineering-change rule
rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence. It is never used to hold a date or win a campaign. P&W's published terms say the same. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we say so first, with P&W. No date of any kind is given for our content entering the engine [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476].

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture engine on offer to any new single-aisle, on standard terms
rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard 'win-win' terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no dates, no launch-style terms. Our answer to any doubt on readiness is in-service durability data. We are not after market share [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582].

rolls_royce.move: Trent durability and UltraFan technology pull-through inside the existing budget
rolls_royce.detail: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine and life-limited-part durability work continues inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). UltraFan demonstrator technology, and the technology from the folded UltraFan NB, keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing, inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope. This is not a Trent upgrade programme [RX-0123, RX-0214].

boeing.move: Step the MAX build rate down with demand on the same six KPIs, and consolidate lines one at a time
boeing.detail:
This is Pope's ladder (inference), in steps of 5 at least 6 months apart: 42 a month in 2050-51; 37 then 32 in 2052; 32 to 2055; 27 from about 2056; 22 from about 2058. Over 2050-60 it builds 4,014 aircraft against demand of 3,962, and the running gap stays under two months of output. Four steps in about six years, never a cliff [BX-1310].
- Each step is taken on rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. If a KPI degrades on a step, we hold that rate and fix it before the next one.
- Lines are consolidated one at a time. Which line goes is a KPI call, not a date.
- No target is published ahead of stability [BX-1268]. The board doesn't price this move.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot through the downturn; give the supply chain the step-down skyline early; LEAP-1B allocation reviews continue
boeing.detail:
Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Fragile or financially weak suppliers stay funded and producing at or above our rate, while strong ones burn down inventory. Every supplier gets the step-down skyline within the planning window [B-1616].

LEAP-1B is still a watch item, and an easing one. Our call falls from about 1,026 engines (2050) to 496 (2060), so the risk has turned from rationing to low volume at the supplier. CFM's own LEAP fleet-support priority stands. Nothing is attributed to anyone before exposure [BX-1264, BX-1325].

boeing.move: Keep trained labour through low-rate production; redeploy before releasing anyone
boeing.detail: This protects the production system and the supply chain at falling volume [B-1618]. People on lines being consolidated move first to Everett, the 787 at Charleston, Defense, or the fps risk-reduction team.

boeing.move: Put the 2050 fps case on the record as tested, and keep the risk-reduction team and the hiring and transfer plan warm; launch nothing
boeing.detail:
THE CASE AS TESTED
- 10-year at Renton, Code 7 (CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture, two sources), with Code 3 as the fallback if a Joint Venture durability problem is reported.
- Pope's signed, conditional Renton wind-down.
- Cost-plus or risk-share terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].
- Against Do Nothing: -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92.

THE TREND AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050).
- Decision-year dollars: -$7.8B, -$10.5B, -$11.9B, -$9.4B.

MALAVE'S RESET, OWNED [BX-1319]: the lost lead isn't a loss against Do Nothing, and the 20-year window slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. Net of the clock that is +$0.22B, real on this board. The gain stream would still have to double ($3.66B PV against $1.80B) to clear +$1B.

No later round remains on this board, so this hold means no new airplane in this game. The team and the funded hiring and transfer plan [B-1941, B-0729, B-1593] stay because readiness doesn't keep by itself, not as a bridge to a dated launch. No date [B-2315].

airbus.move: Four items for the full Board's twice-yearly safety review
airbus.detail:
Wagner's drafts:
(1) NGSA at full rate: 1,339 aircraft in 2050 (about 112 a month), with capacity of 1,366 (about 114) from 2053. It runs on two engine sources (CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture) from three makers, at 2,568-2,732 engines a year, below the 2044 peak of 2,770.
(2) The Joint Venture engine's in-service durability by operating environment, hot and sandy included, as Pratt & Whitney reports it. It is a watch item, not a constraint.
(3) Rolls-Royce content enters that engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, with no date compressed.
(4) In-service A320 fleet support after the 2047 line closure: sustaining engineering staffed, and the makers running the LEAP shop material and GTF Advantage kits fleet first. Also, the A350 flies a single widebody engine source, the Trent XWB [A-0253]. With the A350 at Do Nothing, that becomes a permanent standing watch.
A quality escape, a safety event or an engine supply crunch comes back to the Board at once [AX-0056].

airbus.move: Record of the A350 decision: Do Nothing as a final, deliberate choice
airbus.detail:
This goes on the Board record at the Board's request.
- The A350 Re-engine is held in its last window on this board. The A350 stays at Do Nothing for good, as a deliberate choice and not by default of analysis.
- The case was tested in full and failed two independent ExCo tests: Toepfer's $1B added-move test (+0.57 in S1-S5, -0.42 in S6 / S7) and Wagner's engine readiness (no mature widebody engine for a 2055 EIS).
- My own within-$1B default rule decides it as well.
- The A350 family, including the A350F, competes on product and price, as older widebodies have before [A-0090, A-0091, A-0003, A-0440].
- Wagner keeps a non-public technical dialogue with Rolls-Royce on Trent XWB in-service durability, on standard terms. It carries no commitment, price, date or Re-engine signal. Any announcement is a capital-markets matter for the Board [AX-0004].

airbus.move: Capital-allocation paper for the Audit Committee
The generation after NGSA kept on a technology clock (Board off-site)
airbus.detail: The Board's annual off-site keeps the technologies for the generation after NGSA on their own maturity clock, inside the R&D budget, with no launch implied [AX-0020, AX-0006, AG-0039]. The board counts NGSA's market only to 2056 and pay looks about four years ahead, so the off-site carries the long view that neither prices.

airbus.move: Close-of-game governance record
airbus.detail:
Recorded for the Board:
- Delay Tactics were never ordered in any round (2030-2050), and the team's stricter condition was never set aside.
- The CEO's one override was never used.
- No item reached the Board through an override.
- NGSA was launched in 2030 on its own clock, entered service in 2037 and was never re-timed or cancelled in reaction to Boeing.
- Engine supply stayed dual-source from three makers.

cfm.move: OE capacity and the A320neo tail (internal)
cfm.detail:
This is Ghai's flag, and supply load is Ali's ground.
- On the observed data, A320neo slots are already back, so there is no cost on the board.
- Off the board, LEAP-1A OE capacity that is no longer called carries a risk of under-absorption. Freed capacity goes first to shop-visit material for an ageing fleet. The call is made by the cross-functional team on field data. Ali cannot net the lower OE load against more shop visits without hot-section supplier numbers, and he won't do it on analysis.
- We add no LEAP OE capacity to chase the top of Airbus's stated range, which sits below its 2044 level.
- In public we don't repeat Airbus's range, any CFM slice of it, or the A320neo slots coming back. Those are Airbus's numbers to give, or ours with Safran (Ghai's standing terms veto).

cfm.move: Field-data package for the Board, owed by the cross-functional team: standing past the last decision year
RISE test record to the Board (private)
cfm.detail: Our RISE evidence ends in October 2025: compact-core HPT dust testing began, the first Chief Mechanic and Architect for Open Fan durability was named, and open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's in tests with Airbus. No later result is in our evidence, including whether the flight test flew. So the doctrine's G4 test gate is not met for a product. We bring later results to the Board once they are on the record. On Ali's and the Board's advice, this sentence stays private, because it tells the market how old our last result is.

cfm.move: Embraer standing condition
cfm.detail: No Embraer airframe, volume or spend is on the record, and none is proposed. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first. Any real integration or support spend goes to Ghai's capex test and to the Board before it is committed. The partnership's value (+2.11 inside today's row, on Ghai's model) stays out of expected_pv_b until a volume is agreed. Doctrine (profile section 6) drives this, not my record.

cfm.move: Board watch list after the last decision year

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet first on pacing parts through 2056
pratt_whitney.detail: Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]: AOG spares, then shop material [PX-0124], then kit parts, then OE. Decided daily, reviewed weekly [PX-0131]. OE load is 978, 987, 982, 947, 938, 950 and 955 NB engines in 2050-56. The 2051 peak of 987 is 3.6% under the 2044 peak of 1,024, and the largest step is +2.5% (2050). A supplier quality gate comes before each rate step, including each step of the NGSA long-term agreements, because the powder-metal escape came from a ramp [P-1040]. The brief shows no live escape. Eddy's ground 2 passes. If a live escape, rising AOG or a supply break appears: contain it first, give a dated recovery, and OE gives way.

pratt_whitney.move: In-service durability report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first
pratt_whitney.detail: Opening line: after 13 years on NGSA (2037-49), neither our brief nor our files hold any time-on-wing figures, LLP life against plan by part family, shop-visit findings by cause, removal rates or hot-and-sandy fleet-leader data. We also have no 2036 gate data and no evidence that the LLPs were at full life at the 2037 EIS. That is not a finding of a shortfall. We have no data either way, and no news is not good news [PX-0112]. No figure is invented. Method [PX-0122][PX-0128]: report by operating environment, never as a fleet average; track hot-and-sandy fleet leaders separately; report LLP life by part family against the life declared at EIS. Configuration control: Eddy confirms the rule and the record. The engineering-change log is not in his brief, so the log itself goes to the committee [P-1215]. The gear and core stay P&W's [P-1233]. The Board's durability-first test applies [P-1360].

pratt_whitney.move: Record of Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto on any concession for an fps code or NGSA share
pratt_whitney.detail: Mitchill's binding veto, accepted. It is also my own red line [PX-0055][PX-0100]. No concession, discount, free upgrade or launch-style term goes to Boeing, Airbus or a fleet customer, whether to win an fps selection or to defend NGSA share. Grid reason: S2 − S1 = −1.65 − (−1.65) = 0.00. Any 2050 fps enters service in 2057 or 2060, after the board's NB count ends in 2056, so any price paid for a code is pure loss. Recorded here only, never in a public line.

pratt_whitney.move: Final whole-life review and bridge to 2045, for the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Mitchill's review [P-1191], on the board's convention: −1.65 = +0.35 engine value − $2.00B R&D (undiscounted); yield 98.50%; $0.175 of PV per $1 of R&D. Against Do Nothing (0.00): −1.65. Against a $2.00B buyback (about 0 NPV): trails by 1.65. Capitalise ends NOT MET by 1.65. The gap is final and unchanged since 2045. Discounted view, information only: R&D phased over 2030-35 is $1.09B at 2026, giving −0.74 (−0.72 on our +0.374). boeing.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I owe you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane moved our way this year, for the first time in a while. I think it's turning. I don't think it's turned. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. I'd rather tell you plainly that the case isn't there than launch an airplane to avoid saying so. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

One correction from me on the 737. I've been saying we're holding at 57 a month. That's our capacity, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We build to demand, and this year that's about 43 a month. As demand comes down, we'll bring the rate down in steps on those same gates, never off a cliff, and we'll keep our suppliers and our people ready through it. Customers will keep getting honest delivery dates.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.
- No veto stands against the plan, and I take no override.

THE TEAM RULE, APPLIED
(1) Malave's buffer test, the binding check. S3 must be no lower than -2.83 (Do Nothing's -0.83 less $2B).
- Do Nothing: -0.83, $2.00B clear.
- Every Solo row passes. The 10-year at Renton clears by $1.08B; the 7-year by only $0.05-0.19B.
- Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B. Jay's veto on those four binds. None is ordered.
(2) Pope's KPI veto: nothing to bind on. No Rate Increase is offered, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. H6 is not engaged.
(3) Everything else is my call. Within ε, doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] break the tie.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes: Pope's KPI and supplier tests pass. The new task is stability at falling volume, handled in other moves.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305]
- Balance sheet: yes. Net debt is $0.0B since 2029, held in base and stress. Every 10-year row is fundable ($0.0B stress peak).
- Technology: yes. The Joint Venture engine would have 24 years since readiness by a 2060 EIS, and CFM's ducted engine 19.
- Market: no. The best stand-alone fps, the 10-year at Renton, is -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92 against Do Nothing. The three streams haven't converged.
3. What if certification takes longer? Jay costed doctrine's +3-year slip once and in full: $0.74-1.22B against a $1.08B margin. It absorbs the slip on the narrow count only.
- Pope fails the 10-year on predictable delivery: value at the nominal date, certification pacing, and 23 years without a major development.
- She is clear it is not a KPI, supplier or strain failure.
4. Is this doing less, better? Yes. Do Nothing is within ε of every Solo 10-year row and of the Re-engine, and it has the least to execute.

THE NARROWBODY
Expected column: S1, the narrowbody's planning column, with the Re-engine blended at Jay's 30%.
- Do Nothing -0.86; 10-year at Renton -1.72 (-0.86 against Do Nothing); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -1.73 (-0.87).
My debt-first test fails: it needs a plan more than ε ahead. Doctrine's last-round rule (profile §6: launch only if the fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε) fails too; that rule is doctrine, not my record. The tie breaks to Do Nothing on four counts:
- less to execute;
- the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.78);
- no added penalty ($19.1B undiscounted, for scale only; the grid already nets it);
- the higher-confidence plan.
The Board would veto any launch on Business case ($1.86B short of +$1B), so an order would revert to hold anyway.
- The 7-year trails the 10-year by $0.87-0.89B, fails Fundable under Jay's ruling (a stress peak of $1.0-6.4B after 2050 counts as not held) and has thin buffer margins.
- Via Embraer is barred by Jay's veto, trails Solo by $2.45-2.56B in every column and, on Pope's IP test, adds nothing we lack.

THE LAST ROUND, PLAINLY
No later round remains on this board, so this hold means no new airplane in this game. I say that rather than launch to avoid saying it. The Board asked for that, and it's my own standard [BX-1241, BX-1322]. The trend did turn, for the first time:
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050);
- decision-year dollars: -$11.9B (2045) to -$9.4B (2050);
- the market moved +$0.22B our way net of the clock.
Jay owned his miss [BX-1319]. Against Do Nothing, the lost lead isn't a loss, because Do Nothing also loses a point a year; and the window slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" [BX-1300]. The gain stream would have to double to clear +$1B.

Do Nothing erosion, on the record:
- preference 27.7% (2050) to 16.0% (2060);
- operating profit $0.66B (2050), $1.30B (2055) and $1.43B (2060) a year below the game baseline;
- FCF $12.66B or more, and net debt held.
Value erodes; the balance sheet doesn't.

THE 787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD
Item value against hold is 0.44 - 1.04p. At Jay's 30% (Low confidence) that is +0.13; break-even is 42%, and it is never above ε, even at zero odds.
- Tie-breakers: the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.53), doing less, and no added $0.6B penalty.
- The Board vetoes it on Business case.
- Pope passes it on operations, so my hold rests on ε, not on an operations finding.
- Forgone value, logged apart: +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44.

STANDING RULINGS
- H1: stays lifted. The 777X has been in service since 2027 and the MAX 7/10 since 2026; debt was repaired in 2029 [BX-0550, BX-1299, BX-1305, B-2326].
- H2: cannot bind.
- H3: first half lifted. Second half open, since no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4: not engaged. Nothing is launched. A 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years of overlap) would be barred; a 10-year + Re-engine (2 years) is legal with no slack.
- H5: nothing to cancel.
- H6: not engaged.
- H7: no trigger.
- H8: total $0.13B.

MY RED LINES, ALL KEPT
- no rate request without stable KPIs;
- no production-certification concurrency;
- no fixed-price development;
- no blame on the FAA;
- no supplier problem attributed to Airbus.

COSTS AND BIASES
On the grid the decision costs nothing: Do Nothing is the best plan in S2 and inside ε of the best in S1 and S3. Two biases show, both at no cost. Under-disclosure: the step-down ladder isn't published. Cash for readiness: suppliers are kept funded at falling volume.

Decision year 2050, round 4 of dash-2050-cons, the last round.

WHERE WE STAND
- We have launched nothing in rounds 1-3 and are on today's products.
- The 737 MAX holds at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed gates: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate_737 value offered.

- The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are long done. My conditions for the next airplane (debt repaired, developments finished) are met [BX-1305, B-2326, BX-1247].

PUBLIC RECORD
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM + PW + RR, and its ramp is completing. Airbus is on the A320 Alt plan and is extending its NGSA engine slot agreements with CFM and the Joint Venture.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036; CFM's ducted engine since 2041; CFM-Embraer since 2042 (open and not exclusive).
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says "The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus."
- Observed narrowbody delivery share: 29.9% in 2048 (543 aircraft) and 27.0% in 2049 (483 against Airbus's 1,306).

DO NOTHING (-0.83 / -0.93 / -0.83)
- S1 = rivals hold; S2 = Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine; S3 = risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics (covert). With no fps, S3 equals S1.
- Demand now sits below the line. MAX deliveries are 513 (2050), 388 (2053), 346 (2055) and 248 (2060), against 684 of capacity: 75%, 57%, 51% and 36% used. The waiting backlog is 0.
- Preference: 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- Operating profit runs $0.66B (2050), $1.30B (2055) and $1.43B (2060) a year below the game baseline. FCF stays at $12.66B or more, and net debt is held. Value erodes; the balance sheet doesn't.

OBJECTIVES UNDER DO NOTHING
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 27.7%).
- Met: balance-sheet repair, kept in base and stress.
- Engine enabler: dual sources not met (the MAX flies CFM only), and no 2050 order can meet it, since the earliest fps EIS is 2057. Three narrowbody makers: met.

THE GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3; my calc in work/r4_ceo_frame_calc.py)
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44. Best plan in S1 and S3.
- 10-year at Renton: -0.86 / -0.85 / -0.92. At the new site: -0.96 / -0.95 / -1.02.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -0.56 / -1.60 / -0.62. Best fps row in S1 and S3.
- 7-year at Renton: -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.81. It trails the 10-year by $0.87-0.89B alone (inside ε) and by $1.00-1.02B with the Re-engine.
- Via Embraer: -3.12 to -4.26. It trails the Solo 10-year by $2.45-2.56B in every column.
- Renton adds +0.10 on a 10-year or via Embraer fps and +0.13 to +0.14 on a 7-year. It adds nothing while the fps holds.

TREND OF THE 10-YEAR AT RENTON AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2026 PV: -5.26 (2030), -4.29 (2035), -1.78 (2045), -0.86 (2050).
- Decision-year dollars: -$7.8B, -$10.5B, -$11.9B, -$9.4B.
- Five years of the clock (x0.607) would take 2045's -1.78 to -1.08. The actual is -0.86. So, net of the clock, the market moved +$0.22B our way: the first gain in four rounds. Jay projected -1.08 to -1.28; the grid beat that by $0.22-0.42B. That is evidence an estimate was wrong [BX-1319], and I want to know why.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes, on the brief. Pope's seat to confirm, now at falling volume.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
   - Boeing: yes. Net debt is $0.0B, and every 10-year row holds stress net debt at $0.0B.
   - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give CFM + the Joint Venture, both mature by any EIS from 2057.
   - Market: closer, but no. The best stand-alone fps still loses $0.86B against Do Nothing. A tie isn't convergence [BX-1296, BX-1303].
3. What if certification takes longer than we think? S3 is Jay's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83.
   - Every Solo row passes: 7-year at the new site by only $0.05B; 10-year at Renton by $1.08B; rows with the Re-engine by $0.22-1.38B.
   - Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B.
   - I still want the full cost of a slip, taken once [BX-1318].
4. Is this doing less, better? Do Nothing is within ε of every Solo 10-year row and of the Re-engine, and it has the least to execute [BX-1239].

- launch_via_embraer: Rating first (S3 -4.01 to -4.30), Business case and Downside.
- re787: launch in any combination. Its best column is +0.44, below +$1B at any odds.
- any premium above $2B.
It approves holds, and Renton with Pope's wind-down result. It says a premium can't carry a launch, because its tests read the grid.

- the submitted row beside Do Nothing, and each Board item's default row;
- my expected column;

- my standing rulings;
- every premium logged, with forgone holds shown apart;
- the trend, Jay's account of the beat, the erosion to 2060, and a plain statement that no later round remains;
- no fps date.

- Pass, every Solo row:
  - Do Nothing ($2.00B clear); the Re-engine ($2.44B);
  - 7-year at the new site ($0.05B), at Renton ($0.19B), + Re-engine ($0.22B), at Renton + Re-engine ($0.36B);
  - 10-year at the new site ($0.98B), at Renton ($1.08B), + Re-engine ($1.28B), at Renton + Re-engine ($1.38B).

Confirm or correct, and name the rows you veto. Is a $0.05-0.19B pass on the 7-year robust?

2. "FUNDABLE WHEN THE 777X TURNS" [BX-0547]. The Board asks you to rule on the stress flags.

- The 7-year rows ($1.0-6.4B) and via Embraer ($6.0-12.4B) read 'yes' only because the last checkpoint is 2050. Their peaks come after it.

3. CASH TIMING for a 2050 launch on the brief's standard curve:
- 10-year: $60.32B over 2050-59, peak year about 2056 (14%, about $8.4B);
- 7-year: $65.00B over 2050-56;
- Re-engine: $5B over 2050-54.

4. WHY 2050 BEAT YOUR PROJECTION. You projected -1.08 to -1.28 for the 10-year at Renton; the grid shows -0.86.
- My arithmetic: five years of the clock take 2045's -1.78 to -1.08, so the market moved +$0.22B our way net of the clock, the first gain since 2030. In decision-year dollars: -$11.9B (2045) to -$9.4B (2050).

6. 787 RE-ENGINE.
- Your odds of an A350 Re-engine this round. You had 35% in 2045, and Airbus has now held three times.
- The item is worth 0.44 - 1.04p, with break-even at 42%. It never clears ε.
- The doctrine premium at your odds. The forgone value (+0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44) is logged apart, as the Board asks.

7. EXPECTED COLUMN. I plan the narrowbody on S1, and the Re-engine on S1 blended with S2 at your odds. S3 stays the buffer baseline and is not blended in. At 35%, Do Nothing is -0.87, the Re-engine -0.79, the 10-year at Renton -1.72 and the 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -1.79. Correct me if you'd plan differently.

8. PREMIUM LOG. Confirm three things:
- holding the fps gives up nothing on the grid;
- the objective premium for the 10-year at Renton would be $0.86-0.92B (about $0.94-1.00B with the Re-engine hold at 35%), inside the cap;

- In EIS-year dollars the gain rose 14%, from $47.2B to $53.8B.
- The item in decision-year dollars went from -$11.9B to -$9.4B. The CEO's arithmetic is confirmed.

WHY I MISSED IT (a reset, owned)
(1) I treated the loss of lead (32/68 to 27/73) as a further market loss. Against Do Nothing it isn't one. Do Nothing also loses 1 pp a year (21.0% in 2055, 16.0% in 2060), so the fps climbs the same 11 pp from Do Nothing's share at EIS either way (21 to 32, or 16 to 27). The year-by-year gap over Do Nothing is unchanged by the delay: Do Nothing's own erosion carries the case.
(2) The 20-year window moved from 2055-74 to 2060-79. It drops 2055-59 (demand 1,548-1,647) and adds 2075-79 at the 2070 level, after the post-2060 replacement wave (544 in 2060, 1,244 in 2065; total 2,082 in 2065).
(3) Inference, not confirmed by the brief: from the early 2060s demand outruns Airbus's capacity (1,366 against 2,082 in 2065), and the rules give its slack to Boeing up to our capacity. The MAX is capped at 684 a year, while an fps line lifts that cap toward 1,200.

REAL OR ARTEFACT
- It is real on the board's rules, not an arithmetic error.
- It is partly a feature of the window rule: a later EIS buys later, bigger years.

WHAT IT DOESN'T DO: it doesn't turn the sign.
- To clear +$1B the gain stream must reach $3.66B PV, 2.03 times today's.
- No fps row is ahead of Do Nothing in any column. The closest is the 10-yr at Renton + Re-engine in S1, at -0.56.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
FOR THE fps (2050 is the last round, so a hold means no new airplane in this game)
- I would back a launch on a grid where an fps row beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon in the expected column with stress net debt held. Today the best trails by $0.86B, and the gain stream would need to be 2.03 times today's ($3.66B PV against $1.80B).
- As advice, I would also want an S3 margin that absorbs doctrine's +3-year slip at full cost: about $1.2B or more, against $1.08B today.
- If Pope's seat or the Board shows that my reconstruction misreads the grid, I will re-run it. That covers the window effect, Airbus's post-2060 slack and the Renton ramp.
- If the CEO takes the objective premium on the 10-year at Renton, I don't veto: it passes the slip leg by $1.08B and is fundable. I would log the $0.86-0.92B premium and tell the Board plainly that it is a tie carried by the mission, not a case.
- My binding veto on the four via Embraer rows lifts only on the grid: their S3 would have to reach -2.83.

FOR THE 787 RE-ENGINE
- Odds alone cannot move it: even at zero odds it is +0.44, inside epsilon.
- I would bring it only on a grid where its clean-column value clears $1B and S2 stays inside -$1B.
- An A350 Re-engine on the record closes it under H3.

CONDITIONS ON MY NUMBERS
They hold barring:
- an A350 Re-engine on the public record;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- any change to the stress-case cash path in the brief.
My 30% odds are Low confidence. They move the Re-engine premium between $0 and $0.44B, never past the cap.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.83 in S3, so the limit is -2.83. Every Solo row passes; the 10-year at Renton by $1.08B. Every via Embraer row fails, by $1.18-1.47B, and under the team rule I veto those four. The 7-year passes by only $0.05-0.19B: one to six months of slip. That isn't a baseline. Its stress peaks fall after 2050, and I rule them not held: it isn't fundable.

On the beat, I'm resetting my estimate. I charged the lost lead as a market loss, but against Do Nothing it isn't one. Do Nothing loses a point a year too, so the fps climbs the same 11 points whenever it lands. The window also slid onto the 2060s replacement wave. Net of the clock that is +$0.22B. It's real on this board, but the gain stream would have to double to clear +$1B; nothing on this order sheet does that.

A tie isn't a case. Within ε, Do Nothing has the higher worst column (-0.93 against -1.78) and adds no penalty, against $19.1B. A three-year slip, costed once and in full, takes $0.74-1.22B, most or all of the buffer.

The Re-engine is worth +0.13 at my 30% odds. Hold it; I log $0.13B.

So we hold everything, and say plainly that no later round remains: no new airplane in this game. The balance sheet stays fully restored, barring an A350 Re-engine on the record or a change to the stress path.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase (my veto) [doctrine]
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, each after 2-3 months of stable KPIs and an FAA review. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 1. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. rate_737: hold is the only value offered, so no Rate Increase is on the order sheet. My veto has nothing to act on, and H6 cannot engage. Confirmed.

Is 57 a month stable on the gates? 57 a month is our FAA-agreed capacity: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The line ran at that rate for 13 years, delivering 684 a year from 2035 to 2047, with no problem on the record. Since 2048 it has built to demand, not to 57: 543 (2048), 483 (2049) and 513 (2050), about 45, 40 and 43 a month. The brief gives no KPI series, so this result rests on its no-live-problem record.

Advice on the public line, not binding: say 'capacity of 57 a month on the FAA-agreed gates; we build to demand, about 43 a month in 2050'. The bulletin shows 483 deliveries in 2049. 'Holding at 57 a month' reads as 684 a year, and the public table says otherwise.

tests.name: Stability at falling volume: the MAX lines under Do Nothing [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: The lines stay stable on the six FAA-agreed KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training, ticketing) as volume falls. Any adjustment runs on the same gates and in steps (doctrine's step is 5 a month, at least 6 months apart), never as a cliff. Customers get honest delivery dates.

tests.name: Supplier readiness at falling volume: LEAP-1B and fragile suppliers [doctrine]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, and engine and structures supply that covers the rate, whether it is rising or falling.
tests.numbers:
Answer to asks 1 and 2.

LEAP-1B: our call falls with deliveries, from 1,368 engines at 57 a month to 1,026 (2050), 776 (2053), 692 (2055) and 496 (2060).
- From the observed tables (narrowbody engines = 2 x deliveries x share), CFM delivered about 1,671 narrowbody engines in 2049 (46.7% of 3,578). Our call took 966 of them (58%), against 61% in 2044 and 2048.
- CFM's Airbus load is about 705 engines and falling as A320neo slots return to CFM.
- Verdict: still a watch item, and an easing one. The risk has turned from rationing to low volume at the supplier.
- CFM puts the LEAP fleet first, with kits and shop material ahead of the OE delivery rate (bulletin).
- Keep the allocation reviews running [BX-1264, BX-1325], and attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure [B-1923].

Fragile suppliers at falling volume: the brief names none. Doctrine's answer:
- keep the fragile or financially weak ones funded and producing at or above our rate, and let the strong ones burn down inventory [B-2330, BX-1243];
- keep production infrastructure and trained labour through low-rate production, to protect the health of the production system and the supply chain [B-1618];
- give every supplier the step-down skyline early, because 'suppliers' health and rate readiness will be critical' whenever rates change [B-1616].
This is the frame's cash for readiness.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: Do Nothing and the 787 Re-engine (EIS 2055) [record, applied by inference; the slip prior is doctrine]
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read the risk-case column (S3, Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 9.

Do Nothing has no EIS to deliver. With no fps, S3 equals S1 (-0.83), and the worst column is S2 (-0.93).

787 Re-engine: the item against hold is +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44. S3 equals S1, because Delay Tactics act only from fps EIS. S2 is Airbus's move, not a delivery risk.

The board prices no Re-engine slip. Doctrine's prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). Shifting the S1 item at 10.5% (inference) gives +0.40 at a 1-year slip, +0.36 at 2 years and +0.30 at 4. It stays positive in S1 and S3 across the range, so at most about a third of its value rides on the nominal date.

Readiness:
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade route has been ready since 2033, which gives 22 years by a 2055 EIS, and GE says it will keep improving it. Durability comes first [BX-1298, B-2304].
- Charleston builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone re-engined 787 gaining 1 pp a year from 2055 needs 108.5 a year (9.0 a month) in 2060, 117 (9.7) in 2065 and 134 (11.2) in 2075. That fits inside a footprint being doubled for rates in the teens [B-2336, BX-1317].
- Workforce: nothing is in development, so one derivative fits the one-at-a-time rule [B-0341].
Operations can deliver it. My hold rests on ε, not on an operations finding.

Answer to ask 3. Confirmed:
- A 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) with a 2050 10-year fps (window 2053-60) overlaps 2 years (2053-55), $1.2B undiscounted. That is H4-legal with no slack. A 1-year Re-engine slip makes it 3 years ($1.8B), and doctrine's 2-year central slip makes it 4 ($2.4B); either would breach H4.
- On the grid the pairing costs the Re-engine $0.14-0.15B in every column: it is worth +0.30 / -0.75 / +0.30 beside the 10-year, against +0.44 / -0.60 / +0.44 alone. The fps item beside it is -1.00 / -1.00 / -1.06, which breaks the Board's -$1B limit in S3.

A 2050 7-year fps (window 2050-57) against a 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) overlaps 5 years: $3.0B undiscounted, against a 2-year cap. H4 bars it, and the row is struck if ordered.
