Supplier plan: castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers. Gearbox and shop capacity are shared with P&W; the gear is P&W's work-share under its terms.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
On hold:
- 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045, and 55.2% in 2050 in S1-S3. The worst year is 5.2 points above the line.
- S4 reads 58.0% in 2050 on every plan.

Reading the S4 figure:
- 58.0% is the pre-2042 split (58/100), so in S4 the board appears not to count the GEnx upgrade's 5 points in 2050. That is my inference; I cannot see the board's mechanism.

With the upgrade: still 55.2% in 2050, because it counts from 2053. From 2053 it reads 60.0% (63/105).

Boeing's 787 work with GE:

Trent 1000 on the 787 (ask 7): on this board, durability inside the existing budget (the about £1bn programme) is enough.

No grid adjustment.

tests.name: In-service record against the written standard
tests.threshold: Report the Joint Venture fleet to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against the written standard: time on wing in the specification, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, and aircraft on ground. No figure invented (inference: my maturity rule applied in service).
tests.numbers:
The brief carries deliveries, not fleet data. I have no time-on-wing, shop-visit, life-limited-part or aircraft-on-ground figures. I invent none, and I claim neither compliance nor shortfall.

What we know:
- The fleet is about 7,870 Rolls-Royce engines at end-2049 and about 8,848 at end-2050.
- The first cohorts (7 in 2037, 115 by 2039, 382 by 2040) have been in service 10-13 years, so they are well into shop visits (inference).
- Under P&W's terms the gear and core are P&W's. P&W says its GTF fleet is 'still not where our customers need it to be', so durability is a shared exposure.

One standard, one fleet report, by operating environment (hot and sandy included), as P&W now publishes.

If the data are bad, in this order:
1. Operators and Airbus told first, jointly with P&W.
2. Then the public, with the fix and no recovery date we cannot hold.
3. Spares and lease engines to aircraft on ground first.
4. No engineering change rushed in to cover it.

tests.name: Engineering-change rule and Joint Venture governance
tests.threshold: Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never to hold a date or win a campaign (attr. rule). One engineering interface, one durability standard and one chief engineer per change. Crediting is a valuation only. Changes are rationed, fleet first (inference).
tests.numbers:
Confirmed. The draft statement, option E (i) and P&W's published terms all state the same rule: partner content enters only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and P&W signs durability only on an engine it has tested.

Governance:
- one engineering interface;
- one durability standard and one fleet report;
- one chief engineer per change;
- each change carries its own test plan, certification basis and fleet-introduction gate, reported to the Committee.

Crediting:
- A joint technical valuation of each change, recorded at its gate, feeds the share split as a valuation only: no licence and no cash.
- On this board P&W and RR hold equal narrowbody shares (26.7% each observed in 2049), so crediting is unpriced.
- Share or term questions go to the Board before they are public.

No date is given for any change.

- **A date in public.** I would invoke the veto for any of these:

  - an UltraFan WB date before 2056.
- **A capacity or MRO constraint in the brief.** It would make the capacity test live, and I would ask for the support build to 14,600 engines by 2056 to be re-sized before anything else.
- **A rival-engined 787 Re-engine on the record, or a brief projecting our widebody share near 50%.** Either would trigger the franchise test, with time on wing as the first lever. On this board, any widebody item still needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the permanent strain.
- **Named airline wins and in-service data.** These firm up my confidence in the support ramp. Wins on the Joint Venture engine and time-on-wing data inside the specification would both count.
ops.memo:
All four fields at hold. No Civil veto: nothing compresses maturity, and nothing public carries a date.

Readiness. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037, a year of margin. No other airframe awaits an engine.

The fleet. About 7,870 Rolls-Royce engines at end-2049, 8,848 at end-2050 and 14,600 by 2056. The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data. So I report against the written standard (time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts, aircraft on ground) and invent no figure. One standard and one fleet report with P&W, by operating environment. If the data are bad, operators and Airbus hear it from us and P&W first, then the public, with the fix and no recovery date.

Support. Partner shops on the Singapore model, added to P&W's network. Sized for about 8,850 engines by end-2050, then about 14,600 by 2056.

The rule. Our content goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence. One chief engineer per change, fleet first.

Capacity. 978 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody in 2050. No constraint in the brief. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 stay ring-fenced.

Widebody. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050. The upgrade would count from 2053 and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056. Each carries a permanent $5B strain: −6.73 and −9.00. Trent durability inside the existing budget does the fleet work.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence. It is never used to hold a date or win a campaign. P&W's published terms say the same. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we say so first, with P&W. No date of any kind is given for our content entering the engine [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476].

other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard 'win-win' terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no dates, no launch-style terms. Our answer to any doubt on readiness is in-service durability data. We are not after market share [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582].

other_moves.detail: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine and life-limited-part durability work continues inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). UltraFan demonstrator technology, and the technology from the folded UltraFan NB, keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing, inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope. Joint Venture support network scaled to the fleet

The network is sized for about 8,850 Rolls-Royce engines by end-2050 and is planned to reach about 14,600 by 2056 (about +65%, roughly 960 engines a year), with the fleet growing to about 18,400 by 2060. Support commitments go through the Investment Committee and are funded inside the Civil operating budget [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Supplier and capacity plan; widebody ring-fence

Castings and forgings go with high-performing suppliers. Gearbox and shop capacity are shared with P&W under its terms. In 2050 we deliver about 978 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody, and the brief reports no constraint [RX-0284, RX-0286].

other_moves.move: Capital frame and final Joint Venture lookback to the Audit Committee
Widebody doctrine beyond the game horizon; watch on Boeing's 787 work with GE
other_moves.detail: To the Board only. A widebody programme comes to the Board only with a 787 or A350 Re-engine on the public record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. On this board each item needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the strain. Neither is an option we keep warm [RX-0051, R-1573, R-1574]. We keep watching Boeing's 787 work with GE: today it is 'not a 787 Re-engine order', and the GEnx upgrade is already inside our 55.2%.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA, and we pace it on durability. Our job is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, scales with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core. Our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only once a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the last round. All four fields at hold. The work this round is delivery, not launches.

1. START FROM MY PROPOSAL. I framed all four fields at hold. Both memos recommend the same orders, and neither raises a binding veto against them.
- ultrafan_nb_solo: hold. The Solo was folded in 2035, and hold is the only legal value.
- jv_with_pw: hold. The Joint Venture is formed, ready since 2036 and in service. Hold keeps it as approved, and it is the only legal value.
- ultrafan_wb: hold.
- t1000_upgrade: hold.

2. GRID ROWS, with and without each item (brief §3, S1-S4). Weights are mine, since the brief gives none: 0.75 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05.
- Hold: +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.03 / +11.37. Expected +11.05 on my weights and on the Board's (0.80 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05), +11.10 on the Re-engine stress (0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20), +11.37 on S4 alone. Worst column +11.03. It is the best plan in every column.
- Hold + T1000 upgrade: +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.30 / +4.75. Against hold that is -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.62: -6.72 expected on my weights and the Board's, -6.71 on the stress, -6.62 on S4. Worst column -6.73, beyond its own -$2B bill. It buys about $0.27B of engine value ($0.38B in S4) for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- Hold + UltraFan WB: +2.03 / +2.03 / +2.35 / +3.05. Against hold that is -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32: -8.93 expected on my weights and the Board's, -8.77 on the stress, -8.32 on S4. Worst column -9.00, beyond its own -$4B bill. It is ready in 2056, a year after the earliest Re-engine EIS (2055), and buys $0 / $0 / $0.32B / $0.68B for $9B.
Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights. No later round exists to cancel either item: the full bill and the strain land. Calculations are in /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-cons/work/r4_decide_calc.txt.

3. BINDING VETOES. McCabe withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches: binding, and moot, because I propose neither. Watson's Civil veto is not invoked: nothing is compressed, and no public text carries a date. No plan is struck on a veto, because none was proposed. Overrides: empty.

4. MY TESTS.
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: no 787 or A350 Re-engine has been launched or announced. Boeing calls its GE work 'not a 787 Re-engine order', and Airbus keeps the A350 as its focus. UltraFan WB has no airframe to fly.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: both items fail 'viable business model' on the strain, and UltraFan WB also fails 'large market'.
- Profitable or not at all: both are negative in every column. 'We won't do anything not profitable' [RX-0058].
- Widebody franchise: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 (58.0% in S4). The 50% line is not threatened, so no premium is triggered.
- Premium cap: the shortfalls are $6.72B against the $3B cap and $8.93B against the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Both are declined.
- No options management [RX-0051]: no widebody item launched as a hedge.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]: McCabe's capex (about £0.49bn a year for either item) and the downside were on the table before I chose. The package spends £0.
- On 787 share I said 'Why not?' [RX-0117]. On this board the answer is $6.7B. 'We are not after market share' [R-1582].

5. EXPECTED SCENARIO: S1. Boeing launches nothing and gives no date, there is no Re-engine, and CFM/GE launches no new programme. The best grid plan in S1, and in every other column, is all hold. Premium 0.

6. RED-LINE CHECK BEFORE RETURNING. All hold breaks no company red line.
- McCabe flagged that UltraFan WB with no Re-engine on the record would breach 'no UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it'. I confirm the flag. It is struck by holding: no launch.
- Watson flagged 'No grid adjustment' in public move (iii) as board language. I take that: the phrase is removed from the public text. Last round's public move (ii) carried a grid figure (S2 against S1). This round's public text carries none.
- The public statement is Watson-checked word for word: no dates, nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates, no share claim, and the widebody line conditional.
- No flag is left unresolved.

7. BOARD. No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item. Every guidance point is answered in board_response, with a final status for each round-3 recommendation.

8. WHERE THIS IS DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. I have no evidenced decision on running a formed Joint Venture. The governance, fleet-report, support and lookback moves follow company doctrine (profile.md §4, §9 steps 6-12), Watson's attributed maturity rule and the Board's guidance. The capital frame and the lookback are McCabe's evidence. On the lookback I take her number plainly: 9-12% does not clear the mid-to-high teens. It adds value. It is not good enough by our own hurdle [RX-0033], and I say so to the Audit Committee.

'They are a milestone on our journey, not our final destination' [RX-0062].

Lookback: my figures are recorded as I gave them. $5.71B was spent against the $4B line, a miss. IRR is 9.1-12.0% against a 15-18% hurdle: the Joint Venture adds value but does not clear our hurdle. Treat that as a floor, because my record on engine-launch economics is thin.

Red lines: all hold breaks none. There is no UltraFan launch without an airframe, no overlap and no upgrade beside an UltraFan in development.

One drafting point, advice only. The public line ties a Trent upgrade to 'a Re-engine on the record', which is stricter than our test for the upgrade (it must beat hold, or fall short by no more than a declared premium within $3B). It costs nothing to leave it in.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

veto.ground:
Not invoked. None of the three Civil grounds is met by the final orders, the public statement, the public other moves or the rationale.
(a) Maturity: nothing is compressed. The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036, the bulletin's date carried over from the folded GTF2 schedule (2030 + 6). It has been in service on NGSA since 2037 (2030 + 7), with one year of margin. The rationale does not count on any engine before its ready year. The upgrade (launch + 3, counting from 2053) and UltraFan WB (launch + 6 = 2056, and only once a Re-engine is in service) are both held, so neither has a date that could be broken.
(b) Early date: I read the final public statement sentence by sentence, and it contains no year and no number. The three public other moves contain no ready date, no EIS and no date for Rolls-Royce content entering the engine. Move (ii) now says 'no dates' and no longer carries a grid figure. Move (iii) no longer says 'No grid adjustment'. Nothing is said about Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates.
(c) Support: both narrowbody fields can only be held, so this round has no launch, trigger or commit and creates no new narrowbody EIS. For NGSA, the partner-shop support plan was in place before the 2037 EIS. A private move sizes it for about 8,850 Rolls-Royce engines by end-2050 (8,848 on my sums of the brief) and plans it to about 14,600 by 2056. It adds to P&W's network rather than replacing it.
Had I invoked the veto, the team rule would have made it binding. The ground would have rested on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

ops.note:
I concur. I am not invoking the Civil veto, and the orders break no red line.

For the Board:
- Test fails: none.
- Binding vetoes: none.
- Notes: 4, all advice (below).
- Board items: none. No order differs from the default.

Orders: all four fields are at hold (ultrafan_nb_solo, jv_with_pw, ultrafan_wb, t1000_upgrade). This matches my test memo.

Readiness against the one live airframe:
- Joint Venture engine: ready 2036 (the bulletin's date).
- NGSA EIS: 2037 (2030 + 7). That is one year of margin, and the engine is in service.
- No other airframe is waiting for an engine. Boeing launched nothing and gave no date.
- The earliest EIS for a new single-aisle is 2057 (a 7-year fps launched in 2050) or 2060 (a 10-year fps).

Dates in public:
- The final statement and the three public other moves contain no year.
- Nothing is disclosed earlier than launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), launch + 3 (upgrade) or the bulletin's Joint Venture date.
- No date is given for Rolls-Royce content entering the engine. The engineering-change rule is stated in public and matches P&W's published terms.
- Both drafting points I raised are taken: no grid figure and no 'grid adjustment' wording appear in public text.

Support before EIS: pass. No new narrowbody EIS is created this round. The NGSA plan was in place before 2037, is sized for about 8,850 engines by end-2050 and is planned to about 14,600 by 2056.

Red lines on the final orders:
- Strain is $0. No narrowbody programme is held beside a widebody programme.
- No upgrade while an UltraFan is in development.
- No UltraFan WB without a Re-engine to fly it.
- No maturity is compressed and no early date is disclosed.

Notes, advice only:
1. Widebody share is 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in S4). The worst year is 5.2 points above the 50% line.
2. Narrowbody development money is $5.71B against the $4B objective line. It was missed in 2035, not by this round's orders. It is McCabe's ground and not one of my red lines, and it is reported to the Audit Committee.
3. The brief carries no fleet data. The fleet report goes to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against the written standard, with no figure invented and neither compliance nor shortfall claimed. That obligation continues after the game ends.
4. The support figures (8,850 and 14,600) are plans, not completed capacity. The brief has no MRO data to check them against, and I use my CMD figure of 1,100-1,200 shop visits a year only as a widebody-era reference [RX-0279].

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

boeing.max_rate_source: Research base path: 47 a month cleared 27 May 2026 but not stable (actual 2026 output about 42-43 a month); 52 about mid-2027 with the Everett North Line (opened July 2026); 57, Boeing's stated goal, about mid-2029; flat after. Bounds: MS 52 flat (low), 63 by 2030 (high, the four-line ceiling).
boeing.site_source: Renton: three final assembly lines, held at 47 a month (Boeing, July 2026); Everett North Line: about $1B, capacity about 15-16 a month (Leeham), takes the builds for 52 and beyond.
boeing.rate_increase_note: the board's 737 rate increase: +5 pp of its 2,000-aircraft market from 2032 = +100 aircraft a year (about 8 a month, to about 65: the four-line ceiling of 62-63 plus a second North Line)
boeing.renton_saving_source: Research estimate (2025$): new-site capex for about 50 a month at about $80M per unit of monthly rate = $4.0B, less about $1.0B to convert Renton = $3.0B central ($1.5B-$5.5B). Booked at fps entry into service, as the board books bills.
boeing.fps_ramp_note: fps capacity ramps on the NGSA chart's shape (rate 50 about 4 years after EIS, 100 about 8 years after), shifted to the fps EIS
boeing.total_cap_note: Boeing's single-aisle total capped at 100 a month, the peak of Airbus's Rev. B plan (Boeing's record is 806 deliveries in 2018, 580 of them 737s); as the fps fills it the MAX gives way, down to an Everett tail of 10 a month, until 2050.

demand.growth_source: Airbus GMF 2025: fleet 24,730 (2024) to 49,210 (2044), 34,250 single-aisle deliveries to 2044; Boeing CMO 2025: single-aisle 66% of the fleet in 2024, 72% in 2044; Boeing CMO 2026: fleet growth about 3% a year. Growth is not in the user's data.
demand.firm_backlog_note: the page's firm orders (Cirium, 5 Oct 2026): 737 MAX and A320neo family; delivered first, never lapse or switch maker
demand.lapse_note: share of the still-unserved new customers (not firm orders) who drop out each year: they keep old aircraft longer, defer growth or cancel. Not calibrated; firm-order cancellations run about 2-5% a year and unplaced demand lapses faster.
demand.note: total demand = replacement + growth. New demand(y) = (growth(y) + replacements(y)) x class_share, split by preference; the firm backlog is delivered first. Replacements after 2075 are held at the 2075 value. flex_share: customers flying both types, lessors and unannounced customers, as a share of replacements over the flex window; when their first choice cannot deliver they take the other maker's free slots (each year, from the waiting backlog too).

options._note: User's assumptions of 14 Oct 2026: demand = the conservative-case curve with the firm orders as its first slice (option B); Boeing loses 1 point of share a year after NGSA EIS (while it has no new narrowbody in service) down to the point where Airbus sells all it can and Boeing captures only the slack; Airbus raises capacity 1% a year until it meets its demand.
